Editor's Introduction

George Boole published this book in 1854, when he was thirty-nine and Professor of Mathematics at Queen's College, Cork. He had not been to university. He was the son of a shoemaker in Lincoln, taught himself Latin, Greek and then mathematics, and was supporting his family as a schoolmaster from the age of sixteen. By his late twenties he was publishing original mathematics in the journals and had won a medal from the Royal Society, and in 1849 the new college in Cork made him its first professor of mathematics without his ever having taken a degree.

His idea was that reasoning has laws as definite as the laws of algebra, and that they can be written down as an algebra. Let a letter stand for a class of things: x for sheep, y for white things. Then xy is the class of things that are both, the white sheep; 1 stands for everything under discussion and 0 for nothing; 1 − x is everything that is not a sheep. "All x are y" becomes an equation, and reasoning becomes the solving of equations. Almost every rule of ordinary algebra carries over. The one that does not is the law Boole put at the centre of the book, x2 = x: a class combined with itself is the same class. Of all numbers, only 0 and 1 obey it, and so the algebra of logic turns out to be the algebra of 0 and 1. He had sketched the system in a pamphlet of 1847, The Mathematical Analysis of Logic; this is the full statement.

It was admired and little used in his lifetime. Logicians found the algebra forbidding, and mathematicians found parts of it strange, above all his habit of working through steps that have no logical meaning, such as dividing by zero, and trusting the answer at the end. Jevons, Venn and Peirce rebuilt it in the following decades into a simpler form, and in that form it became the foundation of modern logic. In 1937 Claude Shannon showed that it also describes electrical switching circuits, which is why every digital computer now calculates in Boole's algebra.

This edition retells the first fifteen chapters, the logic. Boole's title promises a second subject as well, probability, and Chapters XVI to XXII apply the method to it; they are not included here, and the places where the first half points ahead to them say so. His prose has been put into plain modern English. His symbols, equations and equation numbers are exactly his, except for a handful of printer's errors in the 1854 edition and the transcription it was set from, corrected against the original and listed in the source files. His numbered articles are kept, so that his own cross-references, such as "(II. 9)", meaning Chapter II, article 9, still work. Where an equation would stop a reader, a few words in the sentence say what it means. And seven short notes marked "Editor's note" say where modern Boolean algebra does things differently, or where an idea of his went next; those are ours, not his.

On the cover. Drawn for this edition, in the manner of the Dover science paperbacks of the 1950s and 60s. It is Boole's "development" from Chapter V: the universe, 1, cut by a class x into x and not-x, each part cut again by y and again by z, until eight constituents stand in the bottom row. A premise says which of them are empty, and those are struck out; reading off what survives is how every problem in the book is solved, and it is the ancestor of the truth table.

Preface

This book is not a reissue of an earlier treatise of mine, “The Mathematical Analysis of Logic.” Its first part does pursue the same object, and it begins by laying down the same system of fundamental laws. But its methods are more general, and it applies them far more widely. It gives the results of some years of study and reflection on a way of investigating the operations of the intellect. My earlier account of that idea was written within a few weeks of first conceiving it.

The part of this book that deals with logic assumes that the reader knows the most important terms of the subject as it is usually taught, and what the subject is for. On these points there is no better guide than Archbishop Whately’s “Elements of Logic” or Mr. Thomson’s “Outlines of the Laws of Thought.” The present revival of interest in studies of this kind seems largely due to the first of these. The reader also needs some algebra, but no more than how to solve simple equations. The chapters on the theory of probability (not included in this edition) call for rather more algebra, especially the method of elimination and the solution of equations with more than one unknown. For background on that subject, see the treatises on probability in “Lardner’s Cabinet Cyclopædia,” by Professor De Morgan, and in the “Library of Useful Knowledge,” by Sir John Lubbock, and an interesting series of letters translated from the French of M. Quetelet. Other references are given in the book itself. On a first reading the reader may skip, as he sees fit, Chapters X., XIV., and XIX. (the last of these is in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition), along with any of the applications he finds uninviting or beside his purpose.

In various places, and especially in the notes to the last chapter (which, like the chapters on probability, is not included in this edition), the reader will find references to writers ancient and modern. They are meant mainly to illustrate a certain view of the history of philosophy. On these I should add one thing. I have never given a citation that I did not believe, after careful examination, to be supported either by other authorities or by the general drift of the work it came from. I would gladly have avoided anything that might be taken for a parade of learning. But I felt I owed it both to my subject and to the truth to give the reader the means of checking the statements in the text.

I now bring to a close a labour whose extent few people will be able to judge from its visible fruits. If I may speak for a single moment of the feelings with which I have pursued this task, and with which I now lay it aside, I would say this. I never doubted that it was worthy of my best efforts. I felt that whatever truth it might bring to light was not a private or arbitrary thing, and did not depend, in its essence, on anyone’s opinion. I knew well that learned and able men held views on logic directly opposed to those on which the whole argument and method of this book rest. I believed their views to be mistaken, but I knew that my own might be bent, without my noticing, by an influence of another kind. I felt especially the danger of the bias that comes from long attention to one particular aspect of the truth. But I trust that out of this conflict of opinions the truth will only emerge the freer from anything merely personal. I trust that its different parts will be seen in their proper proportion, and that none of them will in the end be valued too highly or too lightly because of prejudices attached to the mere form in which it was presented.

To my valued friend the Rev. George Stephens Dickson, of Lincoln, I wish to record my thanks for much kind help in revising this work, and for some important suggestions.

5, Grenville-place, Cork,

Nov. 30th. 1853.

Chapter 1: Nature and Design of This Work

1. This book has four aims. The first is to investigate the fundamental laws of those operations of the mind by which we reason. The second is to express those laws in the symbolic language of a calculus (a system of symbols with fixed rules for working with them, as algebra is), and on that foundation to build the science of logic and its method. The third is to make that method the basis of a general method for applying the mathematical theory of probability (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition). The last is to gather, from the pieces of truth these inquiries bring to light, some likely hints about the nature and make-up of the human mind.

2. That this plan is not entirely new hardly needs saying. Its two main practical branches, logic and probability, have drawn a great deal of attention from philosophers. In its ancient and medieval form, logic is tied almost entirely to one great name, Aristotle. It reached the ancient Greeks in the treatises of his Organon, which are partly technical and partly metaphysical, and it has come down to our own day with hardly any essential change. Original inquiry has flowed instead toward questions of general philosophy. These questions began in the quarrels of the logicians, but they outgrew their origin and gave each later age of speculation its own particular bent. Think of the eras of Porphyry and Proclus, of Anselm and Abelard, of Ramus, and of Descartes, and of the final protests of Bacon and Locke. Each shows the study of logic reaching out to shape the course of human thought, sometimes by raising topics rich in debate, sometimes by provoking protest against logic's own inflated claims.

The history of the theory of probability looks quite different. It has grown steadily, the way a science grows. At its birth it had the young genius of Pascal; in its maturity, the most difficult of all the mathematical researches of Laplace; and other names hardly less distinguished could be added. Logic has been remarkable for the related questions of metaphysics it gave rise to; probability has been remarkable for the push it gave to the higher branches of mathematics. Both subjects, moreover, have rightly been seen as serving a theoretical end as well as a practical one. Logic is not only for drawing correct conclusions from given premises. And probability does more than teach us how to put life insurance on a secure footing, or how to boil down whatever is valuable in countless observations in astronomy, in physics, or in that field of social inquiry which is fast becoming very important. Both studies matter in another way too: they shed light on the powers of the mind. They show how language and number serve as tools for reasoning. They reveal something of how the different powers of the intellect we all share are connected. They set out the essential standards of truth and correctness in the two realms of knowledge, the demonstrative (what can be proved) and the probable. And those standards are not imposed from outside; they are rooted deep in the way the human faculties are made. These theoretical goals are no less interesting, no less dignified, and, I would add, no less important than the practical aims that history has tied them to. Our higher powers of thought give us all our knowledge of the world and of ourselves that goes beyond what the senses simply perceive. To uncover their hidden laws and relations is a goal that no rational mind needs to be persuaded of.

3. Some parts of this plan have occurred to others before me. But its overall conception, its method, and to a large extent its results are, I believe, original. So in this chapter I will offer some preliminary statements and explanations, to make the real aim of the book clear and its subject easier to follow.

The first aim, then, is to investigate the fundamental laws of those operations of the mind by which reasoning is carried out. There is no need to argue here that the operations of the mind really do, in some real sense, obey laws, and therefore that a science of the mind is possible. If anyone doubts this, the way to meet the doubt is not to try to settle it à priori, by argument in advance of the evidence. The way is to point the doubter to the evidence of actual laws, which means pointing him to an actual science. So the answer to that doubt belongs not in the introduction to this book but in the book itself. Let us grant, then, that a science of the powers of the intellect is possible, and consider for a moment how we are to obtain it.

4. Like every other science, the science of the mind's operations must rest first of all on observation. Here, what we observe are the very operations and processes whose laws we want to find. Every science needs this foundation in experience. But there are some special differences in how experience yields general truths when the subject is the mind and when the subject is external nature. We need to look at these differences.

The general laws of nature are not, for the most part, things we directly perceive. Either they are inductive inferences from a large body of facts, stating the truth those facts have in common; or, at least to begin with, they are physical hypotheses about causes, which explain the phenomena with unfailing precision and let us predict new combinations of them. In every case, and in the strictest sense of the word, they are probable conclusions. They come ever closer to certainty as experience confirms them more and more. But they never entirely lose the character of probability, in the strict and proper sense of that term. Knowledge of the laws of the mind is different. It does not need a large collection of observations as its basis. We see the general truth in the particular instance, and repeating the instance does not confirm it any further. An obvious example will show this. There is a rule of reasoning called the dictum of Aristotle, de omni et nullo ("about all and about none": roughly, whatever is affirmed or denied of a whole class is affirmed or denied of everything in it). We may ask whether this rule expresses a primary law of human reasoning. But there is no question that it expresses a general truth of logic. And reflecting on a single instance of it is enough to show that truth in all its generality. This is evidence that the rule rests on some general law or laws of the mind. It also illustrates the point that we do not reach such general truths by induction from many instances: they are contained in seeing one instance clearly. Alongside this comes another truth that is just as important. Our knowledge of the laws on which the science of the intellect rests, however much or little of it we have, is not probable knowledge. For in the particular example we see not only the general truth but also that it is a certain truth, a truth in which our confidence will not keep growing as we see it confirmed again and again in practice.

5. But if the general truths of logic win our agreement the moment the mind sees them, what makes it hard to build a science of logic? Not, we may answer, gathering the material, but sorting it out: telling what kind of truth each one is, and settling its place and its relation to the rest. Every science consists of general truths, but only some of those truths are primary and fundamental; the rest are secondary and derived. Kepler's laws of elliptical motion are general truths of astronomy, but they are not its fundamental truths. The same holds in the purely mathematical sciences. An almost endless variety of known theorems, and an infinite number of others still unknown, all rest together on the foundation of a few simple axioms; and yet all of them are general truths. I would add that to a mind refined enough, these truths would shine out by their own light. It would not need the connecting links of thought, the steps of tiring and often painful deduction, by which we actually come to know them. Let us call fundamental those laws and principles from which all the other general truths of a science can be deduced, and into which they can all be broken down again. Are we wrong, then, to count this as the true science of logic: one that lays down certain elementary laws, confirmed by the mind's own testimony; that lets us deduce from them, by uniform processes, the whole chain of their secondary consequences; and that supplies, for practical use, methods of perfect generality? Consider whether any science, taken either as a system of truth or as the basis of a practical art, can properly have any other test of whether its laws are complete and fundamental. The test is how complete its system of derived truths is, and how general the methods it supports. Other questions may certainly come up. Convenience, custom and personal preference may press their claims, and they deserve attention. But on the question of what makes a science in its pure, abstract integrity, I believe nothing besides the test above really counts.

6. The second aim of this book is to express the fundamental laws of reasoning in the symbolic language of a calculus. Here it is enough to say that the laws themselves suggest this way of expressing them, and make it uniquely fit for our purposes. There is a close analogy between the operations of the mind in reasoning generally and its operations in the particular science of algebra. More than that: to a large extent the two kinds of operation follow exactly the same laws. Of course, the laws must be worked out separately in each case. Any agreement in form between them can only be established à posteriori, after the fact, by actually comparing them. To borrow the notation of the science of number and simply assume that the rules for using it will stay the same in a new use would be mere hypothesis. There are, it is true, certain general principles, grounded in the very nature of language, that govern how symbols are used; and symbols are just the elements of a scientific language. Up to a point these elements are arbitrary. What they mean is purely a matter of convention: we may use them in any sense we like. But that freedom has two essential limits. First, once we have fixed a symbol's meaning, we must never depart from it within the same piece of reasoning. Second, the laws by which we reason with the symbols must be based only on that fixed meaning. Under these principles, if the laws of the symbols of logic turn out to agree with those of algebra, the result can only be an agreement of processes. The two fields of meaning stay separate and independent, each with its own laws and conditions.

Now, the investigations in the following pages present logic, on its practical side, as a system of processes carried out with symbols that have a definite meaning and that obey laws based on that meaning alone. But at the same time they show those laws to be identical in form with the laws of the general symbols of algebra, with one single addition: the symbols of logic obey a further special law (Chap. II.), which the symbols of quantity, as such, do not obey. I will not dwell here on what this law is or on the evidence for it; those questions are fully discussed later. But this law is the essential ground of difference between the kinds of inference logic deals with and those that arise in the particular science of number, and so it deserves more than a passing mention. It may be said to lie at the very foundation of general reasoning. It governs those acts of conception or imagination that come before the processes of logical deduction, and it gives those processes much of their actual form and expression. So we may say that this law is the seed, the first principle, and that every approach to a general method in logic is a more or less complete growth from it.

7. We have already laid down the principle (5) that, in the science of logic, whether an assumed system of laws is sufficient and truly fundamental must be seen partly in how perfect the methods are that it leads to. It remains, then, to ask what a general method in logic requires, and how far the system of this book meets those requirements.

Logic deals with two kinds of relation: relations among things, and relations among facts. But facts are expressed by propositions, so the second kind can, at least for the purposes of logic, be turned into relations among propositions. Suppose we say that the fact or event A always follows the fact or event B. To this extent, at least, that is the same as saying that the truth of the proposition asserting that the event B happens always implies the truth of the proposition asserting that the event A happens. So instead of saying that logic deals with relations among things and relations among facts, we may say that it deals with relations among things and relations among propositions. An example of the first kind is the proposition “All men are mortal”; of the second, the proposition “If the sun is totally eclipsed, the stars will become visible.” The first expresses a relation between “men” and “mortal beings”; the second, a relation between the simple propositions “The sun is totally eclipsed” and “The stars will become visible.” I count among such relations those that affirm or deny that things exist, and those that affirm or deny that propositions are true. Now let us call the things or propositions among which a relation is expressed the elements of the propositions that express it. With this definition we can say that the premises of any logical argument express given relations among certain elements, and that the conclusion must express an implied relation among those elements, or among some of them: that is, a relation that the premises imply, or contain by way of inference.

8. With this settled, a general method in logic seems to need the following.

First, since the conclusion must express a relation among all or some of the elements in the premises, we need a way of eliminating the elements we do not want to appear in the conclusion, and of finding the full relation the premises imply among the elements we want to keep. In the language of ordinary logic, the elements that do not appear in the conclusion are called middle terms. The kind of elimination shown in logic textbooks takes two propositions that share an element, the middle term, and deduces a conclusion connecting the two terms that remain. But the problem of elimination as this book sees it is much wider. It aims not just to eliminate one middle term from two propositions, but to eliminate middle terms from propositions in general, however many terms and propositions there are and however they are connected. Neither logic nor algebra, as they now stand, offers any exact parallel to this. In algebra, as is well known, elimination (combining equations so that a symbol drops out) is limited in this way: from two equations we can eliminate one symbol of quantity; from three equations, two symbols; and in general, from n equations, n−1 symbols. This condition, necessary in algebra, seems to hold in the existing logic too, but it has no essential place in logic as a science. There, no relationship at all can be proved between the number of terms to be eliminated and the number of propositions they are to be eliminated from. From the equation representing a single proposition we can eliminate any number of the symbols that stand for terms or elements in logic; and from any number of equations representing propositions, we can eliminate one such symbol, or any other number of them, in the same way. One general process does this in every case. This is one of the many remarkable consequences of that distinctive law of the symbols of logic which I have already pointed out.

Second, a general method in logic should be able to express the final relation among the elements of the conclusion as any admissible kind of proposition, or with the terms in any chosen order. Among the kinds we may count those that logicians call categorical, hypothetical, disjunctive, and so on (plain statements, “if” statements, “either-or” statements). Under the choice of order we may put everything that depends on which elements appear in the subject or in the predicate, or in the antecedent or in the consequent (the “if” part or the “then” part), of the proposition that forms the “conclusion.” But setting aside the technical language of the old schools, let us ask what genuinely different kinds of problem may come up. We have seen that the elements of the final, inferred relation may be either things or propositions. Take the first case. We might be asked to deduce from the premises a definition or description of some one thing, or class of things, among the elements of the conclusion, in terms of the other things it involves. Or we might form the idea of some thing or class of things that involves more than one of the elements of the conclusion, and ask for its expression in terms of the other elements. Now take the second case, where the elements kept in the conclusion are propositions. Then we might want to settle questions like these. Given the premises, is any of these propositions, taken by itself, true or false? Are particular combinations of them true or false? If we assume a particular proposition to be true, does anything follow about the other propositions, and if so, what? If we assume some particular condition about certain of the propositions, does anything follow about the others, and what? And so on. These, I say, are general questions, and a general method in logic ought to be able to answer them. Perhaps we can gather them all into one statement of the final problem of practical logic. Given a set of premises expressing relations among certain elements, whether things or propositions: required, explicitly, the whole relation that follows among any of those elements, under any proposed conditions, and in any proposed form. That this problem can be solved in all its aspects will appear later. But I have not gone into the nature and functions of a general method in logic just to point that out. The reader needs to understand the specific goals of the investigation we are now beginning, and the principles that are to guide us toward them.

9. It might be said at this point that Aristotle's logic, in its rules of syllogism and conversion, already sets out the elementary processes of which all reasoning consists, and that beyond these there is neither room nor need for a general method. (A syllogism draws a conclusion from two premises that share a middle term; conversion swaps the subject and predicate of a proposition.) I have no wish to point out the defects of the common logic, and I will refer to it only as far as I must to show the real nature of this book in its true light. With that purpose alone, I would make two remarks. First, syllogism, conversion and the rest are not the ultimate processes of logic. This book will show that they rest on, and can be broken down into, deeper and simpler processes, and that these are the real elements of method in logic. Nor is it in fact true that all inference can be reduced to the particular forms of syllogism and conversion (see Chap. xv.). Second, even if all inference could be reduced to these two processes (and some have held that it can be reduced to syllogism alone), a general method would be just as necessary. We would still have to decide in what order the processes should follow one another, as well as what each one is, in order to reach the relation we want. By the relation we want, I mean the full relation that, given the premises, connects any elements we choose from them, and that expresses this relation in any form and order we choose. If we may judge by the mathematical sciences, which are the most perfect examples of method we know, this directive function, deciding what to do and in what order, is method's chief task and its mark of distinction. The fundamental processes of arithmetic, for example, are in themselves only the elements of a possible science. Saying what they are is the first business of its method; arranging their order is its later and higher task. In the more complex examples of logical deduction, and especially in those that underlie the solution of hard questions in the theory of probability (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition), we cannot do without the help of a directive method, and only a calculus can supply one.

10. Why the ultimate laws of logic are mathematical in form; why they are identical, except at a single point, with the general laws of number; and why they differ at that one point: on these questions it would come close to presumption to try to give a firm answer. They probably lie beyond the reach of our limited faculties. The mind may perhaps be allowed to know the laws it is itself subject to without being given any understanding of their ground and origin, or even, except to a very limited degree, of how well they suit their purpose compared with other systems of law we can imagine. Science does not need that knowledge anyway. Science properly concerns itself with what is; it does not look for reasons why one thing was preferred or appointed over another. These considerations are a sufficient answer to every protest against presenting logic in the form of a calculus. We do not adopt this form because we choose to give logic this way of showing itself. We adopt it because the ultimate laws of thought make it possible, dictate its character, and seem to rule out presenting the science perfectly in any other form. We should remember that the business of science is not to create laws but to discover them. We do not make the constitution of our own minds, however much it may be in our power to shape their character. And just as the laws of the human intellect do not depend on our will, so the forms of the science built on them are, in everything essential, independent of personal choice.

11. Besides setting out the principles of this method in general, the book will apply it to the analysis of a wide variety of propositions, and of chains of propositions that form the premises of demonstrative arguments. These examples are taken from various writers; they differ greatly in complexity, and they cover a wide range of subjects. Some may feel that I have allowed myself too much freedom in choosing them, but I do not think I need to apologize for that. Everyone admits that logic, as a science, can be applied very widely; and it is just as certain that its ultimate forms and processes are mathematical. So any objection à priori to using such forms and processes on a problem of morals or of general philosophy must rest on a misunderstanding or a false analogy. It is not of the essence of mathematics to deal with the ideas of number and quantity. Whether it would be good, as a general habit of mind, to apply symbolic processes to moral argument is another question. Perhaps, as I have said elsewhere, the perfection of the method of logic may be valuable chiefly as evidence that its principles are true in theory. The last thing that anyone who knows the value of mental toil and struggle would want is to replace ordinary reasoning, or to bind it to the rigor of technical forms. That toil and struggle give the mind an athlete's strength; they teach it to wrestle with difficulties and to rely on itself in an emergency. Still, there may be cases, even among matters that everyone agrees belong to ordinary reasoning, where the value of a scientific procedure comes to be felt and recognized. Some examples of this kind will be found in this book.

Footnote: Mathematical Analysis of Logic. London: G. Bell. 1847.

12. The general doctrine and method of logic explained above also form the basis of a theory of probability, and of a method to go with it. So building that theory and method on these principles will be a separate aim of this book (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition). It may help to say something here about the nature of this application, and especially about the kind of solutions it leads to. For that purpose I will need to say a little more about the forms in which the results of the logical analysis are presented.

Why must a method in logic come first, as the basis of a theory of probability? The reason can be put in a few words. Suppose we want to know how the expected frequency of some event depends on the known frequencies of other events. Before we can find that out, we must know how the events themselves depend on one another. To put it technically, we must be able to express the event whose probability we are looking for as a function of the events whose probabilities are given. And working out that expression always belongs to logic. Probability, however, in its mathematical sense, can be measured in numbers. So the subject of probability belongs equally to the science of number and to logic. This book differs from all earlier ones in recognizing that both these elements stand side by side. That difference decides, in a great many cases, whether a problem can be solved at all, and it also brings new and important elements into the solutions. So I think it necessary to set out here, at some length, the particular consequences of the theory developed in the following pages.

13. The measure of the probability of an event is usually defined as a fraction. Its numerator is the number of cases favourable to the event, and its denominator is the whole number of cases, favourable and unfavourable, all of them supposed equally likely to happen. This book adopts that definition. At the same time, it shows that there is another way of looking at the subject (I will come to it shortly) that could just as well be taken as fundamental, and that would lead to exactly the same methods and conclusions. I may add this. As far as the accepted conclusions of the theory of probability go, and as far as they follow from its basic definitions, they do not differ from the results of the method of this book (which I take to be equally sound as inference).

Questions in the theory of probability come in many shapes, and algebraic and other conditions can change them in many ways. Even so, there seems to be one general type to which every such question can be brought, or at least as much of each question as truly belongs to the theory of probability. In terms of the data (what is given) and the quæsitum (what is sought), that type can be described as follows. First, the data are the probabilities of one or more given events. Each is either the probability that its event simply happens, or the probability that it happens under certain stated conditions. Second, the quæsitum, the thing sought, is the probability that some other event happens, either simply or under conditions. This event is expressed differently from those in the data, but it involves, more or less, the same elements. As for the data, they are either causally given, as when we work out the probability of a particular throw of a die from what we know of how the die is made, or they come from watching repeated cases of events succeeding or failing. In the second case, the probability of an event can be defined as the limit that the ratio of favourable cases to all observed cases approaches as the observations go on without end (assuming that nature is uniform). Last, one important distinction remains about the nature of the events, or how they relate. Events are either simple or compound. A compound event is one whose expression in language, or whose conception in thought, depends on the expression or conception of other events, which may be called simple in relation to it. To say “it rains” or “it thunders” is to state that a simple event happens. But to say “it rains and thunders,” or “it either rains or thunders,” is to state that a compound event happens, because the expression of that event depends on the elementary expressions “it rains” and “it thunders.” So the test of a simple event is not that its nature is somehow simple. It rests entirely on the way the event is expressed in language or conceived in thought.

14. Now one general problem that the existing theory of probability can solve is this: given the probabilities of any simple events, find the probability of a given compound event, that is, of an event put together in a given way out of those simple events. The problem can also be solved when the compound event whose probability is sought is subject to given conditions, that is, to conditions that also depend in a given way on the given simple events. Besides this general problem, there are some particular problems whose principle of solution is known. Various questions about causes and effects can be solved by known methods on the particular assumption that the causes exclude one another, but apparently not otherwise. Beyond this, it is not clear that anyone has made progress toward what may be called the general problem of the science, namely: given the probabilities of any events, simple or compound, conditional or unconditional, find the probability of any other event, just as freely chosen in its expression and conception. In stating this problem I do not even require that the events whose probabilities are given and the event whose probability is sought should share some elements. It is the job of a method to decide whether the data of a problem are enough for the purpose, and, when they are not, to show where they fall short.

The method of this book can solve this problem in its most unrestricted form. To be more precise, its theoretical solution is given completely, and its practical solution comes down to purely mathematical processes, such as solving and analysing equations. The order and character of the general solution can be described as follows.

15. First, it is always possible, by the preliminary method of the calculus of logic, to express the event whose probability is sought as a logical function of the events whose probabilities are given. The result looks like this. Suppose that X stands for the event whose probability is sought, and A, B, C, &c. for the events whose probabilities are given, simple or compound. Then the whole relation of the event X to the events A, B, C, &c. comes out in the form of what mathematicians call a development. In the most general case it has four distinct classes of terms. The first class expresses those combinations of the events A, B, C that both necessarily go with the event X and necessarily signal that it has happened. The second class expresses the combinations that necessarily go with the event X but do not necessarily imply it. The third class expresses the combinations that cannot happen together with the event X, though they are not otherwise impossible. The fourth class expresses the combinations that cannot happen under any circumstances. I will not dwell on this account of what the logical analysis of the problem yields, except to remark that its elements are exactly the ones by which our expectation of the event X, as it depends on what we know of the events A, B, C, is affected, and the only ones by which it can be. General reasoning would confirm this conclusion. But general reasoning would not usually manage to untangle the complicated web of events and circumstances out of which the solution just described has to be drawn. Reaching that result is the first step toward the complete solution of the question I set. Note that up to this point the process is logical, that is, it is carried out with symbols that have a logical meaning, and it ends in an equation that can be interpreted as a proposition. Let us call this result the final logical equation.

The second step of the process deserves close attention. From the final logical equation that the first step has led us to, we read off, by inspection, a series of algebraic equations that contain the complete solution of the problem implicitly. Of how this passage is made, it is enough to say this. There is a definite relation between two sets of laws: the laws by which the probabilities of events are expressed as algebraic functions of the probabilities of the other events they depend on, and the laws by which the logical connection of the events is itself expressed. Like the other agreements of formal law mentioned already, this relation is not founded on a hypothesis. We learn it by observation (I.4) and reflection. If, however, we assumed it à priori, in advance of the evidence, as the very basis of the definition of probability, strict deduction would lead from it to the accepted numerical definition as a necessary consequence. As I have already remarked (I.12), the theory of probability stands in an equally close relation to logic and to arithmetic. As far as results go, it makes no difference whether we regard it as springing from arithmetic, or as founded on the relations that connect the two together.

16. The general solutions this method yields have some features, of interest perhaps to the mathematician, that are worth pointing out.

First, since the method does not depend on how many data there are or what kind, it still works when the data are not enough to fix the value sought. When that happens, the final expression of the solution will contain terms with arbitrary constant coefficients. Matching these, there will be terms in the final logical equation (I. 15). Interpreting those terms tells us what new data we need to fix the values of the constants, and so to make the numerical solution complete. If such data cannot be had, we can still give the constants their limiting values 0 and 1, and so find the limits within which the probability sought must lie, whatever further experience may show. When the event whose probability is sought is quite independent of those whose probabilities are given, the limits found this way will be 0 and 1, just as they plainly ought to be, and interpreting the constants will only lead us back to a restatement of the original problem.

Second, the expression of the final solution will always involve one particular quantity, found by solving an algebraic equation. When that equation is of high degree, there may seem to be a difficulty about which root to choose. In some cases, it is true, both the given elements and the element sought are so obviously restricted by necessary conditions that no choice is left. But in complicated cases it would be hopeless to find such conditions by unaided reasoning. A separate method is needed for this purpose, one that might fairly be called the Calculus of Statistical Conditions. I will not go further into it here than to say two things. Like the first method, it is based on the use of the “final logical equation.” And it definitely fixes, first, the conditions that the numbers in the data must satisfy for the problem to be real, that is, drawn from a possible experience; and second, the numerical limits within which the probability sought would have had to fall if, instead of being found by theory, it had been found directly by observation of the same system of phenomena the data came from. Clearly these limits will be actual limits of the probability sought. Now, if the data are taken to satisfy the conditions just assigned to them, then in every case I have examined there turns out to be one root, and only one, of the final algebraic equation that meets the required limits. Every source of ambiguity is thus removed. It even seems that new truths about the theory of algebraic equations come to light along the way. It is remarkable that this special quantity depends only on the data of the problem, and not at all on its quæsitum. So solving one particular problem unties the knot for a whole system of problems, namely all the problems that share the same data, whatever their quæsita may be. This matters whenever we need to draw a series of connected conclusions from one particular set of data. It also gives the solutions of particular problems the family likeness, drawn from their dependence on one central and fundamental unity, that often marks the use of general methods.

17. These considerations, and others like them, justify calling the method of this book a general method for solving questions in the theory of probability. But it does not follow that we can always do without hypotheses. As I have noted, a solution may consist entirely of terms with arbitrary constant coefficients; it may, in fact, be wholly indefinite. If we used only the data of experience, the method of this book would give results of that kind for some of the most important questions it covers. To get a definite solution in such cases, we must fall back on hypotheses that have more or less probability of their own but cannot be exactly verified. Generally such hypotheses differ from the direct results of experience in being logical rather than numerical in character: they lay down the conditions under which phenomena occur, rather than how often they occur. That difference, however, does not matter. Whatever their nature, once assumed, the hypotheses must be counted among the actual data, though they will obviously give the solution itself something of a hypothetical character. Understood this way, with these possible sources for the data actually used, the method is perfectly general. But it is no more answerable for the correctness of the hypotheses brought in than for the correctness of the numerical data taken from experience.

To illustrate, the theory of reducing astronomical observations rests partly on hypotheses. It makes certain assumptions about the nature of error, such as that an error is equally likely to fall on the side of excess or of defect, and so on. Without them it would be impossible to draw any definite conclusions from a set of observations that disagree. But once such assumptions are granted, the rest of the investigation falls strictly within the theory of probability. The same holds for the important problem of working out, from the records of the majorities of a deliberative assembly, the average probability that any one of its members judges correctly. Applied to the bare numerical data, the method of this book gives a solution of the wholly indefinite kind described above. And, to show still more strikingly how insufficient those data are on their own, the interpretation of the arbitrary constants (I. 16) in the solution merely gives back a restatement of the original problem. But if we admit the hypothesis that each mind forms its opinion independently, either absolutely, as in the speculations of Laplace and Poisson, or within limits set by the actual data, as will be seen in this treatise, Chap. XXI. (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition), the problem takes on a far more definite character. Clearly, then, the further value of the theory of probability must depend a great deal on forming such intermediate hypotheses correctly, wherever the purely experimental data are not enough for a definite solution and the further experience that the interpretation of the final logical equation points to cannot be had. On the other hand, too ready a habit of forming hypotheses on subjects that by their very nature lie beyond human knowledge is bound to damage the credit of the theory of probability, and to throw doubt, in the public mind, on even its most legitimate conclusions.

Footnote: The author designs to treat this subject either in a separate work or in a future Appendix. In the present treatise he avoids the use of the integral calculus.

18. It would perhaps be premature to speculate here on whether the methods of abstract science are ever likely to serve the study of social problems as well as they have served the various branches of physical inquiry. Trying to settle that question on purely à priori grounds, by argument in advance of the evidence, would very likely mislead us. For example, the fact of human free will would seem at first sight to rule out the idea that the movements of society should ever show the kind of orderly development we expect under the rule of physical necessity. Yet the researches of the statistician already reveal facts that contradict that expectation. The records of crime and poverty, for instance, show a degree of regularity unknown in regions untouched by the disturbing influence of human wants and passions. On the other hand, bad seasons, volcanic eruptions, the spread of blight among plants or of epidemic disease among animals, things apparently or mainly the product of natural causes, refuse to be brought under regular laws that we can grasp. “Fickle as the wind” is a proverb. Reflecting on these points teaches us to correct our first judgments somewhat. We learn not to expect, under the rule of necessity, an order that human observation can perceive, unless the interplay of the causes producing it is simple enough. Nor should we think, on the other side, that free agency in the individual cannot coexist with regularity in the movements of the system he is one unit of. Human freedom stands out as an apparent fact of our consciousness. It is also, I believe, a highly probable conclusion by analogy (Chap. XXII., not included in this edition) from the nature of that part of the mind whose scientific constitution we are able to investigate. But whether we accept it as a fact resting on consciousness or as a conclusion approved by reason, it must be understood in a way that does not conflict with an established result of observation. That result is this: phenomena that involve large masses of people do actually show a very remarkable degree of regularity. This lets us collect, in each age, the materials on which any estimate of its state and progress, as far as these show in outward results, must depend. So there is no sound à priori objection to the possibility of the kind of data needed as the experimental foundation of a science of social statistics. Further, whatever else this book may accomplish, I expect it to leave no doubt that there exists a system of abstract principles, and of methods founded on them, by which any collection of social data can be made to yield, explicitly, whatever information it implicitly contains. Where the data are extremely complex, getting this information out may be very hard. The difficulty would not come from any flaw in the theory, but from the sheer labour of the calculations it calls for. It is quite possible that in many cases the difficulty would be one that only combined effort could overcome. But this much, I believe, can be affirmed with perfect safety: we have in theory in every case, and in practice as far as the necessary labour of calculation can be supplied, the means of drawing out from statistical records the seeds of general truths that lie buried in the mass of figures.

19. Beyond these general positions, though, I do not venture to speak with confidence. Applying scientific methods to statistical records might produce results beyond those that can be found without such help. Whether those extra results would repay the labour enough to make it worth carrying out such investigations on a proper scale is a question that perhaps only experience could settle. It is to be hoped, and it might be expected without much presumption, that here as elsewhere the abstract doctrines of science will serve more than intellectual pleasure. Consider the apparent order in which the sciences have developed and, one after another, lent their help to the service of mankind. In that light it does not seem very unlikely that a day may come when similar help will come from branches of knowledge still more closely bound up with human welfare. For the present, though, let the speculations of this book rest simply on their claim to be true.

20. Last, I intend to try to draw from the scientific results of the earlier inquiries some general hints about the nature and constitution of the human mind (in the final chapter, not included in this edition). There is no need here to go into the grounds on which such an inference is possible. One or two general remarks may show the path I will try to follow. It must be admitted that our views of the science of logic are bound to influence greatly, perhaps mainly to decide, our opinions about the nature of the intellectual faculties. Take, for example, this question. Does reasoning consist merely in applying certain first or necessary truths that were stamped on the mind from the start? Or is the mind itself a seat of law, whose working is as plain and as conclusive in the particular case as in the general formula? Or, as some writers of note seem to hold, is all reasoning about particulars? This question, I say, does not merely affect the science of logic. It also bears on forming sound views of how the intellectual faculties are constituted. Again, suppose we conclude that the mind is by its original constitution a seat of law. Then the question of what kind of subjection to law this is also has deep speculative interest. Is it, for instance, an obedience founded on necessity, like the obedience that keeps the heavens turning and preserves the order of nature? Or is it a subjection of some quite different kind? Further, if the mind really is shown to be subject to law, and if its laws are correctly stated, then the question of how those laws are likely, or bound, to influence the course of human thought in different ages is one of great importance. It well deserves patient investigation, as a matter both of philosophy and of history. These and other questions I propose to discuss, however imperfectly, in the concluding part of this book. They belong, perhaps, to the domain of probable or conjectural knowledge rather than to that of positive knowledge. But it may happen that where there is not enough warrant for the certainties of science, there are grounds of analogy good enough to suggest highly probable opinions. It has seemed better to me to keep this discussion entirely for after the main business of this book, which is the investigation of scientific truths and laws. Experience teaches us clearly enough that the right order of progress in every search for truth is from the known to the unknown. There are parts, even of the philosophy and constitution of the human mind, that have been put fully within reach of our investigation. To make a proper knowledge of those parts of our nature the basis of every attempt to see into the shadows and uncertainties of the conjectural realm that lies beyond and above them: that is the course best suited to the limits of our present condition.

Chapter 2: Signs and Their Laws

1. Language is a tool of human reason, not just a way of expressing thought. That much is generally agreed. In this chapter I want to ask what it is that makes language able to serve the most important of our intellectual powers in this way. Along the way we will look at how language is built, treating it as a system designed for a purpose. We will pick out its elements, try to settle how they relate to and depend on one another, and ask how each of them, as a working part of the system, helps it reach the end it serves.

We need not, for these inquiries, enter the famous old debate of the schools: is language an essential tool of reasoning, or could we reason without it? I take that question to lie outside the plan of this book, and here is why. The business of science is to investigate laws. We may regard signs as standing for things and their relations, or as standing for the conceptions and operations of the human intellect. Either way, in studying the laws of signs we are in effect studying the laws of reasoning as they show themselves. If the two inquiries differ at all, the difference does not touch the scientific statement of formal laws, which is what this part of the book is after. It touches only the way the results are presented to the mind. When we investigate the laws of signs à posteriori, from the outside, what we examine directly is language and the rules that govern its use. When we take the inner processes of thought as our direct subject, we appeal more immediately to our own consciousness. But in both cases, as we will find, the results come out formally the same. Nor could we easily believe that the countless languages and dialects of the earth would have kept so much in common, over so many ages, unless their agreement had some deep foundation in the laws of the mind itself.

2. All language is made of signs, or symbols. Words are signs. Sometimes words are said to stand for things. Sometimes they stand for the operations by which the mind combines the simple notions of things into complex conceptions. Sometimes they express relations of action, of being acted on, or of mere quality, which we see among the objects of our experience. Sometimes they express the feelings of the mind that perceives. But words, though they serve as signs in these ways and others, are not the only signs we can use. Arbitrary marks that speak only to the eye, and arbitrary sounds or gestures that speak to some other sense, are signs just as much, provided that what they stand for is defined and understood. In the mathematical sciences, letters and the symbols +, −, =, and so on, are used as signs. There the word “sign” is usually kept for the second kind, the symbols that stand for operations or relations, rather than for the letters, which stand for the elements of number and quantity. What a sign really means does not depend on the particular shape it takes, and neither do the laws that govern its use. In this book, however, we are dealing with written signs, and the word “sign” will be used for these alone. The essential properties of signs are listed in the following definition.

Definition.—A sign is an arbitrary mark, having a fixed interpretation, and susceptible of combination with other signs in subjection to fixed laws dependent upon their mutual interpretation.

In plainer words: a sign is a mark chosen at will, which has a fixed meaning, and which can be combined with other signs according to fixed laws, laws that depend on what the signs mean.

3. Let us take the parts of this definition one at a time.

(1.) First, a sign is an arbitrary mark. It clearly makes no difference which word or token we attach to a given idea, as long as the attachment, once made, is kept. The Romans said “civitas” for what we call a “state.” But they and we could just as well have used any other word for the same conception. In fact nothing in the nature of language would stop us from using a single letter in that sense. If we did, the laws governing the letter would be essentially the same as the laws governing “civitas” in Latin and “state” in English, at least so far as those words are governed by general principles common to all languages.

(2.) Second, each sign must have a fixed meaning throughout any one discussion or chain of reasoning. The need for this is obvious; it seems to come from the very nature of the subject. There is, however, a dispute about exactly what words or symbols stand for when they are used as names in reasoning. Some hold that they stand only for the conceptions of the mind; others, that they stand for things. The question matters little here, since its answer cannot change the laws by which signs are used. My own view is this. In reasoning, signs take the place of the mind's conceptions and operations and do their work. Those conceptions and operations represent things and the connections and relations of things, and so the signs represent things with their connections and relations too. And because signs take the place of the mind's conceptions and operations, they are subject to the laws of those conceptions and operations. This view will be explained more fully in the next chapter. Here it serves to explain the third part of the definition of a sign, namely, that its combinations are subject to fixed laws, and that these laws depend on what it means.

4. The following Proposition analyses and classifies the signs by which reasoning is carried on.

Proposition I.

Everything language does as a tool of reasoning can be done by a system of signs made of the following elements:

First, literal symbols, such as x, y, and so on, standing for things as objects of our conceptions.

Second, signs of operation, such as +, −, ×, standing for those operations of the mind by which conceptions of things are combined or taken apart to form new conceptions out of the same elements.

Third, the sign of identity, =.

These symbols of logic obey definite laws in their use. Those laws partly agree with, and partly differ from, the laws of the matching symbols in algebra.

Let us take this as our test of the true elements of rational discourse: they should combine in the simplest forms and by the simplest laws, and by combining in this way they should produce every other form of language, known or conceivable. With that principle in hand, consider the following classification.

Class I.

5. Naming or describing signs: signs that give the name of a thing, or some quality or circumstance belonging to it.

To this class we can plainly assign the noun, proper or common, and the adjective. The two really differ in only one respect. The noun states outright that the individual thing or things it refers to exist; the adjective takes that existence for granted. If we attach to an adjective the subject everyone understands anyway, “being” or “thing,” it becomes in effect a noun, and for every essential purpose of reasoning the noun can replace it. Perhaps, in every shade of the mind's view, it is not quite the same to say “Water is a fluid thing” as to say “Water is fluid.” But for expressing the processes of reasoning the two are at least equivalent.

It is also clear that this class must include any sign used by convention for some circumstance or relation that would otherwise take many signs to spell out. The epithets of poetry are very often of this kind. They are usually compound adjectives, each doing the work of a description of many words. Homer's “deep-eddying ocean” packs a whole description into the single word βαθυδίνης. In the same way, any other description, whether aimed at the imagination or at the intellect, could by agreement be represented by a single sign. That sign would obey, in every essential point, the same laws as the adjective “good” or “great.” Joined to the subject “thing,” it would become in effect a noun, and a single noun could then carry the combined meaning of the thing and the quality.

6. Now, since a sign has been defined as an arbitrary mark, we are free to replace every sign of the kind just described by a letter. So let us agree to represent by a single letter, such as x, the class of individuals to which a particular name or description applies. If the name is “men,” for instance, let x stand for “all men,” or the class “men.” By a class we usually mean a collection of individuals, each of which the particular name or description fits. In this book the term is stretched a little. It includes the case where just one individual answers to the name or description. It also includes the cases named by the words “nothing” and “universe,” which as classes must be understood to contain “no beings” and “all beings” respectively. Next, if an adjective such as “good” is used to describe, let a letter, say y, stand for all the things the description “good” fits, that is, “all good things,” or the class “good things.” Let us further agree that the combination xy shall stand for the class of things to which the names or descriptions represented by x and y both apply at once. So if x alone stands for “white things” and y for “sheep,” let xy stand for “white sheep.” Likewise, if z stands for “horned things,” while x and y keep their meanings, let zxy stand for “horned white sheep,” that is, the collection of things to which the name “sheep” and the descriptions “white” and “horned” all apply together.

Let us now look at the laws that the symbols x, y, and so on, used in this sense, obey.

7. First, it is plain that in combinations like these, the order in which two symbols are written makes no difference. The expressions xy and yx both stand for the class of things to every member of which the names or descriptions x and y both apply. So we have xy=yx.(1)

If x stands for white things and y for sheep, either side of this equation stands for the class of “white sheep.” We may form the conception in a different order, but the individual things it covers are the same. In the same way, if x stands for “estuaries” and y for “rivers,” the expressions xy and yx both stand, without distinction, for “rivers that are estuaries” or “estuaries that are rivers.” In ordinary language this combination joins two nouns, rather than a noun and an adjective as in the first example. Let a third symbol, z, stand for the class of things to which the word “navigable” applies. Then any one of the expressions zxy,zyx,xyz,&c., will stand for the class of “navigable rivers that are estuaries.”

Sometimes one descriptive term carries a hidden reference to another. Then all we need do is write that reference openly into its stated meaning, and the remarks above apply again. For instance, if x stands for “wise” and y for “counsellor,” we must say whether x means wisdom in the absolute sense or only wisdom in giving counsel. Once that is settled, the law xy=yx holds as before.

So we may use the symbols x, y, z, and so on, in place of nouns, adjectives, and descriptive phrases, subject to two conditions. The first is a rule of interpretation: any expression in which several of these symbols are written together stands for all the objects or individuals to which their meanings all apply at once. The second is a law: the order in which the symbols follow each other makes no difference.

The rule of interpretation has now been illustrated enough. So I will not always bother to state the subject “things” when I give the meaning of a symbol that stands for an adjective. When I say, let x represent “good,” it will be understood that x means just “good” only when some other symbol supplies a subject for that quality; used alone, it means “good things.”

8. A few remarks can be added about the law just found. They will also apply, more or less, to some other laws to be derived later.

First, this law is a law of thought, not, strictly speaking, a law of things. A difference in the order of the qualities or attributes of an object, setting aside all questions of cause, is merely a difference in how we conceive it. The law (1) states as a general truth that the same thing can be conceived in different ways, and it says what that difference amounts to. It does nothing more.

Second, as a law of thought, it is actually worked out in a law of language, which is both the product and the tool of thought. Prose tends toward a uniform order. Yet even in prose, when several adjectives with a fixed meaning are applied to the same subject, the order in which they come makes no difference. And poetry owes much of its rich variety to extending this same lawful freedom to the noun as well. Milton's language is especially marked by this kind of variety. The noun often comes before the adjectives that qualify it, and it is often placed right in the middle of them. In the first few lines of his invocation to Light we meet examples like these:

	“Offspring of heaven first-born.”
	“The rising world of waters dark and deep.”
	“Bright effluence of bright essence increate.”

These inverted forms are not just the fruit of poetic license. They are the natural expression of a freedom that the deep laws of thought allow, but that ordinary speech, for convenience, does not use.

Third, the law expressed by (1) can be summed up by saying that the literal symbols x, y, z, are commutative, like the symbols of algebra: their order can be swapped. In saying this, I do not claim that multiplication in algebra, whose fundamental law is expressed by the equation xy=yx, is in itself anything like the process of logical combination that xy has been made to stand for above. I claim only that if the arithmetical process and the logical process are written in the same way, their symbolic expressions will obey the same formal law. The evidence that they obey it is quite separate in the two cases.

9. The combination of two literal symbols in the form xy expresses the whole class of objects to which the names or qualities represented by x and y both apply. It follows that if the two symbols mean exactly the same thing, their combination expresses no more than either symbol alone. In that case we should have xy=x. But since y is supposed to mean the same as x, we may put x in its place in this equation, and we get xx=x. that is, a class combined with itself gives that same class. Now in ordinary algebra the combination xx is written more briefly as x2. Let us adopt the same notation here. The way we write down a particular sequence of mental operations is just as arbitrary as the way we write down a single idea or operation (II. 3). In this notation, then, the equation above takes the form x2=x,(2) and it is, in fact, a second general law of the symbols by which names, qualities, or descriptions are represented.

The reader should keep in mind that, although in the earlier examples the symbols x and y were given meanings different from each other, nothing stops us from giving them exactly the same meaning. Clearly, the closer their actual meanings come to each other, the closer the class named by the combination xy comes to being the same as the class named by x, and the same as the class named by y. The case assumed in proving equation (2) is that of absolute sameness of meaning. Language shows this law at work in practice. To say “good, good” about anything, though a clumsy and useless repetition, is the same as saying “good.” So “good, good” men are just “good” men. People do sometimes repeat words in this way to heighten a quality or strengthen a statement. But that effect is secondary and a matter of convention; it is not rooted in the inner relations of language and thought. Most of the operations we see in nature, or carry out ourselves, have a greater effect when repeated. This prepares us to expect the same thing in language, and even to repeat ourselves when we want to speak with emphasis. But neither in strict reasoning nor in exact speech is there any real justification for the practice.

10. We now turn to another class of the signs of speech, and to the laws connected with their use.

Class II.

11. Signs of the mental operations by which we gather parts into a whole, or separate a whole into its parts.

We can do more than form conceptions of objects marked out by names, qualities, or circumstances that apply to each individual in the group we are thinking about. We can also form the combined conception of a group of objects made up of smaller groups, each named or described on its own. For this we use the conjunctions “and,” “or,” and so on. “Trees and minerals” and “barren mountains, or fertile vales” are examples of this kind. Strictly speaking, when the words “and” or “or” are placed between the terms describing two or more classes of objects, they imply that those classes are entirely separate, so that no member of one is found in another. In this respect, and in every other, the words “and” and “or” are like the sign + in algebra, and their laws are the same. So the expression “men and women,” setting aside conventional meanings, is equivalent to “women and men.” Let x stand for “men” and y for “women,” and let + stand for “and” and “or.” Then we have x+y=y+x,(3) an equation that would hold just as well if x and y stood for numbers and + were the sign of arithmetical addition.

Let the symbol z stand for the adjective “European.” Since it comes to the same thing to say “European men and women” as to say “European men and European women,” we have z(x+y)=zx+zy.(4) This equation, too, would hold just as well if x, y, and z were symbols of number and writing two letters side by side meant their algebraic product, just as, in the logical meaning given earlier, it means the class of objects to which both of the joined descriptions apply.

Those are the laws governing the sign +, used here for the positive operation of gathering parts into a whole. But the very idea of an operation that makes some positive change seems to suggest the idea of an opposite, negative operation, one that undoes what the first has done. We cannot think it possible to gather parts into a whole without also thinking it possible to separate a part from a whole. In ordinary speech we express this operation by the word “except,” as in “All men except Asiatics,” or “All states except those which are monarchical.” Here it is understood that the things excepted are part of the things they are excepted from. Just as we wrote the operation of gathering with the sign +, so we may write this negative operation with −, the minus sign. So if x stands for men and y for Asiatics, that is, Asiatic men, then the conception “All men except Asiatics” will be written x−y, the class of men with the Asiatic men taken out. And if x stands for “states” and y for the descriptive property “having a monarchical form,” then the conception “All states except those which are monarchical” will be written x−xy: from the states, take away the states that are monarchical.

Editor's note: Boole's plus sign is not the modern "or". He uses it only to join classes that have no members in common, so that "x plus y" means things that are either x or y but never both, and he allows "x minus y" only when all the y's are already among the x's. Modern Boolean algebra, following Jevons in 1864 and later Peirce, reads plus as an inclusive "or" (either one, or both) and replaces subtraction with the complement, "not-y". Boole's results still come out right in his own system, but a reader who knows modern notation should not read his plus as "or".

For every essential purpose of reasoning it makes no difference whether we mention the excepted cases first or last. In the same way, it makes no difference in what order we write a series of terms, some of which carry the sign −. So we have, as in ordinary algebra, x−y=−y+x.(5) Still letting x stand for the class “men” and y for “Asiatics,” let z stand for the adjective “white.” Now to apply the adjective “white” to the group of men described by the phrase “Men except Asiatics” is the same as to say “White men, except white Asiatics.” So we have z(x−y)=zx−zy.(6) This too agrees with the laws of ordinary algebra.

Equations (4) and (6) can be seen as two cases of a single general law: the literal symbols x, y, z, and so on, are distributive in their operation. The general fact this law expresses is this. Suppose some quality or circumstance is ascribed to all the members of a group, where the group was formed by gathering smaller groups together or by excluding some of them. The resulting conception is the same as if the quality or circumstance had first been ascribed to the members of each smaller group, and the gathering or excluding done afterwards. Whatever is said of the members of the whole is said of the members of all its parts, however those parts are put together.

Class III.

12. Signs that express relation, and by which we form propositions.

All verbs could properly be put in this class. But for the purposes of logic it is enough to include only the verb “to be,” in the form is or are. Every other verb can be broken down into this element plus one of the signs of Class I. Those signs express quality or circumstance of every kind, so they can express the subject's relation of acting or being acted on, whether in the past, present, or future. Thus the proposition “Cæsar conquered the Gauls” can be broken down into “Cæsar is he who conquered the Gauls.” My reason for this analysis is as follows. Unless we understand what it means to have conquered the Gauls, that is, what the expression “One who conquered the Gauls” means, we cannot understand the sentence. So that expression is truly an element of the sentence. “Cæsar” is another element. And one more is needed: the copula is, to show the connection between the two. I do not claim that this is the only way to view the relation expressed by the proposition “Cæsar conquered the Gauls.” I claim only that this analysis is correct from the particular point of view we have taken, and that it is enough for the purposes of logical deduction. It may be noted that the passive and future participles of the Greek language imply the principle asserted here, namely, that the sign is or are can be treated as an element of every personal verb.

13. This sign, is or are, can be represented by the symbol =. Next we consider the laws, or as they would usually be called, the axioms, that this symbol brings with it.

Take the proposition “The stars are the suns and the planets,” and let stars be represented by x, suns by y, and planets by z. Then we have x=y+z.(7) Now if it is true that the stars are the suns and the planets, it follows that the stars, except the planets, are suns. That gives the equation x−z=y,(8) which must therefore follow from (7). So a term z has been moved from one side of an equation to the other by changing its sign. This agrees with the algebraic rule of transposition.

But rather than dwell on particular cases, we can state the general axioms at once:

First, if equal things are added to equal things, the wholes are equal.

Second, if equal things are taken from equal things, the remainders are equal.

It follows that we may add or subtract equations, and use the rule of transposition just given, exactly as in ordinary algebra.

Again: suppose two classes of things, x and y, are identical; that is, every member of the one is a member of the other. Then the members of the one class that have a given property z will be identical with the members of the other that have the same property z. So if we have the equation x=y; then whatever class or property z may stand for, we also have zx=zy. This is the same in form as the algebraic law: if both sides of an equation are multiplied by the same quantity, the products are equal.

In the same way it can be shown that if the matching sides of two equations are multiplied together, the resulting equation is true.

14. Here, however, the likeness between this system and algebra, as algebra is usually stated, seems to stop. Suppose it is true that the members of a class x that have a certain property z are identical with the members of a class y that have the same property z. It does not follow that the members of the class x, all of them, are identical with the members of the class y. So we cannot infer from the equation zx=zy, that is, “the x's that are z are the same as the y's that are z,” that the equation x=y is also true. In other words, the algebraists' axiom that both sides of an equation may be divided by the same quantity has no formal equivalent here. I say no formal equivalent because, in keeping with the general spirit of these inquiries, we do not even try to decide whether the mental operation represented by removing a logical symbol z from a combination zx is in itself like division in arithmetic. That mental operation is in fact what is usually called abstraction, and it will appear later that its laws depend on the laws already derived in this chapter. What has been shown now is that nothing among those laws matches, in form, a commonly accepted axiom of algebra.

But a little thought will show that even in ordinary algebra this axiom is not as general as the other axioms we have looked at. Deducing the equation x=y from the equation zx=zy is valid only when we know that z is not equal to 0. So if the value z=0 is allowed in the algebraic system, the axiom stops applying, and the analogy shown before remains, at least, unbroken.

15. However, there is little point, except as a matter of speculation, in tracing such likenesses with the symbols of quantity in general. We have seen (II. 9) that the symbols of logic obey the special law x2=x. Now among the symbols of number there are only two, namely 0 and 1, that obey the same formal law.
