We know that 02=0, and that 12=1; and the equation x2=x, taken as an equation of algebra, has no roots other than 0 and 1. So instead of measuring how far the symbols of logic agree in form with the symbols of number in general, the more natural step is to compare them with symbols of quantity admitting only of the values 0 and 1. Let us imagine, then, an algebra in which the symbols x, y, z, etc. can take the values 0 and 1, either one, and these values only. The laws, the axioms, and the processes of such an algebra will be identical, through their whole range, with the laws, the axioms, and the processes of an algebra of logic. Only a difference of interpretation will separate them. This is the principle on which the method of this book is built.

16. It remains to show that the parts of ordinary language not yet considered in this chapter either break down into the same elements we have considered, or serve those elements by helping to define them more precisely.

We have already dealt with the noun, the adjective, and the verb, along with the particles and and except. The pronoun can be treated as a particular form of the noun or the adjective. The adverb modifies the meaning of the verb but does not change its nature. Prepositions help to express circumstance or relation, and so they add precision and detail to the meaning of the literal symbols. The conjunctions if, either, or, are used mainly to express relations among propositions. It will be shown later that those same relations can be fully expressed by elementary symbols that are similar in meaning, and identical in form and law, to the symbols whose use and meaning have been explained in this chapter. As for any remaining elements of speech, examination will show that they do one of two things. Either they give a more definite meaning to the terms of discourse, and so enter into the interpretation of the literal symbols already considered; or they express some emotion or feeling that goes with the utterance of a proposition, and so do not belong to the province of the understanding, which is our only concern here. Experience in using this classification will show that it is sufficient.

Chapter 3: Derivation of the Laws

1. The object of science, in the proper sense of the word, is the knowledge of laws and relations. One of the most important conditions of scientific progress is the ability to tell what is essential to that end from what is only accidentally attached to it. I say tell apart, because a steady devotion to science does not require us to turn our attention away completely from other speculations, often metaphysical ones, with which science is frequently bound up. Take questions like these: whether there is some underlying ground that sustains the phenomena we observe; whether causes are real; whether it is proper to speak as if one state of things leads to the next by some operation. Questions of this kind may have deep interest and meaning in relation to science without being, in their essence, scientific. In fact it is hardly possible to state the conclusions of natural science without borrowing the language of these ideas. Nor does this necessarily cause any practical trouble. Some people believe that there is more to the relation of cause and effect than a fixed order in which one thing follows another; some refuse to believe it. Both sides read the conclusions of physical astronomy in exactly the same way. But they agree only because they recognise a shared element of scientific truth, one that does not depend on their particular views about what causation is.

2. If this distinction matters in physical science, it deserves even more attention in the science of the powers of the intellect. For the questions this science raises are almost bound to get mixed up, at least in how they are expressed, with ways of thinking and speaking that betray a metaphysical origin. The idealist would state the laws of reasoning in one form; the sceptic, if he were true to his principles, in another. Some people regard the phenomena we are studying here as nothing more than a series of states of the thinking subject, with no causal link between them. Others trace them to the operations of an active intelligence. If each side were consistent, they would state those laws differently too. A different way of classifying the faculties of the mind would produce differences of the same kind. Amid so much variety, some of it only apparent and some of it real, I want to assert one principle as our only firm and stable ground. It is this: if the laws in question really are drawn from observation, then they have a real existence as laws of the human mind, whatever metaphysical theory their wording may seem to involve. They contain an element of truth that no later criticism of the nature of the mind's operations, or even of whether those operations are real, can essentially touch. Grant, if you like, that the mind is nothing but a succession of states of consciousness: a series of passing impressions, caused neither from outside nor from within, rising out of nothing and sinking back into nothing again. That is the last refinement of the sceptical intellect. Even so, the results that observation had led us to would remain true as laws of succession, or at least of a succession that has already happened. They would have to be translated into a language whose vocabulary had been stripped of every term like cause and effect, operation and subject, substance and attribute. But they would still be valid as scientific truths.

There is more. Any statement of the laws of thought that rests on actual observation must contain scientific elements that do not depend on metaphysical theories about the nature of the mind. So the practical use of those elements, in building a system or method of reasoning, must also be independent of metaphysical distinctions. For any practical application will rest on the scientific elements contained in the statement of the laws. In the same way, the practical conclusions of physical astronomy do not depend on any theory of what causes gravitation; they rest only on knowing its observed effects. And so, both in finding the laws of thought and in putting them to use once found, we are, for every truly scientific purpose, not concerned with whether any metaphysical speculation whatever is true or false.

3. Under these circumstances, the course I think best is to use the language of everyday speech as far as I can, without regard to any theory of the nature and powers of the mind that it might be thought to carry with it. For instance, it is ordinary usage to say that we talk with each other by communicating ideas, or conceptions, and that communicating them is the job of words. It is also ordinary usage to say that, when particular ideas or conceptions are presented to the mind, it has certain powers or faculties for dealing with them. By these it can fix its regard on some ideas and shut out others, or combine the given conceptions or ideas in various ways. These faculties or powers have been given different names, such as Attention, Simple Apprehension, Conception or Imagination, Abstraction, and so on. These names have not only supplied the titles of separate branches of the philosophy of the human mind; they have also passed into the common language of people. So whenever I have occasion to use these terms, I shall use them without implying that I accept the theory that the mind has such and such powers and faculties as distinct parts of its activity. Nor is it really necessary to ask whether these powers of the understanding exist separately or not. We may gather all these different titles under one general name, the Operations of the human mind. We can define these operations as far as this book needs, and then try to express their ultimate laws. That is the general plan I shall follow, though now and then I will refer to the names that common agreement has given to the particular states or operations of the mind that come up along the way.

It will be most convenient to divide the more definite results of the investigation that follows into separate Propositions.

Proposition I.

4. To deduce the laws of the symbols of Logic from a consideration of those operations of the mind which are implied in the strict use of language as an instrument of reasoning.

In every discourse, whether it is the mind talking with its own thoughts or a person talking with others, there is a limit, assumed or stated, within which the subjects being talked about are confined. The most unrestricted discourse is the one in which our words are taken in the widest possible sense; for such words, the limits of discourse are as wide as those of the universe itself. But more often we confine ourselves to a smaller field. Sometimes, when we speak of men, we mean (without saying so) men only under certain circumstances and conditions: civilized men, for example, or men in the prime of life, or men under some other condition or relation. Now, whatever the extent of the field within which all the objects of our discourse are found, that field may properly be called the universe of discourse.

5. Furthermore, this universe of discourse is, in the strictest sense, the ultimate subject of the discourse. Under the limits we have just described, the job of any name or descriptive term is not to call up in the mind the conception of every being or object it could apply to. It is to call up only those that exist within the assumed universe of discourse. If that universe of discourse is the actual universe of things, as it always is when our words are taken in their real and literal sense, then by men we mean all men that exist. But if the universe of discourse is limited by some understanding implied in advance, then we are speaking of men under the limit so introduced. In both cases the business of the word men is to direct a certain operation of the mind: from the proper universe of discourse, we pick out, or fix upon, the individuals the word signifies.

6. The mental operation implied by using an adjective is of exactly the same kind. Suppose, for instance, that the universe of discourse is the actual Universe. The word men tells us to select in our minds, from that Universe, all the beings the term "men" applies to. In just the same way the adjective "good," in the combination "good men," tells us to go further and select from the class of men all those who have the further quality "good." And if another adjective were put in front of "good men," it would direct a further operation of the same kind, concerning whatever further quality it was chosen to express.

It is important to notice carefully what the operation described here really is, because it is conceivable that it might have been different. If the adjective were simply attributive, that is, if it simply attached a quality, then once a particular set of beings had been marked out by men, putting the adjective good in front would tell us to attach the quality of goodness, in our minds, to every one of those beings. But that is not what the adjective really does. The operation we actually perform is one of selection according to a prescribed principle or idea. It does not matter here which faculties of the mind such an operation would be assigned to under the accepted classification of its powers. I suppose it would be thought to depend on two of them, Conception or Imagination, and Attention. To the first we might assign the forming of the general conception; to the second, the fixing of the mind's regard on those individuals, within the prescribed universe of discourse, that answer to the conception. But it seems quite possible that the power of Attention is nothing more than the power of keeping up the exercise of some other faculty of the mind. If so, we might properly assign the whole mental process just described to the single faculty of Imagination or Conception. The first step of the process would be the conception of the Universe itself, and each step after that would narrow, in a definite way, the conception so formed. Taking this view, I shall call each such step, or any definite combination of such steps, a definite act of conception. And I shall stretch this term to cover not only the conception of classes of objects named by particular words or by simple qualities, but also the combining of such conceptions in any way that the powers and limits of the human mind allow. In fact it covers any intellectual operation short of the one involved in building a sentence or proposition. We must now consider the general laws that such operations of the mind obey.

7. I shall now show that the laws found in the preceding chapter for the use of the literal symbols of Logic, which there were reached à posteriori, after the fact, from the structure of language, are really the laws of the definite mental operation just described. We begin our discourse with a certain understanding about the limits of its subject, that is, about the limits of its Universe. Every name, every descriptive term we use, directs the person we are speaking to to carry out a certain mental operation on that subject. That is how thought is communicated. But on this view each name or descriptive term is only the representative of an intellectual operation, and that operation comes first in the order of nature. So it is clear that the laws of the name or symbol must be derived ones. They must, in fact, come from the laws of the operation they represent. I shall now show that the laws of the symbol and the laws of the mental process are identical in expression.

8. Let us suppose, then, that the universe of our discourse is the actual universe, so that words are used in the full extent of their meaning. And let us consider the two mental operations implied by the words "white" and "men." The word "men" implies the operation of selecting in thought, from its subject, the universe, all men; and the resulting conception, men, becomes the subject of the next operation. The operation implied by the word "white" is that of selecting, from its subject, "men," all members of that class who are white. The final resulting conception is that of "white men." Now it is perfectly plain that if these operations had been performed in the reverse order, the result would have been the same. We may begin by forming the conception "men" and then, by a second act of the intellect, narrow it to "white men." Or we may begin by forming the conception "white objects" and then narrow it to those members of that class who are "men." As far as the result goes, it makes no difference at all. Clearly, the order of the mental processes would make no difference either if we put any other descriptive or naming terms in place of "white" and "men," provided only that their meaning was fixed and absolute. So the fact that the order of two successive acts of the faculty of Conception does not matter, where one act supplies the subject that the other works on, is a general condition of the use of that faculty. It is a law of the mind. And it is the real origin of the law of the literal symbols of Logic that is its formal expression, law (1) of Chap. II, the law that xy is the same as yx.

9. It is just as clear that this mental operation is of such a kind that repeating it does not change its effect. Suppose that by one definite act of conception the attention has been fixed on men, and that by another exercise of the same faculty we narrow it to those of the race who are white. Then repeating the second mental act any further, narrowing the attention to white objects again, does not change in any way the conception we have reached, namely, that of white men. This too is an example of a general law of the mind, and its formal expression is the law ((2) Chap, II.) of the literal symbols, the law that xx is the same as x.

10. Again, it is plain that from the conceptions of two distinct classes of things we can form the conception of the collection of things that the two classes make up together. And it obviously makes no difference in what order of position or of priority the two classes are presented to the mind. This is another general law of the mind, and its expression is found in (3) Chap. II, the law that x + y is the same as y + x.

11. There is no need to carry this line of inquiry and comparison further. Enough illustration has been given to make the following two positions clear.

First, the operations by which the mind, using its power of imagination or conception, combines and modifies the simple ideas of things or qualities are subject to general laws, no less than those operations of the reason that work on truths and propositions.

Second, those laws are mathematical in their form, and they are actually worked out in the essential laws of human language. So the laws of the symbols of Logic can be deduced from a consideration of the operations of the mind in reasoning.

12. The rest of this chapter deals with questions about the law of thought whose expression is x2=x (II. 9). As has been implied (II. 15), this law is what marks off the operations of the mind in its ordinary discourse and reasoning from its operations when it is busy with the general algebra of quantity. An important part of the inquiry that follows will be to prove that the symbols 0 and 1 have a place among the symbols of Logic, and can be given a meaning there. But first it may be necessary to show how particular symbols like these can properly, and usefully, be used to represent quite separate systems of thought.

This propriety cannot rest on any shared meaning. Logic and Arithmetic (I use the second term in its widest sense, as the science of Number) are truly separate systems of thought, and properly speaking they have no subject in common. The one deals with the very conceptions of things; the other takes account only of their numerical relations. But the forms and methods of any system of reasoning depend directly on the laws the symbols obey, and only indirectly, through that link, on what the symbols mean. So it can be both proper and useful to use the same symbols in different systems of thought, provided they can be given meanings that make their formal laws identical and their use consistent. The ground for using them will then not be a shared meaning but the shared formal laws they obey in their respective systems. And that sharing of formal laws must be established on no other ground than careful observation and comparison of the results that are seen to follow, separately, from the meanings within each system under consideration.

These remarks explain the line of inquiry taken in the next Proposition. The literal symbols of Logic all obey, without exception, the law whose expression is x2=x. Among the symbols of Number there are only two, 0 and 1, that satisfy this law. But each of these two symbols also obeys a law of its own in the system of numerical quantity. This suggests the question: what meanings must we give to the literal symbols of Logic so that these same special formal laws hold in the logical system too?

Proposition II.

13. To determine the logical value and significance of the symbols 0 and 1.

The symbol 0, as used in Algebra, satisfies the following formal law, 0×y=0, or 0y=0,(1) whatever number y may stand for. For this formal law to hold in the system of Logic, we must give the symbol 0 a meaning such that the class represented by 0y is identical with the class represented by 0, whatever the class y may be. A little thought will show that this condition is met if the symbol 0 stands for Nothing. Following an earlier definition, we may call Nothing a class. In fact, Nothing and Universe are the two limits of how far a class can extend. They are the limits of the possible meanings of general names, since no general name can refer to fewer individuals than Nothing contains, or to more than the Universe contains. Now, whatever the class y may be, the individuals it shares with the class "Nothing" are identical with those contained in the class "Nothing," for there are none. So by giving 0 the meaning Nothing, we satisfy law (1); and no other meaning satisfies it consistently with the perfectly general character of the class y.

Second, in the system of Number the symbol 1 satisfies the following law, namely, 1×y=y, or 1y=y, whatever number y may stand for. Suppose this formal equation holds equally in the system of this book, in which 1 and y stand for classes. Then the symbol 1 must stand for a class such that all the individuals found in any proposed class y are also all the individuals 1y that the class y shares with the class represented by 1. A little thought will show here that the class represented by 1 must be "the Universe," since this is the only class in which all the individuals that exist in any class are found. So the meanings of the symbols 0 and 1 in the system of Logic are, respectively, Nothing and Universe.

14. The idea of any class of objects, such as "men," brings to mind the idea of the opposite class, the beings that are not men. And the whole Universe is made up of these two classes together, since of every individual in it we may say either that it is a man or that it is not a man. So it becomes important to ask how such opposite names are to be expressed. That is the object of the following Proposition.

Proposition III.

If x represent any class of objects, then will 1−x represent the contrary or supplementary class of objects, that is, the class including all objects which are not comprehended in the class x.

To make the idea clearer, let x stand for the class men, and, following the last Proposition, let us express the Universe by 1. Now if from the conception of the Universe, as made up of "men" and "not-men," we take away the conception of "men," what remains is the conception of the opposite class, "not-men." So the class "not-men" will be represented by 1−x. And in general, whatever class of objects the symbol x stands for, the opposite class will be expressed by 1−x, which reads as "the Universe, leaving out the x's."

15. Strictly speaking, the following Proposition belongs to a later chapter of this book, the one devoted to maxims or necessary truths. But the law of thought it concerns is so important that it seemed right to introduce it here.

Proposition IV.

That axiom of metaphysicians which is termed the principle of contradiction, and which affirms that it is impossible for any being to possess a quality, and at the same time not to possess it, is a consequence of the fundamental law of thought, whose expression is x2=x.

Let us write this equation in the form x−x2=0, from which we get x(1−x)=0;(1) both of these steps being justified by the axiomatic laws of combination and transposition (II. 13). In words, the equation (1) says that the class of things that are both x and not-x is empty. To make the idea simpler, let us give the symbol x the particular meaning men. Then 1−x will represent the class of "not-men" (Prop. III.). Now the formal product of the expressions for two classes represents the class of individuals common to both (II. 6). So x(1−x) will represent the class whose members are at once "men" and "not men," and the equation (1) thus expresses the principle that a class whose members are at the same time men and not men does not exist. In other words, it is impossible for the same individual to be at the same time a man and not a man. Now let us widen the meaning of the symbol x from "men" to any class of beings marked out by having any quality whatever. The equation (1) will then express that it is impossible for a being to have a quality and not to have that quality at the same time. But this is exactly the "principle of contradiction" that Aristotle described as the fundamental axiom of all philosophy. "It is impossible that the same quality should both belong and not belong to the same thing.…This is the most certain of all principles.…Wherefore they who demonstrate refer to this as an ultimate opinion. For it is by nature the source of all the other axioms."

Footnote: Τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ ἅμα ὑπάρχειν τε καὶ μὴ ὑπάρχειν ἀδύνατον τῷ αὐτῷ καὶ κατὰ τὸ αὐτό… Αὕτη δὴ πασῶν ἐστὶ βεβαιοτάτη τῶν ἀρχῶν… Διὸ πάντες οἱ ἀποδεικνύντες εἰς ταύτην ἀνάγουσιν ἐσχάτην δόξαν· φύσει γὰρ ἀρχὴ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἀξιωμάτων αὕτη πάντων.—Metaphysica, III, 3.

I have brought in this interpretation not for its immediate value in the present system, but to illustrate a significant fact in the philosophy of the powers of the intellect. What has commonly been regarded as the fundamental axiom of metaphysics is only the consequence of a law of thought, and that law is mathematical in form. I also want to draw attention to the fact that the equation (1), which expresses this fundamental law of thought, is an equation of the second degree: x appears in it squared. I will not speculate in this chapter about whether this has to be so by its very nature. But we may venture to say that if it were not so, the whole working of the understanding would be different from what it is. It is because the fundamental equation of thought is of the second degree that we analyse and classify by dividing things into pairs of opposites, or, as the technical term has it, by dichotomy (cutting in two). Now if the equation in question had been of the third degree, and could still be interpreted as such, the mind's division of things would have had to be threefold. We would have had to proceed by a kind of trichotomy (cutting in three). With the faculties we actually have, we cannot properly conceive what that would really be like; but we could still investigate its laws as an object of intellectual speculation.

Footnote: Someone might object here that if the equation x2=x exists, then so must the equation x3=x, which is of the third degree, and ask whether that equation does not point to a process of trichotomy. The answer is that the equation x3=x cannot be interpreted in the system of logic. For if we write it in either of the forms x(1−x)(1+x)=0,(2)x(1−x)(−1−x)=0,(3) we see that its interpretation, if it has one at all, must involve the meaning of the factor 1+x, or of the factor −1−x. The first cannot be interpreted, because we cannot conceive of adding any class x to the universe 1. The second cannot be interpreted, because the symbol −1 does not obey the law x(1−x)=0, which all class symbols obey. So the equation x3=x admits of no interpretation like that of the equation x2=x. Suppose, however, that the former equation were true independently of the latter. That is, suppose the act of the mind denoted by the symbol x were such that doing it a second time over, three times in all, reproduced the result of doing it once, while doing it just twice did not. Then presumably we would be able to interpret one of the forms (1), (2), which under the actual conditions of thought we cannot do. Mathematicians know of operations whose law can be fully expressed by the equation x3=x. But they are of a nature entirely foreign to the field of general reasoning. When I say it is conceivable that the law of thought might have been different from what it is, I mean only that we can frame such a hypothesis and study its consequences. Being able to do this implies no such doctrine as that the actual law of human reason is the product either of chance or of arbitrary will.

Editor's note: This is the step that made Boolean algebra the algebra of two values. Once every class symbol must obey the law that x times x is x, and the only numbers that obey it are 0 and 1, the whole system can be worked as if each symbol were either 0 or 1, nothing or everything, false or true. In 1937 Claude Shannon showed that electrical switching circuits, with each switch either open or closed, obey these same laws. That is why every digital computer calculates in Boole's algebra.

16. For reasons that the discussion above makes plain, the law of thought expressed by the equation (1) will sometimes be referred to as the "law of duality."

Chapter 4: Division of Propositions

1. We have now investigated the laws of the mental operations involved in conception, or imagination, and explained the matching laws of the symbols that represent them. The next step is to put these results to practical use. There are three uses: first, expressing the complex terms of propositions; second, expressing propositions themselves; and last, building a general method of deductive analysis. This chapter deals mainly with the first of these. As an introduction to it, we need to establish the following Proposition:

Proposition I.

All logical propositions may be considered as belonging to one or the other of two great classes, which may be called "Primary" or "Concrete Propositions," and "Secondary" or "Abstract Propositions."

Every assertion we make belongs to one of two kinds. Either it states a relation among things, or it states (or amounts to stating) a relation among propositions. An assertion about the properties of things, or the phenomena they show, or the circumstances they are in, is strictly the assertion of a relation among things. For the purposes of logic, to say that "snow is white" is the same as to say that "snow is a white thing." An assertion about facts or events, and how they connect with and depend on one another, usually amounts, for the same purposes, to saying that certain propositions about those events are related in their truth or falsehood. The first class of propositions, about things, I call "Primary." The second class, about propositions, I call "Secondary." In practice this distinction nearly, but not quite, lines up with the usual logical division of propositions into categorical and hypothetical.

For instance, the propositions "The sun shines" and "The earth is warmed" are primary. The proposition "If the sun shines the earth is warmed" is secondary. To say "The sun shines" is to say "The sun is that which shines." It states a relation between two classes of things, namely "the sun" and "things which shine." The secondary proposition, on the other hand, states a relation of dependence between the two primary propositions "The sun shines" and "The earth is warmed." I do not claim that the relation between these propositions is a relation of cause and effect, as the relation between the facts they express is. I claim only that the relation among the propositions implies the relation among the facts, and is implied by it, so closely that for the purposes of logic it can stand in for it.

2. Suppose that instead of the proposition "The sun shines" we say "It is true that the sun shines." Then we are no longer speaking directly about things. We are speaking about a proposition concerning things, namely the proposition "The sun shines." So the proposition in which we say this is a secondary one. In this way every primary proposition can give rise to a secondary proposition: the one that asserts its truth, or declares its falsehood.

The little words if, either, and or will usually signal that a proposition is secondary, but they do not have to. The proposition "Animals are either rational or irrational" is primary. It cannot be broken into "Either animals are rational or animals are irrational," and so it does not state a relation of dependence between the two propositions joined in that second, disjunctive sentence. The words either and or are in fact no test of what kind a proposition is, even though they turn up more often in secondary propositions. Even the word if can appear in a primary proposition. "Men are, if wise, then temperate," is an example. It cannot be broken into "If all men are wise, then all men are temperate."

3. It is not my purpose to discuss the strengths or weaknesses of the usual division of propositions. I will only say this about the classification used here. Its principle is clear and definite in use; it marks a real and fundamental difference among propositions; and it is essential to developing a general method of reasoning. Nor is it any objection that a primary proposition can be put into a form in which it becomes secondary. In that case we take no direct account of the things connected in the primary proposition. We consider only the proposition itself, as true or as false.

4. In this book the same symbols will be used to express both primary and secondary propositions, and, as we shall see, they obey the same laws. The difference between the two cases is not a difference of form but of interpretation. In both, the relation the proposition sets out to express will be written with the sign =. In primary propositions, the two sides joined by this sign will usually stand for the "terms" of the proposition, or, to give them their more specific names, its subject and predicate.

Proposition II.

5. To work out a general method, based on listing the possible cases, for expressing any class or collection of things that can be a "term" of a Primary Proposition.

First, suppose the class or collection is defined only by names or qualities that all its members share. Then its expression is a single term, in which the symbols for those names or qualities are joined with no sign between them, as in algebraic multiplication. So if x stands for opaque substances, y for polished substances, and z for stones, we have xyz= opaque polished stones; xy(1−z)= opaque polished substances which are not stones; x(1−y)(1−z)= opaque substances which are not polished, and are not stones; and so on for any other combination. Notice that each of these expressions obeys the same law of duality as the single symbols it contains. So xyz×xyz=xyz;xy(1−z)×xy(1−z)=xy(1−z); and so on: taking the opaque polished stones together with the opaque polished stones gives nothing new. Any term like these we shall call a "class term," because it expresses a class of things through the properties or names its members have in common.

Second, suppose we are speaking of a collection whose different portions are defined by different properties, names, or attributes. Then the expressions for those portions must be formed separately and joined by the sign +. But if the collection was formed by removing a defined portion from some wider collection, the sign − must be placed before the symbolic expression of the portion removed. A few more remarks on these symbols are in order.

6. Broadly speaking, the symbol + is the equivalent of the words "and" and "or," and the symbol − the equivalent of the word "except." Of "and" and "or," the first is usually used when the collection described is the subject of a proposition, the second when it is the predicate. "The scholar and the man of the world desire happiness" illustrates the first case. "Things possessing utility are either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain" illustrates the second. Now whenever an expression with these words appears in a primary proposition, it matters a great deal whether the groups they separate in thought are meant to be completely distinct and mutually exclusive, or not. Does "Scholars and men of the world" include or exclude those who are both? Does "Either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain" include or exclude things that are both? My view is that, strictly speaking, "and" and "or" do have this power of separating, or excluding. On that view the statement "All x’s are either y’s or z’s," taken rigorously, means "All x’s are either y’s, but not z’s," or "z’s but not y’s." But it must also be admitted that the "jus et norma loquendi" (the law and rule of speech, that is, ordinary usage) seems rather to favour the opposite reading. "Either y’s or z’s" would generally be understood to include things that are y’s and z’s at once, along with things that are one but not the other. Remember, though, that the symbol + does have this separating power. So we must break any disjunctive expression we meet into parts that really are separate in thought, and then join their expressions with the symbol +.

So, depending on the meaning intended, the expression "Things which are either x’s or y’s" will have two different symbolic equivalents. If we mean "Things which are x’s but not y’s, or y’s but not x’s," the expression will be x(1−y)+y(1−x); the symbol x standing for x’s, and y for y’s. If, however, we mean "Things which are either x’s, or, if not x’s, then y’s," the expression will be x+y(1−x). This expression allows for things that are both x’s and y’s at once. It could be written out more fully as xy+x(1−y)+y(1−x); but adding the first two terms of this, the x’s that are y’s and the x’s that are not, simply gives back all the x’s, and so the previous expression.

Notice that the expressions just given obey the fundamental law of duality (III. 16). So we have {x(1−y)+y(1−x)}2=x(1−y)+y(1−x),{x+y(1−x)}2=x+y(1−x). We shall see later that this is only one case of a general law of expressions that stand for "classes or collections of things."

7. The results of these inquiries can be summed up in the following rule of expression.

Rule.—Express simple names or qualities by the symbols x, y, z, etc., and their contraries by 1−x, 1−y, 1−z, etc. Express classes of things defined by common names or qualities by joining the corresponding symbols as in multiplication. Express collections of things made up of portions that differ from one another by joining the expressions for those portions with the sign +. In particular, express "Either x’s or y’s" by x(1−y)+y(1−x) when the classes denoted by x and y are exclusive, and by x+y(1−x) when they are not exclusive. In the same way, express "Either x’s, or y’s, or z’s" by x(1−y)(1−z)+y(1−x)(1−z)+z(1−x)(1−y) when the classes denoted by x, y, and z are meant to be mutually exclusive, and by x+y(1−x)+z(1−x)(1−y) when they are not meant to be exclusive; and so on.

8. On this rule of expression rests the reverse rule, the rule of interpretation. The following examples should illustrate both well enough. For brevity, leaving out the universal subject "things" or "beings," let us take x=hard,y=elastic,z=metals; and we get the following results:

"Non-elastic metals" will be expressed by z(1−y), the metals that are not elastic;

"Elastic substances with non-elastic metals," by y+z(1−y);

"Hard substances, except metals," by x−z;

"Metallic substances, except those which are neither hard nor elastic," by z−z(1−x)(1−y), or by z{1−(1−x)(1−y)} (see (6), Chap. II.).

In the last example, what we really had to express was "Metals, except not hard, not elastic, metals." Words like "and" placed between adjectives usually add nothing, and so they must not be expressed in symbols.

So "Metals hard and elastic" is the same as "Hard elastic metals," and is expressed by xyz.

Take next the expression "Hard substances, except those which are metallic and non-elastic, and those which are elastic and non-metallic." Here the word those means hard substances. So the expression really means hard substances, except hard substances that are metallic and non-elastic, and hard substances that are non-metallic and elastic; the word except covers both of the classes that follow it. The complete expression is x−{xz(1−y)+xy(1−z)};or, x−xz(1−y)−xy(1−z). that is, the hard things, with the hard non-elastic metals and the hard elastic non-metals taken away.

9. The Proposition just given, with its illustrations, is a necessary first step toward the next one, which will complete the plan of this chapter.

Proposition III.

To work out, by examining their possible kinds, a general method for expressing Primary or Concrete Propositions.

A primary proposition, in the most general sense, consists of two terms and asserts that a relation holds between them. These terms need not be names of one word. They may stand for any collection of objects, of the sort we have just been considering. How to express the terms is therefore already covered by the general rules above. What remains is to find out how to express the relations between them. This will plainly depend on the kind of relation, and above all on whether, in that relation, the terms are understood to be universal or particular. That is, it depends on whether we speak of the whole of the collection a term refers to, or speak indefinitely of the whole or of a part of it, which is what the word "some" usually means.

Suppose we want to express a relation of identity between the two classes "Fixed Stars" and "Suns," that is, to express that "All fixed stars are suns" and "All suns are fixed stars." Here, if x stands for fixed stars and y for suns, we have x=y as the equation required. It reads: the fixed stars and the suns are one and the same class.

In the proposition "All fixed stars are suns," the term "all fixed stars" would be called the subject, and "suns" the predicate. Let us stretch the meaning of subject and predicate as follows. By subject we will mean the first term of any affirmative proposition, the term that comes before the copula is or are. By predicate we will mean the second term, the one that comes after the copula. And let us allow that either of them may be universal or particular, so that either the whole class is meant, or only a part of it. Then we have the following Rule for cases like the last example:—

10. Rule.—When both Subject and Predicate of a Proposition are universal, form the separate expressions for them, and connect them by the sign =.

This case usually comes up in the definitions of a science, or of subjects handled in the manner of pure science. Mr. Senior’s definition of wealth is a good example:

"Wealth consists of things transferable, limited in supply, and either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain."

Before putting this definition into symbols, notice that the word and here adds nothing. Wealth is defined by having three properties or qualities, not by being made up of three classes or collections of objects. So, leaving out the and, let us set w=wealth.t=things transferable.s=limited in supply.p=productive of pleasure.r=preventive of pain.

Now it is clear from the subject that the phrase "Either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain," in this definition, is meant to say "Either productive of pleasure; or, if not productive of pleasure, preventive of pain." So the class of things this phrase would define on its own would consist of all things productive of pleasure, together with all things that are not productive of pleasure but are preventive of pain. Its symbolic expression would be p+(1−p)r. that is, the pleasure-giving things, plus the things that give no pleasure but prevent pain.

Now we put this expression in brackets, to show that both its terms are meant, and attach to it the symbols s and t, which limit it to things "transferable" and "limited in supply." That gives the following symbolic equivalent of the original definition: w=st{p+r(1−p)}.(1) In words: wealth is exactly the class of things that are transferable, limited in supply, and either pleasure-giving or, failing that, pain-preventing.

Suppose instead that "Either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain" were meant to pick out only things productive of pleasure without being preventive of pain, p(1−r), or preventive of pain without being productive of pleasure, r(1−p), leaving out the things that are both. Then the definition in symbols would be w=st{p(1−r)+r(1−p)}.(2)

All this agrees with what was said earlier in more general terms. The reader may wonder what would happen if we translated the phrase "Things productive of pleasure or preventive of pain" word for word, as p+r, making the equation of the definition w=st(p+r).(3)

The answer is that this would be equivalent to (2), with one extra implication: that the classes of things denoted by stp and str are quite distinct. In other words, it would imply that among things transferable and limited in supply there exist none in the universe that are at once productive of pleasure and preventive of pain. How to find the full meaning of any equation will be explained later. What has been said may show that before we try to translate our data into the strict language of symbols, it is above all necessary to find out what our words are intended to mean. But no one who values correct thinking, and who regards the right use of language as both its tool and its safeguard, will count this necessity as a burden.

11. Let us next consider the case in which the predicate of the proposition is particular, for example "All men are mortal."

Here our meaning is clearly "All men are some mortal beings," and we must find the expression for the predicate, "some mortal beings." So let v stand for a class indefinite in every respect but one: some of its members are mortal beings. And let x stand for "mortal beings." Then vx will stand for "some mortal beings." So if y stands for men, the equation we want is y=vx. It reads: the men are some of the mortal beings, that is, the class of men is some part, we do not say which, of the class of mortals.

Editor's note: The indefinite class v is Boole's way of saying "some." Later logic stopped using it. Today "Some X are Y" is read as saying that the class of things that are both X and Y is not empty, and the idea of "some" became what logicians call the existential quantifier, "there exists at least one."

From these considerations we get the following Rule for expressing an affirmative universal proposition whose predicate is particular:

Rule.—Express as before the subject and the predicate, attach to the latter the indefinite symbol v, and equate the expressions.

Clearly v is a symbol of the same kind as x, y, and the rest, and it obeys the general law v2=v,orv(1−v)=0. that is, the indefinite class, like every class, taken together with itself is just itself.

So to express the proposition "The planets are either primary or secondary," we would follow the rule like this. Let x represent planets (the subject); y=primary bodies;z=secondary bodies; then, assuming that the word "or" separates the class of "primary" bodies completely from the class of "secondary" bodies, as far as they come into the proposition, we find as the equation of the proposition x=v{y(1−z)+z(1−y)}.(4) that is, the planets are some of the things that are either primary and not secondary, or secondary and not primary.

It is worth noticing that in this case the literal translation of the premises into the form x=v(y+z)(5) would be exactly equivalent, because v is an indefinite class symbol. Still, form (4) is the better one, because the expression y(1−z)+z(1−y) consists of terms that stand for classes quite distinct from each other, and it obeys the fundamental law of duality.

Take the proposition "The heavenly bodies are either suns, or planets, or comets," and represent these classes of things by w, x, y, z, respectively. If we suppose that none of the heavenly bodies belongs to two of these divisions at once, its expression will be w=v{x(1−y)(1−z)+y(1−x)(1−z)+z(1−x)(1−y)}

But suppose it were meant that the heavenly bodies were either suns, or, if not suns, planets, or, if neither suns nor planets, fixed stars. That meaning does not rule out some of them belonging at once to two, or to all three, of the divisions of suns, planets, and fixed stars. Then the expression required would be w=v{x+y(1−x)+z(1−x)(1−y)}.(6)

The examples above are descriptions, not definitions. In fact the predicates of propositions are usually particular. When they are not, either the predicate is a singular term (the name of one individual), or instead of the copula "is" or "are" we use some other form of connection that tells us the predicate is to be taken universally.

12. Consider next the case of universal negative propositions, for example "No men are perfect beings."

Plainly we are not speaking here of a class called "no men" and asserting that all its members are "perfect beings." What we are really doing is making an assertion about "all men": that they are "not perfect beings." So the true meaning of the proposition is this:

"All men (subject) are (copula) not perfect (predicate);" so if y stands for "men," and x for "perfect beings," we have y=v(1−x), that is, the men are some of the beings that are not perfect; and the same goes for any other case. So we have the following Rule:

Rule.—To express any proposition of the form "No x’s are y’s," convert it into the form "All x’s are not y’s," and then proceed as in the previous case.

13. Consider, last, the case in which the subject of the proposition is particular, for example "Some men are not wise." Here, as we have noted, the negative not may properly be attached, at least for the purposes of logic, to the predicate wise. We do not mean to say that it is untrue that "Some men are wise." We mean to say of "some men" that they lack wisdom. So the proper form of the proposition is "Some men are not-wise." Now put y for "men," and x for "wise," that is, "wise beings." Bring in v as the symbol of a class indefinite in every respect but this one: it contains some individuals of the class it is placed before. Then we have vy=v(1−x). It reads: some men are the same as some not-wise beings, that is, some part of the class of men lies inside the class of the not-wise.

14. We can gather everything we have settled into the following general Rule:

General Rule for the Symbolic Expression of Primary Propositions.

First, if the proposition is affirmative, form the expression of the subject and that of the predicate. If either of them is particular, attach to it the indefinite symbol v, and then equate the resulting expressions.

Second, if the proposition is negative, first express its true meaning by attaching the negative word to the predicate, then proceed as above.

One or two more examples should be enough to illustrate it.

Ex.—"No men are placed in exalted stations, and free from envious regards."

Let y stand for "men," x for "placed in exalted stations," and z for "free from envious regards."

Now the class described as "placed in exalted station" and "free from envious regards" is expressed by xz. So the opposite class, those to whom this description does not apply, will be represented by 1−xz, and all men are referred to this class. So we have y=v(1−xz). that is, the men are some of the beings who are not both highly placed and free from envy. If the proposition had been put in the equivalent form "Men in exalted stations are not free from envious regards," its expression would have been yx=v(1−z). We shall see later that this expression really is equivalent to the previous one, given the assumption involved, namely that v is an indefinite class symbol.

Ex.—"No men are heroes but those who unite self-denial to courage."

Let x = "men," y = "heroes," z = "those who practise self-denial," and w = "those who possess courage."

What is really asserted is that "men who do not possess courage and practise self-denial are not heroes."

So we have x(1−zw)=v(1−y) as the equation required: the men who do not have both self-denial and courage are some of the beings who are not heroes.

15. To close this chapter, it may be interesting to set side by side the great leading types of propositions as expressed in symbols. If we agree to let X and Y stand for the symbolic expressions of the "terms," the things related, these types will be X=vY,X=Y,vX=vY. In the first, only the predicate is particular; in the second, both terms are universal; in the third, both are particular. Some lesser forms are really included under these. For instance, if Y=0, the second form becomes X=0; which says that there is no such thing as an X; and if Y=1 it becomes X=1; which says that X is the whole universe of discourse. Both these forms can be interpreted. Notice also that the expressions X and Y, if they rest on a careful enough analysis of what the "terms" of the proposition mean, will obey the fundamental law of duality, which requires that X2=XorX(1−X)=0,Y2=YorY(1−Y)=0.

Chapter 5: Principles of Symbolic Reasoning

1. The chapters so far have done three things. They have investigated the fundamental laws of the operations of the mind in reasoning. They have shown how those laws become the laws of the symbols of logic. And they have set out the principles of expression by which one kind of proposition, the kind called primary, can be written in the language of symbols. All of this was, in the strictest sense, preparation. But it is preparation we cannot do without, because it leads to one of the chief aims of this book: to build a system, or method, of logic on an exact summary of the fundamental laws of thought. Before we start, I think it necessary to point out certain things about the nature of this aim and about the means of reaching it.

2. My first point is that a method in logic can be general only so far as its elementary processes and laws are general. Take one example. In the earlier sections we investigated, among other things, the laws of the logical process of addition, the process symbolized by the sign +. We found those laws by studying instances. In every one of those instances it was a necessary condition that the classes or things added together in thought should be mutually exclusive. Indeed the expression x+y seems to make no sense unless we assume that the things represented by x and the things represented by y are entirely separate, with no individuals in common. Conditions much like this one were also present in the acts of conception from which we learned the laws of the other symbolic operations. So a question arises. Must we restrict our use of these symbolic laws and processes by the same conditions of interpretability under which we first learned them? If we must, then plainly no general method in logic is possible. If we need not, then how are we to think about processes that seem to have no meaning in the very field of thought they are meant to serve? These questions do not belong to logic alone. They apply equally to every developed form of human reasoning that works through a symbolic language.

3. My second point is that this apparent failure of process and interpretation to match up never shows itself in the ordinary uses of human reason. There, no operation is performed whose meaning and use are not seen. Most minds are not satisfied when merely formal reasoning links their premises to their conclusions. Every step of the chain, every intermediate result established along the way, must make sense too. And no doubt this is both how ordinary reasoning actually works and an important safeguard in the reasoning and talk of everyday life.

Perhaps many people would want to extend the same principle to the general use of symbolic language as a tool of reasoning. They might argue like this. The laws or axioms that govern our use of symbols were established by studying only the cases in which interpretation is possible. So we have no right to apply them to other cases, where interpretation is impossible or doubtful, even if (as should be admitted) we apply them only in the intermediate steps of a proof. If this objection were conclusive, we would have to admit that a symbolic method in logic offers little advantage. Perhaps the advantage would shrink to the mechanical gain of using short, handy symbols in place of clumsier ones. But the objection itself is mistaken. Whatever we might expect à priori, it is an unquestionable fact that a conclusion reached by any symbolic process of reasoning is valid whether or not we can interpret the formal results that turned up at the different stages along the way. There are, in fact, certain general principles about the use of symbolic methods. I shall first state them as they apply to logic in particular, and then offer some remarks on their nature and on why they deserve to be accepted.

4. The conditions of valid reasoning with the help of symbols are these.

First, a fixed interpretation must be given to the symbols used to express the data, and the laws by which those symbols combine must be correctly worked out from that interpretation.

Second, the formal processes of solution or proof must be carried out from start to finish in obedience to all the laws found in this way, without asking whether the particular results obtained along the way can be interpreted.

Third, the final result must be interpretable in form, and it must actually be interpreted according to the same system of interpretation that was used to express the data. On these principles the following observations may be made.

5. The need for a fixed interpretation of the symbols has already been discussed enough (II. 3). The need for the final result to be in a form to which that interpretation can be applied rests on an obvious principle. Symbols are a means to an end, and the end is knowledge of some fact or truth we can understand. For that end to be reached, the final result, which expresses the symbolic conclusion, must be in an interpretable form. The greatest difficulty, however, is likely to be felt over the second of the general principles or conditions above (V. 4), and on this point a few more words are needed.

I would say, then, that this principle may be seen as resting on a general law of the mind. We do not know that law à priori, that is, before experience. We learn it the way we learn the other laws of the mind: by seeing the general principle clearly displayed in a particular instance. Take a single example of reasoning in which symbols are used according to laws founded on their interpretation, but without keeping that interpretation constantly in view, so that the chain of proof leads us through intermediate steps that cannot be interpreted to a final result that can. Such an example seems not only to establish that this particular application is valid, but also to reveal the general law at work in it. No pile of further instances can properly add weight to that evidence. More instances may give us a clearer idea of the common element of truth on which the principle rests, and so prepare us to accept it. Where someone does not feel the direct force of the evidence, they may serve as a check, à posteriori, that the principle works in practice. But none of this touches the point I am making: the general principle must be seen in the particular instance, seen to be general in its reach as well as true in the special example. The use of the uninterpretable symbol −1 in the intermediate steps of trigonometry illustrates what I mean. I believe there is no way of explaining that use which does not quietly assume the very principle in question. That principle is not, I think, justified by formal reasoning from any other grounds. But it seems to deserve a place among those self-evident truths which in some sense make general knowledge possible at all, and which may rightly be regarded as expressions of the mind's own laws and make-up.

6. Here is how this principle will be applied in the present work. We have seen that any system of propositions can be expressed by equations in symbols x, y, z. Wherever interpretation is possible, these symbols obey laws identical in form with the laws of a system of number symbols that can take only the values 0 and 1 (II. 15). But the formal processes of reasoning depend only on the laws of the symbols, not on what the symbols are taken to mean. So we are allowed to treat the symbols x, y, z as if they were number symbols of exactly that kind. In practice, we may set aside the logical meaning of the symbols in a given equation; turn them into number symbols that can take only the values 0 and 1; carry out on them, as numbers, every process the solution requires; and at the end give them back their logical meaning. This is the procedure actually used in this book, though I shall not stop each time to restate what kind of change has been made. When the symbols x, y, z are treated as numbers of this kind, the processes we apply to them are not bound by the conditions of thought that would bind them if they were applied to purely logical symbols. That gives us a freedom of operation without which the search for a general method in logic would be hopeless.

Now this system of processes would lead us to nothing intelligible unless the final equations it produced were in a form that could be interpreted once the symbols had their logical meaning back. There is, however, a general method of bringing equations into such a form, and the rest of this chapter is devoted to it. I shall say little here about how the method makes interpretation possible, since that question is kept for the next chapter. Instead I shall confine myself mostly to the process itself, which may be called a process of "development." Before describing it, a few observations will help.

7. Suppose we are looking at some class of things with one question in mind: which of its members have a certain property x, and which lack it? Every individual in the class either has the property or does not. So we can divide the class into two portions: those individuals that have the property, and those that do not. We can make this division in thought before we know anything else about how the class is made up. Whatever else we later learn can only tell us, more or less precisely, what further conditions hold for the portion that has the property and for the portion that lacks it. Suppose, then, we learn this much: the members that have the property x also have a certain property u, and these two conditions together are enough to define them. Then we can represent that portion of the original class by the expression ux (II. 6), that is, the things that are both u and x. Suppose we also learn that the members of the original class that do not have the property x satisfy a condition v, and are defined by it. Then clearly those members will be represented by the expression v(1−x), the things that are v and not x. So the class as a whole will be represented by ux+v(1−x); in words, the x's that are u, together with the not-x's that are v. This may be regarded as a general developed form for expressing any class of objects considered with respect to whether they have or lack a given property x.

The general form we have just reached on purely logical grounds can also be derived by a separate route, from the formal laws that the symbols x, y, z obey equally under their logical and under their numerical interpretation, as mentioned above (V. 6).

8. Definition.—Any algebraic expression containing a symbol x is called a function of x, and may be written in the short general form f(x). Any expression containing two symbols, x and y, is likewise called a function of x and y, and may be written in the general form f(x,y); and so on for any number of symbols.

So the form f(x) could stand for any of the following functions, for instance x, 1−x, 1+x1−x, and so on; and f(x,y) could stand equally for any of the forms x+y, x−2y, x+yx−2y, and so on.

By the same notation, if in any function f(x) we replace x by 1, the result is written f(1); if in the same function we replace x by 0, the result is written f(0). For example, if f(x) stands for the function a+xa−2x, then f(1) will stand for a+1a−2, and f(0) will stand for aa.

9. Definition.—Take any function f(x) in which x is a logical symbol, or a number symbol that can take only the values 0 and 1. The function is said to be developed when it has been brought into the form ax+b(1−x), with a and b chosen so that the result is equivalent to the function we started from. In words, a developed function says how much of it goes with the x's (the coefficient a) and how much with the not-x's (the coefficient b).

This definition assumes that any function f(x) can be written in this form. The following Proposition shows that the assumption is justified.

Proposition I.

10. To develop any function f(x) in which x is a logical symbol.

By the principle laid down in this chapter, we may lawfully treat x as a number symbol that can take only the values 0 and 1.

Let us assume, then, that f(x)=ax+b(1−x), and put x=1. The second term vanishes, because one minus one is zero, and we have f(1)=a. Next, in the same equation, put x=0. Now the first term vanishes, and we have f(0)=b. So the values of a and b are found. Substituting them in the first equation, we get f(x)=f(1)x+f(0)(1−x);(1) which is the development we were looking for. Read aloud, it says: the function equals what it becomes when x is 1, multiplied by x, plus what it becomes when x is 0, multiplied by one minus x. The right-hand side of this equation correctly represents the function f(x), whatever form that function may have. The reason is simple. Regarded as a number symbol, x can take only the values 0 and 1, and for each of these values the development f(1)x+f(0)(1−x), takes the same value as the function f(x). When x is 1, it reduces to the first coefficient; when x is 0, to the second; and those are exactly the values of the function itself.

Footnote: Some readers may be interested to notice that the development of f(x) found in this chapter holds, in the logical system, exactly the place that the expansion of f(x) in ascending powers of x holds in ordinary algebra. In fact it can be obtained by taking the well-known theorem of Taylor, namely f(x)=f(0)+f′(0)x+f′′(0)x21⋅2+f′′′(0)x31⋅2⋅3, &c.(1) and bringing in the condition x(1−x)=0. From that condition we find x2=x, x3=x, and so on, and so f(x)=f(0)+{f′(0)+f″(0)1⋅2+f‴(0)1⋅2⋅3+ &c.}x.(2) But putting x=1 in (1), we get f(1)=f(0)+f′(0)+f″(0)1⋅2+f‴(0)1⋅2⋅3+ &c. so that f′(0)+f″(0)1⋅2+ &c.=f(1)−f(0), and (2) becomes, on substitution, f(x)=f(0)+{f(1)−f(0)}x,=f(1)x+f(0)(1−x), which is the form in question. This proof assumes that f(x) can be expanded in a series of ascending powers of x, so it is less general than the one in the text.

As an illustration, suppose we are asked to develop the function 1+x1+2x. When x=1, we find f(1)=23, and when x=0, we find f(0)=11, or 1. So the required expression is 1+x1+2x=23x+1−x; and this equation holds for each of the values the symbol x can take. (Try it: with x equal to 1 both sides come to two-thirds, and with x equal to 0 both sides come to 1.)

Proposition II.

To expand or develop a function of any number of logical symbols.

Let us begin with the case of two symbols, x and y, and let us write the function to be developed as f(x,y).

First, we treat f(x,y) as a function of x alone and expand it by the general theorem (1). This gives f(x,y)=f(1,y)x+f(0,y)(1−x);(2) where f(1,y) stands for what the given function becomes when, in place of x, we write 1 in it; and f(0,y) stands for what the same function becomes when, in place of x, we write 0 in it.

Now we take the coefficient f(1,y), treat it as a function of y, and expand it in the same way. We get f(1,y)=f(1,1)y+f(1,0)(1−y),(3) where f(1,1) stands for what f(1,y) becomes when y is set equal to 1, and f(1,0) for what f(1,y) becomes when y is set equal to 0.

In the same way, the coefficient f(0,y) expands to f(0,y)=f(0,1)y+f(0,0)(1−y).(4) Now put into (2), in place of f(1,y) and f(0,y), their values from (3) and (4), and we have f(x,y)=f(1,1)xy+f(1,0)x(1−y)+f(0,1)(1−x)y(5)+f(0,0)(1−x)(1−y),(6) which is the expansion required. Here f(1,1) stands for what f(x,y) becomes when we set x=1, y=1 in it; f(1,0) for what f(x,y) becomes when we set x=1, y=0; and so on for the rest. In words, the four terms sort everything into four compartments: things that are x and y; things that are x but not y; things that are y but not x; and things that are neither. Each compartment is multiplied by the value the function takes when x and y are set to 1 or 0 to match it.

So, for example, if f(x,y) stands for the function 1−x1−y, we find f(1,1)=00,f(1,0)=01,f(0,1)=10,f(0,0)=1 and so the expansion of the given function is 00xy+0x(1−y)+10(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y). We shall see in the next chapter that the forms 00 and 10 have a very important logical interpretation in expressions like this one. The first of them, zero over zero, is known to mathematicians as the symbol of an indeterminate quantity.

Next, suppose the function to be expanded contains three symbols, so that we can write it in the general form f(x,y,z). Proceeding as before, we get f(x,y,z)=f(1,1,1)xyz+f(1,1,0)xy(1−z)+f(1,0,1)x(1−y)z+f(1,0,0)x(1−y)(1−z)+f(0,1,1)(1−x)yz+f(0,1,0)(1−x)y(1−z)+f(0,0,1)(1−x)(1−y)z+f(0,0,0)(1−x)(1−y)(1−z) where f(1,1,1) stands for what the function f(x,y,z) becomes when we set x=1, y=1, z=1 in it, and so on for the rest. With three symbols there are eight compartments, one for each way of having or lacking each of the three properties.

11. It is now easy to see the general law that governs the expansion of any given function, and to turn the method of expanding into a rule. But before stating that rule, it will help to make the following observations.

Each expansion we have obtained is made up of certain terms that contain the symbols x, y, and so on, multiplied by coefficients that do not contain those symbols. So the expansion of f(x) consists of the two terms x and 1−x, multiplied by the coefficients f(1) and f(0) respectively. And the expansion of f(x,y) consists of the four terms xy, x(1−y), (1−x)y, and (1−x)(1−y), multiplied by the coefficients f(1,1), f(1,0), f(0,1), f(0,0) respectively. The terms x, 1−x in the first case, and the terms xy, x(1−y), and so on in the second, we shall call the constituents of the expansion. Each constituent names one of the compartments described above: xy the things that are both x and y, x times one minus y the things that are x but not y, and so on down to the things that are neither. Clearly their form does not depend on the form of the function being expanded. In the constituent xy, the symbols x and y are called its factors.

The general rule of development will therefore have two parts. The first tells us how to form the constituents of the expansion; the second, how to find their coefficients. It runs as follows.

First. To expand any function of the symbols x, y, z.—Form a series of constituents in this way. Let the first constituent be the product of all the symbols. In this product change any one symbol, say z, into 1−z, to get the second constituent. Then in both of these change another symbol, say y, into 1−y, to get two more constituents. Then in the four constituents now obtained change another symbol, say x, into 1−x, to get four new ones; and so on, until there are no more symbols left to change. Each change doubles the list, so two symbols give four constituents, three give eight, and so on.

Second. To find the coefficient of any constituent.—If that constituent has x as a factor, change x into 1 in the original function; but if it has 1−x as a factor, change x into 0 in the original function. Do the same for the symbols y, z, and so on. The value of the function once all these changes are made, worked out in full, is the coefficient we want.

The sum of the constituents, each multiplied by its own coefficient, is the expansion required.

Editor's note: What Boole calls the development of a function into its constituents is what is now called its disjunctive normal form, and his constituents are what computer scientists call minterms. Listing all the constituents (two of them, then four, then eight, and so on) and keeping only the ones a premise allows is the very method Jevons teaches by hand in Lesson 23 of his Elementary Lessons in Logic, which is in this collection. It is also the ancestor of the truth table.

12. It is worth noticing that a function can be developed with respect to symbols it does not actually contain. Suppose, for example, that we follow the rule to develop the function 1−x with respect to the symbols x and y. We have,

Whenx=1andy=1the given function=0.
x=1"y=0" "=0.
x=0"y=1" "=1.
x=0"y=0" "=1.

So the development is 1−x=0xy+0x(1−y)+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y); and this is a true development. Adding the terms (1−x)y and (1−x)(1−y) gives back the function 1−x. In words: the not-x's are just the not-x's that are y together with the not-x's that are not y.

The symbol 1, developed by the rule with respect to the symbol x, gives x+1−x. Developed with respect to x and y, it gives xy+x(1−y)+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y). In the same way, developed with respect to any set of symbols, it produces a series made up of all the possible constituents of those symbols. Since 1 stands for the whole universe of discourse, this says that the compartments together fill the universe.

13. A few more remarks on the nature of these general expansions are in order. Let us take as our example the general theorem (5), the pattern of development for functions of two logical symbols.

First, that theorem is entirely true and meaningful when x and y are number symbols of the kind considered in this chapter, whatever algebraic form the function f(x,y) is given. So it may be used, with full meaning, at any stage of the work between the moment we change the symbols from their logical to their numerical interpretation, as described above, and the moment we finally give them back their logical interpretation.

Second, the theorem is entirely true and meaningful when x and y are logical symbols, provided the function f(x,y) has a form that represents a class or collection of things. In that case the right-hand side can always be interpreted logically. For instance, if f(x,y) stands for the function 1−x+xy, applying the theorem gives 1−x+xy=xy+0x(1−y)+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y),=xy+(1−x)y+(1−x)(1−y), and this result is both meaningful and true. Read in words, the function names the not-x's together with the x's that are y; the expansion names the same things compartment by compartment: the things that are x and y, the y's that are not x, and the things that are neither. Only the compartment of x's that are not y is left out.

So we may regard the theorem as true and meaningful for number symbols of the kind described always, and for logical symbols always when interpretable. Whenever it is used in this book, then, it must be understood that if the expansion obtained cannot be interpreted, the symbols x, y are being taken as number symbols of that particular kind.

But although the expansion cannot always be interpreted directly, it always leads us straight to results that can. For example, the expression x−y gives, on development, the form x(1−y)−y(1−x), which in general cannot be interpreted. We cannot, in thought, take away from the class of things that are x's and not y's the class of things that are y's and not x's, because the second class is not contained in the first. But suppose the form x−y appeared as the left-hand side of an equation whose right-hand side was 0. Then on development we should have x(1−y)−y(1−x)=0. Now it will be shown in the next chapter that this equation, with x and y regarded as number symbols of the kind described, splits at once into the two equations x(1−y)=0,y(1−x)=0, and these equations can be read directly in logic once the symbols x and y are given logical meanings: there is nothing that is x and not y, and nothing that is y and not x. In other words, the x's and the y's are the same things. It should also be remarked that although functions do not necessarily become interpretable when developed, equations can always be brought by this process into interpretable forms.

14. The following Proposition establishes some important properties of constituents. In stating it, the symbol t is used to stand for any constituent of an expansion, whichever it may be. So if the expansion is of a function of two symbols x and y, t stands for any of the four forms xy, x(1−y), (1−x)y, and (1−x)(1−y). Where we need to represent the constituents of an expansion by single symbols and still tell them apart, we shall mark the difference with subscripts. So t1 might be used for xy, t2 for x(1−y), and so on.

Proposition III.

Any single constituent t of an expansion satisfies the law of duality, whose expression is t(1−t)=0. The product of any two different constituents of an expansion is equal to 0, and the sum of all the constituents is equal to 1.

In words: nothing both belongs to a compartment and lies outside it; no two compartments share any member; and all the compartments together make up the universe of discourse.

First, take the particular constituent xy. We have xy×xy=x2y2. But x2=x, y2=y, by the fundamental law of class symbols; so xy×xy=xy. Or, representing xy by t, t×t=t, or t(1−t)=0. In the same way the constituent x(1−y) satisfies the same law. For we have x2=x,(1−y)2=1−y,∴{x(1−y)}2=x(1−y), or t(1−t)=0. Now every factor of every constituent has either the form x or the form 1−x. So the square of each factor equals that factor, and therefore the square of the product of the factors, that is, of the constituent, equals the constituent. So, with t standing for any constituent, we have t2=t, or t(1−t)=0.

Second, the product of any two constituents is 0. This follows plainly from the general law of the symbols expressed by the equation x(1−x)=0, which says that nothing is both x and not x. For whichever two constituents of the same expansion we take, there will be at least one factor x in the one matched by a factor 1−x in the other.

Third, the sum of all the constituents of an expansion is unity, that is, 1. This is plain when we add the two constituents x and 1−x, or the four constituents xy, x(1−y), (1−x)y, (1−x)(1−y). But it is also proved, and more generally, by expanding 1 in terms of any set of symbols (V. 12). The constituents in that case are formed as usual, and all the coefficients are unity.

15. With the Proposition above we may connect the following one.

Proposition IV.

If V stands for the sum of any series of constituents, each with coefficient 1, then the condition V(1−V)=0 is satisfied. In words, any collection of whole compartments, taken together, obeys the law of duality just as a single class symbol does.

Let t1, t2 …tn be the constituents in question. Then V=t1+t2…+tn. Squaring both sides, and noting that t12=t1, t1t2=0, and so on, we have V2=t1+t2…+tn; so that V=V2. Therefore V(1−V)=0.

Chapter 6: Of Interpretation

1. We have seen that when any function is fully expanded by the general rule proved in the last chapter, the expansion is made of two distinct sets of elements: the constituents of the expansion, and their coefficients (the numbers standing in front of them). In this chapter I will ask, first, how the constituents are to be interpreted, and then how that interpretation is changed by the coefficients attached to them.

I will use the terms "logical equation," "logical function," and the like in a general sense. They mean any equation or function involving the symbols x, y, and so on, that turns up either in expressing a set of premises or in the chain of symbolic results that runs between the premises and the conclusion. If such a function or equation is in a form that cannot be read straight off in logic, then the symbols x, y, and so on, must be treated as symbols of quantity of the special kind described in earlier chapters (II. 15), (V. 6): quantities that obey the law x(1−x)=0. that is, quantities that can only be 0 or 1.

So by the problem of the interpretation of a logical function or equation, I mean two things. The first is to reduce it to a form which becomes readable once the symbols x, y, and so on, are given their logical meanings. The second is the reading that results. These agreed definitions follow the general principles for conducting the method of this book, laid down in the last chapter.

Proposition I.
