2. The constituents of the expansion of any function of the logical symbols x, y, and so on, can be interpreted. They stand for the separate, non-overlapping divisions of the universe of discourse that we get by affirming and denying, in every possible combination, the qualities the symbols x, y, and so on, denote.

To make this concrete, suppose the function involves two symbols, x and y, and has been expanded with respect to both. The constituents are then: xy,x(1−y),(1−x)y,(1−x)(1−y). Clearly the first, xy, stands for the class of things that have both of the qualities named by x and y. The second, x(1−y), stands for the class that has the property x but not the property y. In the same way the third constituent stands for things that have the property represented by y but not the one represented by x. And the fourth, (1−x)(1−y), stands for things that have neither quality.

So in this case the constituents stand for all four classes of things that can be described by affirming or denying the properties expressed by x and y. These classes are distinct. No member of one is a member of another, because each class has some quality that contradicts a quality of every other class. And together they make up the universe. Any object at all can be described by whether it has or lacks a given quality, so every single thing in the universe falls into one or other of the four classes formed by combining the two given classes x and y and their contraries (their opposites, "not-x" and "not-y").

What has been said here about the constituents of f(x,y) holds in general. The constituents of any expansion stand for classes; those classes are kept distinct by having contrary qualities; and together they make up the universe of discourse.

3. These properties of constituents are expressed in the theorems proved at the end of the last chapter, and could have been deduced from them. Every constituent obeys the fundamental law that the single symbols obey; from that, one might have guessed that each constituent stands for a class. The product of any two constituents of an expansion is zero; from that, one might have concluded that the classes they stand for exclude one another. And the sum of all the constituents of an expansion is 1; from that, one might have inferred that their classes together make up the universe.

4. The analysis and interpretation of logical equations rest on these laws of constituents and on the way of interpreting them just set out. We have already said that every such equation can be interpreted by means of the theorem of development. Here I want to examine the forms of solution that come out at the end of a train of reasoning, and to show how they arise. Strictly speaking they are all versions of one basic type of expression. Still, it will be clearer to present their minor varieties one at a time.

There are three such forms, as follows:

Form I.

5. The first form arises when a logical equation V=0 is developed, broken up into its component equations, and the result is to be interpreted. We assume the function involves the logical symbols x, y, and so on, in combinations that are not fractions. Fractions in fact arise only in the kind of problem we will meet under the third form of solution.

Proposition II.

To interpret the logical equation V=0.

For simplicity, suppose V involves just two symbols, x and y, and write the development of the given equation as axy+bx(1−y)+c(1−x)y+d(1−x)(1−y)=0;(1) where a, b, c, and d are definite numbers.

Now suppose some coefficient, say a, is not zero. Multiply both sides of the equation by the constituent xy that this coefficient belongs to. Since the product of two different constituents is zero, every other term drops out, and we have axy=0, and so, since a is not zero, xy=0, This result does not depend at all on what the other coefficients are. Giving x and y their logical meaning, it reads: "No individuals exist that belong both to the class represented by x and to the class represented by y."

But if the coefficient a is zero, the term axy does not appear in the development (1), and we cannot deduce xy=0 from it.

In the same way, if the coefficient b is not zero, we have x(1−y)=0, which reads: "There are no individuals that belong to the class x and do not belong to the class y."

Either of these readings can also be put in a different form, as we will show later.

Taken together, the separate readings we get from all the terms of the expansion whose coefficients are not zero make up the complete interpretation of the equation V=0. The argument does not depend on how many logical symbols the function V contains. So the aim of the proposition is always reached by the following Rule:

Rule.—Develop the function V, and set equal to 0 every constituent whose coefficient is not zero. The readings of these results, taken together, make up the interpretation of the given equation.

6. As an example, take the definition of "clean beasts" in the Jewish law (Leviticus 11): "Clean beasts are those which both divide the hoof and chew the cud." Let

x = clean beasts;
y = beasts dividing the hoof;
z = beasts chewing the cud;

Then the proposition is represented by the equation x=yz that is, the clean beasts are exactly the beasts that both divide the hoof and chew the cud. We bring it to the form x−yz=0, and look for the kind of interpretation this method leads to. Developing the left-hand side fully, we get 0xyz+xy(1−z)+x(1−y)z+x(1−y)(1−z)−(1−x)yz+0(1−x)y(1−z)+0(1−x)(1−y)z+0(1−x)(1−y)(1−z). The terms whose coefficients are not zero give xy(1−z)=0,xz(1−y)=0,x(1−y)(1−z)=0,(1−x)yz=0. These equations deny that certain classes of things exist. They deny:

First, beasts that are clean and divide the hoof but do not chew the cud.

Second, beasts that are clean and chew the cud but do not divide the hoof.

Third, beasts that are clean and neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud.

Fourth, beasts that divide the hoof and chew the cud but are not clean.

All of these denials are really contained in the original proposition. And the other way round: grant these denials, and the original proposition follows necessarily. They are, in fact, the separate pieces of that proposition. In this way every primary proposition can be broken down into a series of denials that certain defined classes of things exist, and can be rebuilt from that set of denials. Someone may ask how an assertion can be made out of a series of denials. Where does the positive part come from? My answer is that the mind assumes the existence of a universe. It does not assume it à priori, as a fact independent of experience. It assumes it either à posteriori, as something learned from experience, or hypothetically, as the ground that makes assertive reasoning possible at all. Take the proposition "There are no men who are not fallible." It is a denial: it denies that "infallible men" exist. From it we may infer either hypothetically, "All men (if men exist) are fallible," or absolutely, since experience has assured us that the human race exists, "All men are fallible."

The form in which this Proposition's method presents its conclusions may be called the form of "Single or Conjoint Denial."

Form II.

7. The previous form came from developing and interpreting an equation whose right-hand side is 0. The present form, which complements it, comes from developing and interpreting an equation whose right-hand side is 1. The analysis of the last Proposition points straight to it.

In the example just discussed, we deduced from the equation x−yz=0 a joint denial that the classes represented by the constituents xy(1−z),xz(1−y),x(1−y)(1−z),(1−x)yz, exist, since their coefficients were not 0. It follows that the remaining constituents stand for classes that together make up the universe. So we have xyz+(1−x)y(1−z)+(1−x)(1−y)z+(1−x)(1−y)(1−z)=1. This amounts to saying that everything that exists belongs to one or other of the following classes:

First, clean beasts that both divide the hoof and chew the cud.

Second, unclean beasts that divide the hoof but do not chew the cud.

Third, unclean beasts that chew the cud but do not divide the hoof.

Fourth, things that are not clean beasts, do not chew the cud, and do not divide the hoof.

This form of conclusion may be called the form of "Single or Disjunctive Affirmation": single when only one constituent appears in the final equation, disjunctive when, as here, more than one does.

Any equation V=0 in which V obeys the law of duality can also be made to yield this form of interpretation. We rewrite it as 1−V=1 and develop the left-hand side. But this case is really included in the next general form. Both of the forms so far are of little importance next to the one that follows.

Form III.

8. In the two cases so far, the function to be developed was set equal to 0 and to 1 respectively. Now I will suppose it set equal to any logical symbol w. Our task is then to interpret the equation V=w, where V is a function of the logical symbols x, y, z, and so on. First, though, I think it necessary to show how the equation V=w, or, as it will usually appear, w=V, comes about.

Let us go back to the definition of "clean beasts" used in the previous examples: "Clean beasts are those which both divide the hoof and chew the cud." Suppose we want to find how "beasts chewing the cud" are related to "clean beasts" and "beasts dividing the hoof." The equation expressing the proposition is x=yz, and we will have what we want if we can find z as an interpretable function of x and y.

Treating x, y, z as symbols of quantity subject to their special law, we can solve the equation above to get z=xy.

But this equation is not yet in a form we can read. If we can bring it to such a form, it will give us the relation we want.

Developing the right-hand side of the equation, we get z=xy+10x(1−y)+0(1−x)y+00(1−x)(1−y), and we will show later (Prop. 3) that it can be read as follows:

"Beasts which chew the cud consist of all clean beasts (which also divide the hoof), together with an indefinite remainder (some, none, or all) of unclean beasts which do not divide the hoof."

9. This is one case of a problem of the widest generality in logic, which can be stated like this: "Given any logical equation connecting the symbols x, y, z, w, find an interpretable expression for the relation of the class represented by w to the classes represented by the other symbols x, y, z, and so on."

In every case the solution consists in finding, from the given equation, an expression for the symbol w in terms of the other symbols, and then making that expression readable by development. Now the given equation is always of the first degree in each of its symbols (no symbol appears squared, since the square of each equals the symbol itself). So the expression for w can always be found. In fact, whatever the form of the given equation with respect to w, if we develop it we get an equation of the form Ew+E′(1−w)=0,(1) where E and E′ are functions of the remaining symbols. In words: E is what multiplies the class w, and E′ what multiplies everything outside it. From this we have E′=(E′−E)w. Therefore w=E′E′−E(2) and once the right-hand side is expanded by the rule of development, all that is left is to interpret the result in logic by the next proposition.

If the fraction E′E′−E has factors common to its top and bottom, we are not allowed to cancel them unless they are mere numbers. The reason is that the symbols x, y, and so on, taken as quantities, may take such values of 0 and 1 as make the common factors equal to 0, and then the algebraic rule of cancelling fails. This is the case we had in mind when we remarked on the failure of the algebraic axiom of division (II. 14). The course this book follows is strictly in line with its general principles: we express the solution in the form (2), attempt no unauthorized cancelling, and interpret the result by the theorem of development.

If we want the relation of the class expressed by 1−w to the other classes x, y, and so on, we deduce from (1), just as above, 1−w=EE−E′, and the method of the following Proposition applies to interpreting this as well.

Proposition III.

10. To find the interpretation of any logical equation of the form w=V, where w is a class symbol and V is a function of other class symbols, of any form whatever.

Expand the right-hand side of the equation fully. Each coefficient in the result will fall into one of four kinds. We now take them in turn, with what each means.

First, let the coefficient be 1. This is the symbol of the universe, and the product of two class symbols stands for the individuals found in both classes. So any constituent with 1 as its coefficient must be read without limit: the whole of the class it stands for is included.

Second, let the coefficient be 0. In logic, just as in arithmetic, this is the symbol of Nothing. No part of the class represented by its constituent is to be taken.

Third, let the coefficient have the form 00. In arithmetic the symbol 00 stands for an indefinite number, unless some special circumstance fixes it. So analogy suggests that in the system of this book the same symbol should stand for an indefinite class. The following example will make clear that this is its true meaning.

Take the proposition "Men not mortal do not exist." Let us put it into symbols, and then, obeying the laws those symbols have been shown to follow, look for a reverse definition: a definition of "mortal beings" in terms of "men."

If we let y stand for "men" and x for "mortal beings," the proposition "Men who are not mortals do not exist" is expressed by the equation y(1−x)=0, from which we are to find the value of x. The equation above gives y−yx=0, or yx=y. that is, the men who are mortal are all the men there are. If this were an ordinary algebraic equation, our next step would be to divide both sides by y. But we remarked in Chap. II. that the operation of division cannot be performed with the symbols we are now using. What we can do instead is express the division, and then develop the result by the method of the last chapter. So we have, first, x=yy, and, expanding the right-hand side as directed, x=y+00(1−y). This says that mortals (x) consist of all men (y), together with whatever remainder of beings who are not men (1−y) the coefficient 00 indicates. Now let us ask what remainder of "not men" the premise implies. The remainder might include all the beings who are not men; it might include some of them and not others; or it might include none. Any one of these suppositions fits our premise perfectly. In other words, the premise in effect asserts that all men are mortal, and its truth is untouched whether all, some, or none of the beings who are not men are mortal. So the expression 00 here means that all, some, or none of the class it is attached to are to be taken.

This account of the meaning of the symbol 00 rests on one particular case. But the principle behind the argument is general, and the symbol can turn up in no circumstances where the same analysis would not apply. We may properly call 00 an indefinite class symbol, and, where convenient, replace it by a single symbol v, subject to the fundamental law v(1−v)=0.

Fourth, a coefficient of a constituent in an expansion may belong to none of the kinds above. To find its true meaning in that case, we must first prove the following theorem.

11. Theorem.—If a function V, meant to represent some class or collection of objects w, is expanded, and if the numerical coefficient a of any constituent in its development does not satisfy the law a(1−a)=0, then the constituent in question must be set equal to 0. In words: if a coefficient is anything other than 0 or 1, its constituent must be empty.

To prove the theorem in general, write the given expansion in the form w=a1t1+a2t2+a3t3+&c.,(1) where t1, t2, t3, and so on, are the constituents and a1, a2, a3, and so on, the coefficients. Suppose also that a1 and a2 do not satisfy the law a1(1−a1)=0,a2(1−a2)=0; but that all the other coefficients do obey it, so that we have a32=a3, &c. Now multiply each side of equation (1) by itself. The result is w=a12t1+a22t2+ &c.(2) This is clear because it must be the development of the equation w=V2, (and the square of w is just w). But it can also be proved by actually squaring (1) and noting that t12=t1,t22=t2,t1t2=0, &c. by the properties of constituents. Now subtracting (2) from (1), we have (a1−a12)t1+(a2−a22)t2=0. or, which is the same thing, a1(1−a1)t1+a2(1−a2)t2=0. Multiply this last equation by t1. Then, since t1t2=0, we have a1(1−a1)t1=0, whence t1=0. In the same way, multiplying the same equation by t2, we have a2(1−a2)t2=0, whence t2=0. (In each case the number in front is not zero, so the constituent itself must be.)

In this way it can be shown in general that any constituent whose coefficient does not obey the same fundamental law as the symbols themselves must be set equal to 0 on its own. Such coefficients usually appear in the form 10. This is the algebraic symbol of infinity. And the closer a number comes to infinity (if we may put it that way), the further it is from satisfying the fundamental law just mentioned.

The symbol 00, whose meaning we discussed earlier, does not necessarily break the law we are now considering, since it can take the numerical values 0 and 1 equally well. But its actual meaning, as an indefinite class symbol, cannot in my view be deduced from its arithmetical properties, except on the ground of analogy. It has to be established by trial, as we did above.

Editor's note: Boole's division, and the symbols 0/0 and 1/0, are formal devices, not arithmetic. A coefficient 0/0 marks an indefinite portion of a class (the v of Chapter IV), and a coefficient 1/0 marks a constituent that must be empty. His contemporaries found this the hardest part of the book, and Jevons, Venn and Peirce rebuilt the algebra without any division at all; modern Boolean algebra has none. His conclusions are correct; only his route to them was abandoned.

12. We can now gather the results we have reached into the following summary.

First, the symbol 1, as the coefficient of a term in a development, means that the whole of the class that constituent stands for is to be taken.

Second, the coefficient 0 means that none of the class is to be taken.

Third, the symbol 00 means that a completely indefinite portion of the class is to be taken: that is, some, none, or all of its members.

Fourth, any other symbol as a coefficient means that the constituent it stands in front of must be set equal to 0.

It follows that if the solution of a problem, found by development, has the form w=A+0B+00C+10D, that solution can be split into the two following equations: w=A+vC,(3)D=0,(4) where v is an indefinite class symbol. Equation (3) says that the class w is all of A together with some, none, or all of C; equation (4) says that the class D has no members. The reading of (3) shows what elements make up, or may make up, the class w whose definition we want. The reading of (4) shows what relations hold among the elements of the original problem, quite independently of w.

These are the rules of interpretation. I may add that they apply universally, and that using them never runs into an exception or a failure.

13. Corollary.—If V is an independently interpretable logical function, it will satisfy the symbolic law V(1−V)=0.

By an independently interpretable logical function I mean one that can be interpreted without assuming any relation among the things its symbols stand for. So x(1−y) is independently interpretable, but x−y is not. The second function assumes, as a condition of its having any meaning, that the class represented by y is wholly contained in the class represented by x. The first makes no such demand.

Now suppose V is independently interpretable, and let w stand for the collection of individuals it contains. Then the equation w=V holds true without forcing any of the constituents in the development of V to vanish, since a vanishing constituent would mean some relation among the classes of things the symbols in V denote. So the development of V will have the form a1t1+a2t2+&c. with the coefficients a1, a2, and so on, all satisfying the condition a1(1−a1)=0,a2(1−a2)=0,&c. that is, every coefficient is 0 or 1.

So, by the reasoning of Prop. 4, Chap. v., the function V will obey the law V(1−V)=0. that is, nothing is both in the class V and outside it.

This result is obvious à priori, since V is supposed to stand for a class or collection of things. But we now see that it also follows from the properties of the constituents that make it up. The condition V(1−V)=0 may be called "the condition of interpretability of logical functions."

14. The general form of solution, or of logical conclusion, set out in the last Proposition may be called a "Relation between terms." As before, I use the word "terms" for the parts of a proposition, simple or complex, that are joined by the copula "is" or "are." The classes of things represented by the single symbols may be called the elements of the proposition.

15. Ex. 1.—Going back to the definition of "clean beasts" (VI.6), we want a description of "unclean beasts."

As before, with x standing for "clean beasts," y for "beasts dividing the hoof," and z for "beasts chewing the cud," we have x=yz;(5) so 1−x=1−yz; and developing the right-hand side, 1−x=y(1−z)+z(1−y)+(1−y)(1−z); which reads as the following proposition: Unclean beasts are all those which divide the hoof without chewing the cud, all those which chew the cud without dividing the hoof, and all those which neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud.

Ex. 2.—With the same definition, we want a description of beasts that do not divide the hoof.

From the equation x=yz we have y=xz; therefore, 1−y=z−xz; and developing the right-hand side, 1−y=0xz+−10x(1−z)+(1−x)z+00(1−x)(1−z). Here, by the Rule, the term whose coefficient is −10 must be set equal to 0 on its own, and so we have 1−y=(1−x)z+v(1−x)(1−z),x(1−z)=0; The first of these equations reads as the proposition: Beasts which do not divide the hoof consist of all unclean beasts which chew the cud, and an indefinite remainder (some, none, or all) of unclean beasts which do not chew the cud.

The second equation reads as the proposition: There are no clean beasts which do not chew the cud. This is one of the independent relations mentioned above. We were looking for the direct relation of "beasts not dividing the hoof" to "clean beasts" and "beasts which chew the cud." But it happens that the premise also sets up a separate relation between clean beasts and beasts that chew the cud, quite apart from any relation to beasts not dividing the hoof. The process necessarily gives us this relation too.

Ex. 3.—Take the following definition: "Responsible beings are all rational beings who are either free to act, or have voluntarily sacrificed their freedom," and apply the same analysis to it.

Letxstand forresponsible beings.
y"rational beings.
z"those who are free to act,
w"those who have voluntarily sacrificed their freedom of action.

In expressing this definition, I will assume that its two alternatives, "rational beings free to act" and "rational beings whose freedom of action has been voluntarily sacrificed," exclude each other, so that no one is found in both. This lets us translate the proposition literally into the language of symbols, as follows: x=yz+yw.(6) that is, the responsible beings are the rational beings who are free, together with the rational beings who have given up their freedom.

First let us find from this the relation of "rational beings" to responsible beings, beings free to act, and beings who have voluntarily given up their freedom of action. Perhaps it is better to put our aim this way: we want to express the relation among the elements of the premise in a form that lets us decide how far rationality can be inferred from responsibility, freedom of action, a voluntary sacrifice of freedom, and their opposites.

From (6) we have y=x(z+w), and developing the right-hand side, but leaving out the terms whose coefficients are 0, y=12xzw+xz(1−w)+x(1−z)w+10x(1−z)(1−w)+00(1−x)(1−z)(1−w), so, setting equal to 0 the terms whose coefficients are 12 and 10, we have y=xz(1−w)+xw(1−z)+v(1−x)(1−z)(1−w);(7) xzw=0;(8) x(1−z)(1−w)=0;(9) and these read as follows.

Direct Conclusion.—Rational beings are all responsible beings who are either free to act, not having voluntarily sacrificed their freedom, or not free to act, having voluntarily sacrificed their freedom, together with an indefinite remainder (some, none, or all) of beings not responsible, not free, and not having voluntarily sacrificed their freedom.

First Independent Relation.—No responsible beings are at the same time free to act, and in the condition of having voluntarily sacrificed their freedom.

Second.—No responsible beings are not free to act, and at the same time in the condition of not having sacrificed their freedom.

The independent relations just found can, however, be put in another and handier form. Thus (8) gives xw=0z=0z+00(1−z), on development; or, xw=v(1−z);(10) and in the same way (9) gives x(1−w)=01−z=00z+0(1−z); or, x(1−w)=vz;(11) and (10) and (11), interpreted, give the following propositions:

First, Responsible beings who have voluntarily sacrificed their freedom are not free.

Second, Responsible beings who have not voluntarily sacrificed their freedom are free.

These, however, are only different forms of the relations found before.

16. In looking at these results, the reader must remember that the only business of a method of inference or analysis is to find the relations required by the connexion of the terms in the original proposition, that is, by the way the proposition joins them. So in judging how completely the method does its job, we have nothing at all to do with other relations that the meaning of the words may suggest to us, as distinct from their stated connection. For example, it seems obvious that "They who have voluntarily sacrificed their freedom are not free." That relation is implied in the very meaning of the words. So it might seem that the first of the two independent relations the method gave us is, on the one hand, needlessly narrow, and on the other, unnecessary. But if we look only at how the terms are connected in the original premise, we will see that the relation is open to neither charge. The solution, given by the direct conclusion and the independent relations together, is perfectly complete, and nothing in it is superfluous.

If we want to take into account the unstated relation just mentioned, "They who have voluntarily sacrificed their freedom are not free," we can do so by making it a separate proposition. Its proper expression would be w=v(1−z). that is, those who have sacrificed their freedom are some portion of those who are not free.

We would then have to use this equation together with the one expressing the original premise. How such an examination is to be carried out will appear when we come to the theory of systems of propositions in a later chapter. The only difference this makes to the result is that the first of the independent relations found above is replaced.

17. Ex. 4.—Taking the same definition as in Example 2, we want a description of irrational persons.

We have 1−y=1−xz+w=z+w−xz+w =12xzw+0xz(1−w)+0x(1−z)w−10x(1−z)(1−w)+(1−x)zw+(1−x)z(1−w)+(1−x)(1−z)w+00(1−x)(1−z)(1−w)=(1−x)zw+(1−x)z(1−w)+(1−x)(1−z)w+v(1−x)(1−z)(1−w)=(1−x)z+(1−x)(1−z)w+v(1−x)(1−z)(1−w), together with xzw=0,x(1−z)(1−w)=0.

The independent relations here are the same ones we reached before, as they clearly ought to be. Whatever relations hold regardless of whether a given class of things y exists must also hold regardless of whether the opposite class 1−y exists.

The direct solution given by the first equation is: Irrational persons consist of all irresponsible beings who are either free to act, or have voluntarily sacrificed their liberty and are not free to act; together with an indefinite remainder of irresponsible beings who have not sacrificed their liberty and are not free to act.

18. The propositions analyzed in this chapter have all been of the kind called definitions. I have discussed none whose second term, the predicate, is particular (that is, speaks only of "some"). The general type of such propositions is Y=vX, where Y and X are functions of the logical symbols x, y, z, and so on, and v is an indefinite class symbol. Their analysis is made much easier, though the step is not essential, by eliminating the symbol v, and that process depends on the method of the next chapter. I also put off another important problem needed to complete the theory of single propositions, because its analysis really depends on the method of reducing systems of propositions, which will be developed later in this work.

Chapter 7: On Elimination

1. In the examples of the last chapter, every element of the original premise came back in the conclusion, only in a different order and with a different connection. But in ordinary reasoning, and especially when there is more than one premise, it is more usual for some of the elements to be kept out of the conclusion. Such elements are commonly called "middle terms." We may think of them as brought into the original propositions only to help set up a connection among the other elements, and those other elements alone are meant to appear in the conclusion.

2. Some mistaken ideas are current about these intermediate elements, or middle terms. It is a general opinion, though the examples of the last chapter contradict it, that inference consists above all in eliminating such terms (combining the premises so that a term drops out). On this view, the basic pattern of the process is the elimination of one middle term from two premises, giving a single conclusion in which that term no longer appears. So it is commonly held that the syllogism is the basis, or at least the common type, of all inference, and that any inference, however complex its form and structure, can be broken down into a series of syllogisms. Whether this view is right will be considered in a later chapter. For now I want to point to a difference, important but so far unnoticed, between the system of logic expressed in symbols and the system of ordinary algebra, in the matter of elimination. In algebra we can eliminate one symbol from two equations, two symbols from three equations, and in general n−1 symbols from n equations. So there is a fixed connection between the number of independent equations we are given and the number of number symbols we can eliminate from them. In logic it is otherwise. There is no fixed connection between the number of equations representing propositions or premises and the number of class symbols that can be eliminated. From a single equation any number of such symbols may be eliminated. On the other hand, from any number of equations, only a single class symbol may be eliminated. We may say that in this unusual system the problem of elimination can be solved in every case alike. This follows from that remarkable law of duality which the symbols of logic obey. To the equations supplied by the given premises, another equation, or system of equations, is added. It is drawn from the fundamental laws of thought themselves, and it supplies what is needed to solve the problem. Of the many consequences of the law of duality, this is perhaps the one that most deserves attention.

3. In algebra, eliminating symbols from a system of equations often leads to a mere identity of the form 0=0, which means that no independent relations connect the symbols that remain. The same thing can happen in logic, and it means the same thing there. This does not weaken the general principle just stated. The method we are about to take up aims to eliminate any number of symbols from any number of logical equations, and to show in the result whatever relations actually remain. It may be that none remain. In that case the method proves its soundness by leading us to a proposition that says nothing, a mere identity.

4. The notation in the Propositions that follow is like that of the last chapter. By f(x) is meant any expression containing the logical symbol x, with or without other logical symbols. By f(1) is meant what f(x) becomes when x is changed into 1 throughout it; by f(0), what the same function becomes when x is changed into 0.

Proposition I.

5. If f(x)=0 is any logical equation containing the class symbol x, with or without other class symbols, then the equation f(1)f(0)=0 will be true, whatever x is taken to mean; and it will be the complete result of eliminating x from the equation we started with. In words: the function with x put equal to 1, multiplied by the function with x put equal to 0, gives nothing.

In other words, we eliminate x from any given equation, f(x)=0, by changing x into 1 in that equation, then changing x into 0, and multiplying the two resulting equations together.

In the same way, the complete result of eliminating any class symbols, x, y, etc.,from any equation of the form V=0, is obtained as follows. Fully expand the left-hand side of the equation in constituents of those symbols; multiply together all the coefficients of those constituents (the numbers standing in front of the compartments); and set the product equal to 0.

Developing the left-hand side of the equation f(x)=0, we have (V. 10) f(1)x+f(0)(1−x)=0;or, [f(1)−f(0)]x+f(0)=0.(1)∴x=f(0)f(0)−f(1);and 1−x=−f(1)f(0)−f(1). Now put these expressions for x and 1−x into the fundamental equation x(1−x)=0, which says that nothing is at once an x and not an x. The result is −f(0)f(1)[f(0)−f(1)]2=0;or, f(1)f(0)=0,(2) which is the form we wanted.

6. This process shows that the elimination really takes place between the given equation f(x)=0 and the equation x(1−x)=0, which is true always and everywhere, because it expresses the fundamental law of logical symbols, qua logical (that is, insofar as they are logical). So we never need more than one premise, or equation, to make it possible to eliminate a term. The necessary law of thought in effect supplies the other premise or equation. The proof of this conclusion can be set out in other forms, but the same element, supplied by the mind itself, will still be present in effect. For instance, we could proceed as follows.

Multiply (1) by x, and we have f(1)x=0,(3) and let us try to eliminate x from this equation and (1) by the methods of ordinary algebra.

Now if we have two algebraic equations of the form ax+b=0, a′x+b′=0; it is well known that the result of eliminating x is ab′−a′b=0(4) But comparing that pair of equations with (1) and (3) respectively, we find a=f(1)−f(0),b=f(0); a′=f(1)b′=0; and these, put into (4), give f(1)f(0)=0, as before. In this form of the proof, the fundamental equation x(1−x)=0 shows up in the step that takes us from (1) to (3).

7. I shall add one more form of the proof. It is half logical in character, and it may show this important theorem in a clearer light.

We have, as before, f(1)x+f(0)(1−x)=0. Multiply this equation first by x, and then by 1−x, and we get f(1)x=0f(0)(1−x)=0. From these, by solving and developing, we have f(1)=0x=00(1−x), on development,f(0)=01−x=00x. Read directly, these equations say two things.

First, whatever individuals are included in the class represented by f(1) are not x's.

Second, whatever individuals are included in the class represented by f(0) are x's.

So, by ordinary logic, there are no individuals that are at once in the class f(1) and in the class f(0); that is, there are no individuals in the class f(1)f(0). Therefore f(1)f(0)=0.(5) Or it would be enough to multiply the two developed equations together, and the result would follow at once.

8. The theorem (5) gives us the following Rule:

To Eliminate any Symbol from a Proposed Equation.

Rule.—First bring all the terms of the equation over to the left-hand side, if necessary. Then give the symbol the value 1, and then the value 0, and multiply the two resulting equations together.

This proves the first part of the Proposition.

9. Next, consider the general equation f(x,y)=0; whose left-hand side stands for any function of x, y, and other symbols.

By what we have shown, the result of eliminating y from this equation will be f(x,1)f(x,0)=0; for that is the form we reach by changing y into 1 in the given equation, then y into 0, and multiplying the results together.

Now take this result, change x into 1, then x into 0, and multiply the results together. We get f(1,1)f(1,0)f(0,1)f(0,0)=0;(6) as the final result of elimination. But the four factors on the left-hand side of this equation are exactly the four coefficients of the complete expansion of f(x,y), the left-hand side of the original equation. So the second part of the Proposition is plain.

Examples.

10. Ex. 1.—We are given the Proposition "All men are mortal," and its symbolic expression in the equation y=vx, where y stands for "men" and x for "mortals." The task is to eliminate the indefinite class symbol v and to interpret the result.

Bringing the terms over to the left-hand side, we have y−vx=0. When v=1 this becomes y−x=0; and when v=0 it becomes y=0; and these two equations, multiplied together, give y−yx=0, or y(1−x)=0, since y2=y.

This last equation is the result of elimination we wanted. It says that there are no men who are not mortals, and its interpretation is: Men who are not mortal do not exist. That is an obvious conclusion.

Now suppose we use this last equation to look for a description of beings who are not mortal. We have x=yy, ∴1−x=0y. So, by expansion, 1−x=00(1−y): the not-mortals are some, none, or all of the things that are not men. Interpreted, this gives: They who are not mortal are not men. This is an example of what ordinary logic calls conversion by contraposition, or negative conversion (turning "All men are mortal" into "Whatever is not mortal is not a man").

Footnote: Whately’s Logic, Book II. chap. II. sec. 4.

Ex. 2.—Take the Proposition "No men are perfect," represented by the equation y=v(1−x), where y stands for "men" and x for "perfect beings." The task is to eliminate v, and from the result to find a description both of perfect beings and of imperfect beings. We have y−v(1−x)=0. So, by the rule of elimination, {y−(1−x)}×y=0, or y−y(1−x)=0, or yx=0; that is, the class of things both men and perfect is empty. This reads as the Proposition: Perfect men do not exist. From that equation we have x=0y=00(1−y)by development; in words, the perfect beings are some, none, or all of the things that are not men. So, by interpretation: No perfect beings are men. Similarly, 1−x=1−0y=yy=y+00(1−y), that is, the imperfect beings are all the men, plus some, none, or all of what is not a man. Interpreted, this gives: Imperfect beings are all men with an indefinite remainder of beings, which are not men.

11. In handling propositions, it will generally be most convenient to eliminate the indefinite class symbol v first, wherever it appears in the equations. This only changes their form; it does not change what they mean. Let us apply this step to one of the examples of Chap. IV. For the Proposition "No men are placed in exalted stations and free from envious regards," we found the expression y=v(1−xz), and for the equivalent Proposition "Men in exalted stations are not free from envious regards," the expression yx=v(1−z); and we observed that these equations, with v an indefinite class symbol, were themselves equivalent. To prove it, we need only eliminate the symbol v from each. The first equation is y−v(1−xz)=0, so, putting first v=1 and then v=0, and multiplying the results, we have (y−1+xz)y=0,or yxz=0. Now the second of the given equations becomes, when its terms are moved across, yx−v(1−z)=0;whence (yx−1+z)yx=0,or yxz=0, the same as before. The reader will easily interpret the result: there is nothing that is at once a man, in an exalted station, and free from envious regards.

12. Ex. 3.—As material for the general method of this chapter, we will take up again Mr. Senior's definition of wealth, namely: "Wealth consists of things transferable, limited in supply, and either productive of pleasure or preventive of pain." As remarked earlier, we shall take this definition to include all things that have both of the qualities named in its last part. On that assumption, our equation is w=st{pr+p(1−r)+r(1−p)},or w=st{p+r(1−p)}, where

wstands forwealth.
s"things limited in supply.
t"things transferable.
p"things productive of pleasure.
r"things preventive of pain.

From this equation we can eliminate any symbols we do not wish to take into account. We can then express the result, by solving and developing, with whatever arrangement of subject and predicate we choose.

Let us first ask what the expression for w, wealth, would be if we eliminated the element r, which refers to the prevention of pain. Bringing the terms of the equation over to the left-hand side, we get w−st(p+r−rp)=0. Putting r=1, the left-hand side becomes w−st, and putting r=0 it becomes w−stp. So, by the Rule, we have (w−st)(w−stp)=0(7) or w−wstp−wst+stp=0;(8) and so w=stpst+stp−1; and developing the right-hand side of this equation gives w=stp+00st(1−p).(9) This gives us the conclusion: Wealth consists of all things limited in supply, transferable, and productive of pleasure, and an indefinite remainder of things limited in supply, transferable, and not productive of pleasure. That is obvious enough.

Notice that we do not have to carry out the multiplication shown in (7), and reduce that equation to the form (8), in order to find the expression for w in terms of the other symbols. Development can always take the place of multiplication. For instance, if we develop (7) with respect to w, we find (1−st)(1−stp)w+stp(1−w)=0, and so w=stpstp−(1−st)(1−stp); and this equation, developed, gives the same result as before: w=stp+00st(1−p).

13. Suppose next that we want a description of things limited in supply, in terms of how they stand to wealth, to transferability, and to the tendency to produce pleasure, leaving out all reference to the prevention of pain.

From equation (8), which is the result of eliminating r from the original equation, we have w−s(wt+wtp−tp)=0; and so s=wwt+wtp−tp=wtp+wt(1−p)+10w(1−t)p+10w(1−t)(1−p)+0(1−w)tp+00(1−w)t(1−p)+00(1−w)(1−t)p+00(1−w)(1−t)(1−p). We will first give the direct interpretation of this solution, term by term. Then we shall make some general remarks it suggests. Finally, we shall show how the conclusion can be stated a little more briefly.

First, then, the direct interpretation is this. Things limited in supply consist of all wealth that is transferable and productive of pleasure; all wealth that is transferable and not productive of pleasure; and an indefinite amount of what is not wealth, but is either transferable and not productive of pleasure, or intransferable and productive of pleasure, or neither transferable nor productive of pleasure.

To this, the terms whose coefficient is 10 let us add the following independent relations, namely:

First, Wealth that is intransferable, and productive of pleasure, does not exist.

Second, Wealth that is intransferable, and not productive of pleasure, does not exist.

14. I expect the following remarks to be made about this solution.

First, it may be said that in the expression we found for "things limited in supply," the term "All wealth transferable," and so on, is partly redundant. For all wealth is necessarily transferable: the original proposition implies it, and the independent relations state it outright.

My answer is this. In ordinary speech, once another part of our reasoning had shown that there is no wealth that is not transferable, we would not think it necessary to add the word "transferable" to "wealth." But part of what makes this method perfect is that it always defines completely the objects named by each term of the conclusion. It does so by stating how they stand to every quality, every mark of distinction, that we have chosen to use. This is needed to keep the different parts of the solution truly distinct and independent, and it actually prevents redundancy. Suppose the pair of terms we have been looking at had not contained the word "transferable," and had together made up just "All wealth." We could then logically split the single term "All wealth" into two terms, "All wealth transferable" and "All wealth intransferable." But the "independent relations" show that the second of these vanishes. So it is no part of the description we want, and is therefore redundant. The remaining term matches the conclusion we actually obtained.

Solutions that cannot, by any logical division, be made to yield superfluous or redundant terms may be called pure solutions. All the solutions given by the method of development and elimination explained above are of this kind. It is worth noticing that if we used the ordinary algebraic method of elimination, in the cases where that method can be used in this system, we could not count on the solutions being pure. Its lack of generality would not be its only defect.

15. Second, it will be remarked that the conclusion contains two terms whose combined meaning would be more conveniently expressed by a single term. Instead of "All wealth productive of pleasure, and transferable" and "All wealth not productive of pleasure, and transferable," we could simply say "All wealth transferable." This remark is quite fair. But notice that whenever such simplifications are possible, the form of the equation we have to interpret points them out at once; and if that equation is brought to its simplest form, the interpretation it leads to will be in its simplest form too. Thus in the original solution, the terms wtp and wt(1−p), which have unity (that is, 1) as their coefficient, add up to wt; the terms w(1−t)p and w(1−t)(1−p), which have 10 as their coefficient, add up to w(1−t); and the terms (1−w)(1−t)p and (1−w)(1−t)(1−p), which have 00 as their coefficient, add up to (1−w)(1−t). So the complete solution is s=wt+00(1−w)(1−t)+00(1−w)t(1−p), with the independent relation w(1−t)=0, or w=00t. The interpretation would now read like this.

First, things limited in supply consist of all wealth that is transferable, together with an indefinite remainder of what is not wealth and not transferable, and of transferable articles that are not wealth and are not productive of pleasure.

Second, All wealth is transferable.

This is the simplest form in which the general conclusion, with the condition that goes with it, can be stated.

16. When we need to eliminate two or more symbols from an equation, we can either use (6) Prop. I., or eliminate them one after another; the order does not matter. From the equation w=st(p+r−pr), we have already eliminated r, and found the result w−wst−wstp+stp=0. Suppose we had been asked to eliminate both r and t. Taking the step above as the first stage of the process, it remains to eliminate t from this last equation. When t=1, the left-hand side of that equation becomes w−ws−wsp+sp, and when t=0, the same side becomes w. So we have w(w−ws−wsp+sp)=0, or w−ws=0, as the result of elimination we wanted: there is no wealth that is not limited in supply.

If we use this last result to find w, we have w=01−s=00s, so "All wealth is limited in supply." Since p does not appear in the equation, this clearly holds no matter how the elements of the conclusion stand to the quality "productive of pleasure."

Going back to the original equation, suppose we are asked to eliminate s and t. We have w=st(p+r−pr). Instead of eliminating s and t one at a time by the Rule, however, it is enough to treat st as a single symbol, since it satisfies the fundamental law of the symbols, by the equation st(1−st)=0. So we write the given equation in the form w−st(p+r−pr)=0; and, putting st equal first to 1 and then to 0 and taking the product of the results, we have (w−p−r+pr)w=0,or w−wp−wr+wpr=0, as the result we were looking for. In words: there is no wealth that is neither productive of pleasure nor preventive of pain.

As a particular illustration, suppose we are asked to find an expression for "things productive of pleasure" (p) in terms of "wealth" (w) and "things preventive of pain" (r).

Solving the equation, we have p=w(1−r)w(1−r) =00wr+w(1−r)+00(1−w)r+00(1−w)(1−r) =w(1−r)+00wr+00(1−w). This gives the following conclusion: Things productive of pleasure are all wealth not preventive of pain, an indefinite amount of wealth that is preventive of pain, and an indefinite amount of what is not wealth.

From the same equation we get 1−p=1−w(1−r)w(1−r)=0w(1−r), and this, developed, gives 1−p=00wr+00(1−w)⋅r+00(1−w)⋅(1−r)=00wr+00(1−w). So: Things not productive of pleasure are either wealth, preventive of pain, or what is not wealth.

Any similar case could be worked out just as easily.

17. In the last example we eliminated the compound symbol st from the given equation by treating it as a single symbol. The same method works for any combination of symbols that satisfies the fundamental law obeyed by each single symbol. For instance, the expression p+r−pr, multiplied by itself, gives itself back. So if we stand for p+r−pr by a single symbol, say y, the fundamental law will be obeyed, since the equation y=y2, or y(1−y)=0, will be satisfied. The rule of elimination for symbols rests on the assumption that each single symbol obeys that law. So whenever a function or combination of such symbols obeys the law too, it can be eliminated from an equation in a single operation.

The forms of interpretation used in this chapter and the last show, perhaps better than any others, what the symbols 1 and 00 directly mean. But other ways of putting things, closer to everyday speech, are just as true and just as proper. For example, equation (9) can be read like this: Wealth is either limited in supply, transferable, and productive of pleasure, or limited in supply, transferable, and not productive of pleasure. And, the other way round: Whatever is limited in supply, transferable, and productive of pleasure, is wealth. Reverse readings like this one are always available when the final development brings in terms whose coefficient is unity.

18. Note.—The fundamental equation f(1)f(0)=0, which gives the result of eliminating the symbol x from any equation f(x)=0, admits of a remarkable interpretation.

Remember that the equation f(x)=0 stands for some proposition that speaks of the individuals in the class x, say "men," perhaps together with other individuals. Our aim is to find out whether the proposition implies any relation among those other individuals that does not depend on the class men. Now the equation f(1)=0 says what the original proposition would become if men made up the whole universe, and the equation f(0)=0 says what it would become if men ceased to exist. So the equation f(1)f(0)=0 says what, given the original proposition, would be true on either assumption alike: true whether "men" were "all things" or "nothing." The theorem therefore says that whatever is true both when a given class of objects takes in the whole universe and when it vanishes from existence is independent of that class altogether, and vice versâ. Here we have another example of formal results, drawn directly from the mathematical laws of thought, being interpreted as general axioms of philosophy.

Chapter 8: On the Reduction of Systems of Propositions

1. In the preceding chapters we worked out, well enough for the most essential purposes, the theory of single primary propositions; or, to put it more exactly, of primary propositions expressed by a single equation. On that theory we built a method that does the job. We showed how to eliminate any element from the given system of equations, and how to deduce the relation that connects the elements left over, in whatever form is asked for: a denial, an affirmation, or the more usual relation of subject and predicate. What remains is to turn to systems of propositions, and to carry out the same series of investigations for them. We want to know three things. Can we eliminate, ad libitum (as many as we please), any number of the symbols from the equations that express a system of propositions? Can we then deduce, by interpreting the result, every relation that holds among the symbols that remain? And can we find, in particular, the expression of any single element, or of any meaningful combination of elements, in terms of the others, so as to state the conclusion in whatever acceptable form is wanted? The answer to all three will come from showing that any system of equations, or any of the equations in a system, can be reduced to a single equation that is equivalent to it. To that single equation the methods of the previous chapters can be applied at once. We will see, too, that this reduction brings with it an important extension of the theory of single propositions, one we had to do without in the earlier discussion. There is nothing unusual about this. Many special branches of science cannot be fully surveyed from the inside. They have to be studied from an outside point of view as well, and seen in connection with other, related subjects, before their full proportions can be understood.

This chapter will set out two distinct ways of reducing a system of equations to a single equivalent equation. The first uses arbitrary constant multipliers (numbers with no fixed value, multiplied into the equations). It is simple enough in theory, but it makes the later steps of elimination and development, when they come, rather tedious. It was, however, the method of reduction I discovered first, and partly for that reason, partly for its simplicity, I have thought it right to keep it. The second method needs no arbitrary constants, and is better than the first in nearly every respect. So it is the one I will generally use in the rest of this book.

2. We turn to the first method.

Proposition I.

Any system of logical equations can be reduced to a single equivalent equation. Multiply each equation after the first by a different arbitrary constant, and add all the results together, the first equation included.

By Prop. 2, Chap, VI., the interpretation of any single equation f(x,y..)=0 is found by setting equal to 0 those constituents in the development of the left-hand side whose coefficients are not zero. So if we are given two equations, f(x,y..)=0, and F(x,y..)=0, their combined meaning is contained in the set of results we get by setting equal to 0 every constituent that shows up in this way in both, or in either, of the given equations, each developed by the Rule of Chap. VI. For instance, suppose we have the two equations xy−2x=0,(1) x−y=0;(2) and see what each yields.

The development of the first gives −xy−2x(1−y)=0; whence, xy=0,x(1−y)=0.(3) That is, nothing is both x and y, and nothing is x without being y.

The development of the second equation gives x(1−y)−y(1−x)=0; whence, x(1−y)=0,y(1−x)=0.(4) The constituents whose coefficients are not zero, in one development or the other, are xy, x(1−y), and (1−x)y. Together these give the system xy=0,x(1−y)=0,(1−x)y=0;(5) which is equivalent to the two systems the developments give separately, since the equation x(1−y)=0 simply appears in both. Keeping to the case of a pair of equations, then, what we have to find is a single equation which, when developed, yields the same constituents with nonzero coefficients as the given equations do. Now suppose the given equations are V1=0,V2=0, V1 and V2 being functions of the logical symbols x,y,z, &c. Then the single equation V1+cV2=0,(6) c being an arbitrary constant, will do what we want. For let At stand for any term in the full development V1, where t is a constituent and A its numerical coefficient, and let Bt stand for the matching term in the full development of V2. Then the matching term in the development of (6) will be (A+cB)t. The coefficient of t is zero if A and B are both zero, and not otherwise. To see this, suppose A and B are not both zero, and at the same time suppose A+cB=0,(7) then only the following cases can arise.

First, A is zero and B is not. Then the equation above becomes cB=0, and this requires c=0. But that contradicts the assumption that c is an arbitrary constant.

Second, B is zero and A is not. Then (7) reduces to A=0, which breaks the very assumption we started from.

Third, neither A nor B is zero. Then equation (7) gives c=−AB which is a definite value, and so again conflicts with the assumption that c is arbitrary.

So the coefficient A+cB is zero when A and B are both zero, and not otherwise. It follows that exactly the same constituents appear with nonzero coefficients in the development of (6) as in the equations V1=0,V2=0, taken singly or together. And so the equation V1+cV2=0, is equivalent to the system V1=0,V2=0.

By the same kind of reasoning, the general system of equations V1=0,V2=0,V3=0, &c.; can be replaced by the single equation V1+cV2+c′V3+ &c.=0, c,c′, &c., being arbitrary constants. The equation formed this way can be handled in every respect like the ordinary logical equations of the previous chapters. The arbitrary constants c1,c2, &c., are not logical symbols. They do not obey the law c1(1−c1)=0,c2(1−c2)=0. that is, they are not restricted to the values 0 and 1. But bringing them in is justified by the general principle stated in (II. 15) and (V. 6), and used in nearly all our investigations since: equations in the symbols of logic may be treated in every respect as if those symbols were symbols of quantity, subject to the special law x(1−x)=0, until, at the final stage of the solution, they take a form that can be read in the system of thought that logic deals with.

3. The following example will show the method at work.

Ex. 1.—Suppose that a study of the properties of some particular class of substances has led to the following general conclusions.

First, wherever the properties A and B occur together, either the property C or the property D is present as well, but not both together.

Second, wherever the properties B and C occur together, the properties A and D are either both present with them or both absent.

Third, wherever the properties A and B are both absent, the properties C and D are both absent too; and the other way round, wherever C and D are both absent, A and B are both absent too.

From these, suppose we are asked what can be concluded in any particular case from the presence of the property A, about whether the properties B and C are present or absent, leaving the property D out of account. Let us set up the symbols as follows.

Representthe property A by x;
"the property B by y;
"the property C by z;
"the property D by w.

Then the symbolic expression of the premises will be xy=v{w(1−z)+z(1−w)};yz=v{xw+(1−x)(1−w)};(1−x)(1−y)=(1−z)(1−w). In words: the things that are x and y are some of those that are w but not z, or z but not w; the things that are y and z are some of those that are both x and w, or neither; and the things that are neither x nor y are exactly the things that are neither z nor w.

From the first two of these equations, eliminating the indefinite class symbol v from each separately, we have xy(1−w(1−z)−z(1−w))=0; yz(1−xw−(1−x)(1−w))=0. Now we notice that by development 1−w(1−z)−z(1−w)=wz+(1−w)(1−z), and 1−xw−(1−x)(1−w)=x(1−w)+w(1−x), and in these expressions we write, for simplicity, a bar over a letter for "one minus" that letter, replacing 1−x by x‾,1−y by y‾,&c., so that a barred letter means "not" that class. We then get from the last three equations xy(wz+w‾z‾)=0;(1)yz(xw‾+x‾w)=0;(2)x‾y‾=w‾z‾;(3) and from this system we have to eliminate w.

Multiplying the second of these equations by c, and the third by c′, and adding the results to the first, we have xy(wz+w‾z‾)+cyz(xw‾+x‾w)+c′(x‾y‾−w‾z‾)=0. When w is set equal to 1, and so w‾ to 0, the left-hand side of this equation becomes xyz+cx‾yz+c′x‾y‾. And when in the same expression w is set to 0 and w‾ = 1, it becomes xyz‾+cxyz+c′x‾y‾−c′z‾. So the result of eliminating w can be written as the product of these two, set equal to zero: (xyz+cx‾yz+c′x‾y‾)(xyz‾+cxyz+c′x‾y‾−c′z‾)=0;(4) and from this equation we have to find x.

If we went on as in earlier examples, we would multiply out the factors on the left-hand side of this equation. But it is worth showing that this is not needed at all. Let us develop the left-hand side of (4) with respect to x, the symbol whose expression we want. We find yz(yz‾+cyz−c′z‾)x+(cyz+c′y‾)(c′y‾−c′z‾)(1−x)=0; or, cyzx+(cyz+c′y‾)(c′y‾−c′z‾)(1−x)=0; from which we find x=(cyz+c′y‾)(c′y‾−c′z‾)(cyz+c′y‾)(c′y‾−c′z‾)−cyz; and, developing the right-hand side with respect to y and z, x=0yz+00yz‾+c′2c′2y‾z+00y‾z‾; or, x=(1−y)z+00y(1−z)+00(1−y)(1−z); or, x=(1−y)z+00(1−z); Here the coefficient that is a number divided by itself counts as 1, so the things that are z but not y are all among the x's, while of the things that are not z, an indefinite portion are x's. The interpretation is: Wherever the property A is present, either C is present and B absent, or C is absent. And the other way round: Wherever the property C is present and the property B absent, the property A is present.

These results can be reached much more easily by the method I will explain next. Still, it is reassuring to have different routes to the same conclusion, so that each can check the other.

4. We turn to the second method.

Proposition II.

Suppose some equations, V1=0, V2=0, &c., are such that when their left-hand sides are developed, every constituent has a positive coefficient. Then those equations can be combined into a single equivalent equation simply by adding them.

For, as before, let At stand for any term in the development of the function V1, Bt the matching term in the development of V2 and so on. Then the matching term in the development of the equation V1+V2+&c.=0,(1) formed by adding the given equations together, will be (A+B+&c.)t. But by assumption none of the coefficients A, B, &c. is negative. So the combined coefficient A+B, &c. in the new equation can be zero only when the separate coefficients A, B, &c. are all zero together: positive numbers cannot cancel one another out. So the same constituents will appear in the development of equation (1) as in the equations V1=0, V2=0, &c. of the original system taken together. And therefore the interpretation of equation (1) is equivalent to the combined interpretations of the separate equations it was built from.

Proposition III.

5. Let V1=0,V2=0,&c. be any system of equations whose terms have all been moved to the same side. Then the combined interpretation of the system is contained in the single equation V12+V22+&c.=0, formed by adding together the squares of the given equations.

For let any equation of the system, say V1=0, produce on development an equation a1t1+a2t2+&c.=0 in which t1,t2,&c. are constituents, and a1,a2,&c. their coefficients. Then the equation V12=0 will produce on development the equation a12t1+a22t2+&c.=0, with each coefficient squared. This can be proved either from the law of development, or by squaring the function a1t1+a2t2,&c. under the conditions t12=t1, t22=t2,, t1t2=0 laid down in Prop. 3, Chap. v.; that is, each constituent times itself is itself, and any two different constituents multiplied together give zero. So the constituents that appear in the expansion of the equation V12=0, are the same as those that appear in the expansion of the equation V1=0, and now they have positive coefficients, since a square is never negative. The same holds for the equations V2=0,&c. So, by the last Proposition, the equation V12+V22+&c.=0 will be equivalent in interpretation to the system of equations V1=0, V2=0, &c.

Corollary.—Any equation V=0, whose left-hand side already satisfies the condition V2=V, or V(1−V)=0, does not need squaring, since squaring would leave it unchanged. Such equations, in fact, develop at once into a series of constituents with coefficients equal to 1, Chap. v. Prop. 4.

Proposition IV.

6. Suppose the equations of a system have been brought, by the squaring process above or by any other process, to a form in which every constituent in their development has a positive coefficient. Then any equations derived from them by elimination will have the same character, and may be combined with the other equations by addition.

Suppose we have to eliminate a symbol x from an equation V=0, in which none of the constituents in the full development of the left-hand side has a negative coefficient. That expansion can be written in the form V1x+V0(1−x)=0 V1 and V0 each being of the form a1t1+a2t2...+antn, in which t1t2...tn are constituents of the other symbols, and a1a2...an are in each case positive numbers or zero. The result of elimination is V1V0=0; that is, the part multiplying x times the part multiplying one minus x, set equal to zero. And since none of the coefficients in V1 and V0 is negative, there can be no negative coefficients in the product V1V0. So the equation V1V0=0 can be added to any other equation whose constituents all have positive coefficients, and the resulting equation will carry the full meaning of the equations it came from.

Proposition V.

7. To draw from the previous Propositions a practical rule, or method, for reducing systems of equations that express propositions in logic.

The investigations so far have established two points.

First, any equations of the form V=0, where V satisfies the fundamental law of duality V(1−V)=0, can be combined by simple addition.

Second, any other equations of the form V=0 can be brought, by squaring, to a form where the same principle of combining by mere addition applies.

All that remains, then, is to settle which equations, among those that actually express propositions, belong to the first class and which to the second.

Now the general types of propositions were set out at the end of Chap. IV. The division of propositions they represent is as follows.

First, propositions whose subject is universal and whose predicate is particular.

The symbolic type (IV. 15) is X=vY, that is, the X's are some of the Y's, with X and Y satisfying the law of duality. Eliminating v, we have X(1−Y)=0,(1) that is, nothing is an X that is not a Y; and this, we will find, also satisfies the same law. No further reduction by squaring is needed.

Second, propositions both of whose terms are universal, of the symbolic type X=Y, with X and Y each satisfying the law of duality. Writing the equation in the form X−Y=0, and squaring, we have X−2XY+Y=0,or, X(1−Y)+Y(1−X)=0.(2) that is, there is nothing that is X but not Y, and nothing that is Y but not X. The left-hand side of this equation satisfies the law of duality, as its very form makes plain.

We can reach the same equation another way. The equation X=Y is equivalent to the two equations X=vY, Y=vX, (for to say that the X’s are identical with the Y’s is to say both that All X’s are Y’s, and that All Y’s are X’s). Now these equations give, on eliminating v, X(1−Y)=0, Y(1−X)=0, and these, added together, produce (2).

Third, propositions both of whose terms are particular. Such propositions have the form vX=vY, but here v is not entirely arbitrary, and so must not be eliminated. For v stands for some, and though its meaning can include all, it does not include none. So we must move the right-hand side over to the left and square the resulting equation, according to the rule. The result will plainly be vX(1−Y)+vY(1−X)=0. It may be convenient to sum up these conclusions in a Rule, to guide us from now on.

8. Rule.— Express the equations so that the terms X and Y in the following typical forms obey the law of duality. Then change the equations X=vY into X(1−Y)=0, X=Y into X(1−Y)+Y(1−X)=0. vX=vY into vX(1−Y)+vY(1−X)=0.

An equation given in the form X=0 needs no transformation. An equation in the form X=1 can be replaced by 1−X=0, as the second of the transformations above shows.

Once the equations of the system have been reduced in this way, any of them, together with any equations derived from them by elimination, can be combined by addition.

9. Note.—We saw in Chapter IV. that if we translate the terms of a proposition into symbols word for word, without attending to its real meaning, we may produce equations whose terms X and Y do not obey the law of duality. The equation w=st(p+r), given in (3) Prop. 3 of that chapter, is of this kind. Such equations, as we saw, do have a meaning. If, out of curiosity or for any other reason, someone decides to use them, it is best to reduce them by the Rule (VI. 5).

10. Ex. 2.—Let us take the following propositions of elementary geometry.

First, similar figures consist of all those whose corresponding angles are equal and whose corresponding sides are proportional.

Second, triangles whose corresponding angles are equal have their corresponding sides proportional, and vice versâ (the other way round).

To represent these premises, let

s=similar.
t=triangles.
q=having corresponding angles equal.
r=having corresponding sides proportional.

Then the premises are expressed by the following equations: s=qr,(1)tq=tr.(2) that is, the similar figures are exactly those with equal angles and proportional sides, and the triangles with equal angles are exactly the triangles with proportional sides. Reducing by the Rule (or, what comes to the same thing, moving the terms of each equation to the left-hand side, squaring each equation, and then adding), we have s+qr−2qrs+tq+tr−2tqr=0.(3) Suppose we are asked for a description of dissimilar figures in terms of the elements named by the words triangles, having corresponding angles equal, and having corresponding sides proportional.

From (3) we have s=tq+qr+rt−2tqr2qr−1,∴1−s=qr−tq−rt+2tqr−12qr−1.(4) And developing the right-hand side in full, we find 1−s=0tqr+2tq(1−r)+2tr(1−q)+t(1−q)(1−r)+0(1−t)qr+(1−t)q(1−r)+(1−t)r(1−q)+(1−t)(1−q)(1−r).(5)

In this development two of the terms have the coefficient 2. By the Rule these must be set equal to 0. Then, dropping the terms whose coefficients are 0, we have 1−s=t(1−q)(1−r)+(1−t)q(1−r)+(1−t)r(1−q)+(1−t)(1−q)(1−r);(6)tq(1−r)=0;(7)tr(1−q)=0;(8) and the direct interpretation of these is as follows.

First, dissimilar figures consist of all triangles that do not have both their corresponding angles equal and their sides proportional; and of all figures that are not triangles and that have either their angles equal and sides not proportional, or their corresponding sides proportional and angles not equal, or neither their corresponding angles equal nor their corresponding sides proportional.

Second, there are no triangles whose corresponding angles are equal and whose sides are not proportional.

Third, there are no triangles whose corresponding sides are proportional and whose angles are not equal.

11. These are the immediate interpretations of the final equation. We see, just as the general theory says, that when we work out a description of one particular class of objects (here, dissimilar figures) in terms of certain other elements of the original premises, we also get the independent relations that hold among those elements because of the same premises. It is easy to show that this is not wasted information, even for the immediate question we asked. For one thing, the independent relations can always be used, if we wish, to shorten the expression of the relation we were directly looking for. Thus if we write (7) in the form 0=tq(1−r), and add it to (6), we get, since t(1−q)(1−r)+tq(1−r)=t(1−r),1−s=t(1−r)+(1−t)q(1−r)+(1−t)r(1−q)+(1−t)(1−q)(1−r), which, interpreted, gives as the first part of the description of dissimilar figures "Triangles whose corresponding sides are not proportional," in place of the fuller description we had at first. Whether such a reduction is worth making is always a matter of convenience.

12. One reduction is always worth making (VII. 15): gathering the terms of the description we want, such as the right-hand side of (5) or (6), into as few groups as possible. Thus the third and fourth terms on the right-hand side of (6) add up to the single term (1−t)(1−q). If we combine this reduction with the last one, we have 1−s=t(1−r)+(1−t)q(1−r)+(1−t)(1−q), and the interpretation of this is:

Dissimilar figures consist of all triangles whose corresponding sides are not proportional, and of all figures that are not triangles and that have either their corresponding angles unequal, or their corresponding angles equal but their sides not proportional.

So the fullness of the general solution is not something extra we could do without. It gives us all the information we are looking for, and it also gives us the means of stating that information in whatever way suits us best.

13. One more observation remains to be made, illustrating a principle already stated. Two of the terms in the full development of 1−s in (5) have 2 as their coefficient, instead of 10. It will be shown later that this means the two premises were not independent of each other. To check this, let us go back to the premises in their reduced forms, namely s(1−qr)+qr(1−s)=0,tq(1−r)+tr(1−q)=0. Now if the left-hand sides of these equations have any constituents in common, those will show up when we multiply the equations together. Doing so, we get stq(1−r)+str(1−q)=0. From this follow stq(1−r)=0, str(1−q)=0, and these are equations that can be deduced from either of the original premises. Their interpretations are as follows.

Similar triangles that have their corresponding angles equal have their corresponding sides proportional.

Similar triangles that have their corresponding sides proportional have their corresponding angles equal.

And these conclusions can be deduced from either premise on its own. In this respect, by the definitions laid down, the premises are not independent.

14. To finish, let us go back to the problem we used to illustrate the first method of this chapter, and try to find, by the present method, what can be concluded from the presence of the property C about the properties A and B.

On eliminating the symbols v we found the following equations: xy(wz+w‾z‾)=0,(1)yz(xw‾+x‾w)=0,(2)x‾y‾=w‾z‾.(3) From these we have to eliminate w and find z. Now (1) and (2) already satisfy the condition V(1−V)=0. The third equation, when we move its terms to the left-hand side and square, gives x‾y‾(1−w‾z‾)+w‾z‾(1−x‾y‾)=0.(4) Adding (1) (2) and (4) together, we have xy(wz+w‾z‾)+yz(xw‾+x‾w)+x‾y‾(1−w‾z‾)+w‾z‾(1−x‾y‾)=0. Eliminating w, we get (xyz+yzx‾+x‾y‾){xyz‾+yzx+x‾y‾z+z‾(1−x‾y‾)}=0. Now when we multiply the terms of the second factor by those of the first in turn, remembering that xx‾=0, yy‾=0, zz‾=0, (nothing is both a class and its opposite), nearly all of them vanish, and we are left with only xyz+x‾y‾z=0;(5) that is, nothing is z together with both x and y, or z with neither. From this, z=0xy+x‾y‾ =0xy+00xy‾+00x‾y+0x‾y‾ =00xy‾+00x‾y, which gives the interpretation: wherever the property C is found, either the property A or the property B will be found with it, but not both of them together.

From equation (5) we can easily deduce the result we reached earlier by the method of arbitrary constant multipliers, as well as any other requested form of the relation between x, y, and z. For example: If the property B is absent, either A and C will be present together, or C will be absent. And conversely, If A and C are present together, B will be absent. The converse part of this conclusion rests on the presence of a term xz with unity for its coefficient in the developed value of y‾.

Chapter 9: On Certain Methods of Abbreviation

1. The three fundamental methods set out and illustrated in the previous chapters, development, elimination, and reduction, are enough for every practical purpose of logic. Still, there are cases where they can be simplified a great deal, and this is especially true of elimination. Those cases are the subject of this chapter. I will first prove some propositions that contain the principles of these shortcuts, and afterwards apply them to particular examples.

Let us call any terms that satisfy the fundamental law V(1−V)=0 class terms. Each such term, taken alone, is a constituent. But when several occur together, they need not all involve the same symbols, as the terms of a development must. So ax+bxy+cyz can be described as an expression made of three class terms, x, xy, and yz, multiplied by the coefficients a, b, c respectively. The principle used in the next two Propositions, which in some cases shortens elimination a great deal, is the rejection of superfluous class terms. A term counts as superfluous if it adds nothing to the constituents of the final result.

Proposition I.

2. Take any equation V=0 in which V is a series of class terms with positive coefficients. From it we may throw out any term that contains another term as a factor, and we may change every positive coefficient to unity (that is, 1).

Here is why. What a series of positive terms means depends only on the number and kind of the constituents in its final expansion, that is, its expansion with respect to all the symbols it contains. It does not depend at all on the actual values of the coefficients (VI. 5). Now let x be any term of the series, and xy any other term that has x as a factor. The expansion of x with respect to the symbols x and y is xy+x(1−y), and the expansion of the sum of the terms x and xy is 2xy+x(1−y).

By what has just been said, these two expressions are equivalent when they stand on the left-hand side of an equation whose right-hand side is 0 and whose left-hand coefficients are all positive. Either way, the final expansion contains just the two constituents xy and x(1−y), and from them come simply the equations xy=0, x(1−y)=0. That is, nothing is both x and y, and nothing is x without being y. So the pair of terms x+xy can be replaced by the single term x.

The same reasoning covers every case the Proposition describes. For instance, if the term x is repeated, the sum 2x can be replaced by x, because in these circumstances the equation x=0 is bound to appear in the final reduction anyway.

Proposition II.

3. Suppose that in the course of an elimination we have to multiply together two factors, each made up only of positive terms that obey the fundamental law of logical symbols. Then we may throw out of both factors any term they have in common, or throw out of either factor any term that is divisible by a term in the other factor. The condition is that every term thrown out must be added to the product of the factors that remain.

In stating this Proposition, the word "divisible" is a term of convenience, used in the algebraic sense. In that sense xy and x(1−y) are both said to be divisible by x.

To make the meaning of the Proposition clearer, suppose the factors to be multiplied together are x+y+z and x+yw+t. The Proposition says that we may throw the term x out of both factors, and the term yw out of the second factor, as long as these terms are carried over to the final product. The factors that remain are then y+z and t. If to their product yt+zt we add the terms x and yw, we get x+yw+yt+zt, as an expression equivalent to the product of the given factors x+y+z and x+yw+t. It is equivalent, that is, for the purposes of elimination.
