First take the case where the two factors share a term x. Write the factors as x+P and x+Q, where P in the first factor and Q in the second stand for the sum of the positive terms besides x.

Now, (x+P)(x+Q)=x+xP+xQ+PQ.(1) But elimination consists in multiplying certain factors together and setting the result equal to 0. So there are two possibilities. Either the right-hand side of the equation above is itself to be set equal to 0, or it is a factor of some larger expression that is to be set equal to 0.

Take the first possibility. By the last Proposition, we may throw out the terms xP and xQ, since they are positive terms that have another term, x, as a factor. What is left is x+PQ, which is exactly what we get by throwing x out of both factors and adding it to the product of the factors that remain.

Take the second possibility. The only way the right-hand side of (1) can affect the final result of the elimination is through the number and kind of its constituents. Throwing out the terms xP and xQ changes neither. The reason is that the development of x already includes every possible constituent that has x as a factor.

Finally, take the case where one factor contains a term, such as xy, that is divisible by a term, x, in the other factor.

Let the factors be x+P and xy+Q. Now (x+P)(xy+Q)=xy+xQ+xyP+PQ. By the reasoning of the last Proposition, the term xyP may be thrown out, because it contains another positive term, xy, as a factor. So we have xy+xQ+PQ=xy+(x+P)Q. But this is just what we get by throwing the term xy out of the second factor and carrying it over to the final product. So the Proposition is plain.

Proposition III.

4. Let t be any symbol that is kept in the final result when other symbols are eliminated from some system of equations. Then the result of that elimination can be written in the form Et+E′(1−t)=0, in which E is found by putting t=1 in the given system and eliminating the same other symbols, and E′ is found by putting t=0 in the given system and eliminating the same other symbols.

For let ϕ(t)=0 stand for the final result of the elimination. Expanding this equation, we have ϕ(1)t+ϕ(0)(1−t)=0. Now whatever process takes us from the given system of equations to the function ϕ(t), the same process would take us to ϕ(1) if t were changed into 1 in those equations. And the same process would take us to ϕ(0) if t were changed into 0 in them. So the truth of the Proposition is plain.

5. A remark about the three propositions just proved. They are not needed at all for the strict development or application of the general theory. But they serve important practical ends. By Prop. 1 we can simplify the results of addition. By Prop. 2 we can simplify the results of multiplication. And by Prop. 3 we can break any long, tedious elimination into two separate processes, each of which will usually be much less complicated. We will use this method very often when the final aim is to find the value of t in terms of the other symbols that remain after the elimination.

6. Ex. 1.—In the Nicomachean Ethics, Book II. Cap. 3, Aristotle first settles that actions are virtuous not because of some character they have in themselves, but because they imply a certain state of mind in the person who does them. That person must act knowingly, by deliberate choice, for the action's own sake, and on fixed principles of conduct. In the next two chapters he goes on to ask whether virtue belongs to the genus of Passions, or of Faculties, or of Habits, along with some related points. He bases his inquiry on the following premises. From them he also draws the general doctrine and definition of moral virtue that the rest of the treatise lays out.

Premises.

1. Virtue is either a passion (πάθος), or a faculty (δύναμις), or a habit (ἕξις).

2. Passions are not things according to which we are praised or blamed, or in which we exercise deliberate preference.

3. Faculties are not things according to which we are praised or blamed, and which are accompanied by deliberate preference.

4. Virtue is something according to which we are praised or blamed, and which is accompanied by deliberate preference.

5. Whatever art or science makes its work to be in a good state avoids extremes, and keeps the mean in view relative to human nature (τὸ μέσον … πρὸς ἡμᾶς)

6. Virtue is more exact and excellent than any art or science.

This last is an argument à fortiori (from the stronger case). If science and true art avoid falling short and going too far alike, then virtue keeps to the straight line of moderation all the more. If they make their work to be in a good state, we have all the more reason to say that virtue makes her own particular work to be "in a good state." Let the final premise be read in that way. Let us also leave out every mention of praise and blame. In the premises they are mentioned only alongside deliberate preference, and deliberate preference is an element we mean to keep. We may then take as our symbols:

v = virtue.
p = passions.
f = faculties.
h = habits.
d = things accompanied by deliberate preference.
g = things causing their work to be in a good state.
m = things keeping the mean in view relative to human nature.

Using q as the symbol of an indefinite class, we can express our premises by the following equations: v=q{p(1−f)(1−h)+f(1−p)(1−h)+h(1−p)(1−f)}.p=q(1−d).f=q(1−d).v=qd.g=qm.v=qg. Eliminating the symbol q from each of these separately, we get v{1−p(1−f)(1−h)−f(1−p)(1−h)−h(1−p)(1−f)}=0.(1)pd=0.(2)fd=0.(3)v(1−d)=0.(4)g(1−m)=0.(5)v(1−g)=0.(6) We will first eliminate the symbol d from (2), (3), and (4), and then find v in terms of p, f, and h. Adding (2), (3), and (4) gives (p+f)d+v(1−d)=0. Eliminating d from this in the ordinary way, we find (p+f)v=0.(7) That is, nothing is both virtue and either a passion or a faculty. Adding this to (1), and solving for v, we find v=0p+f+1−p(1−f)(1−h)−f(1−p)(1−h)−h(1−f)(1−p). So by development, v=00h(1−f)(1−p). This equation reads: Virtue is a habit, and not a faculty or a passion.

Next we will eliminate f, p, and g from the original system of equations, and then find v in terms of h, d, and m. This time we will eliminate p and f together. Adding (1), (2), and (3), we get v{1−p(1−f)(1−h)−f(1−p)(1−h)−h(1−p)(1−f)}+pd+fd=0.

Developing this with respect to p and f, we have (v+2d)pf+(vh+d)p(1−f)+(vh+d)(1−p)f+v(1−h)(1−p)(1−f)=0. So the result of the elimination will be (v+2d)(vh+d)(vh+d)v(1−h)=0. Now v+2d=v+d+d, and by Prop. I. this can be reduced to v+d. Its product with the second factor is (v+d)(vh+d), which by Prop. II. reduces to d+v(vh) or vh+d.

In the same way, multiplying this result by the third factor gives simply vh+d again. Finally, multiplying it by the fourth factor, v(1−h), gives the final equation vd(1−h)=0(8) that is, there is no virtue accompanied by deliberate preference that is not a habit. It remains to eliminate g from (5) and (6). The result is v(1−m)=0(9) that is, all virtue keeps the mean in view.

Finally, adding the equations (4), (8), and (9) gives v(1−d)+vd(1−h)+v(1−m)=0 from which we have v=01−d+d(1−h)+1−m. And the development of this result gives v=00hdm, of which the interpretation is: Virtue is a habit accompanied by deliberate preference, and keeping in view the mean relative to human nature.

Strictly speaking, this is not a definition of virtue but a description of it. It is, however, all that can correctly be inferred from the premises. Aristotle ties to it the need for prudence, to find the safe middle line of action. And there is no doubt that the ancient theories of virtue were, in general, more intellectual in character than the theories that have mostly prevailed in modern times (the theory of utility excepted). Virtue was seen as the right state and habit of the whole mind, rather than as the sole rule of conscience or of the moral faculty. To some extent those theories were surely right. Unconditional obedience to what conscience commands is an essential part of virtuous conduct. But another part is that those commands should agree with the unchanging principles of right (αἰώνια δίκαια), which are grounded in the constitution of things, or rather are themselves its foundation. And such agreement, at least in any high degree, cannot go along with ignorance and dullness of mind. To come back to Aristotle's own theory: most people, I think, will find it too negative. Merely avoiding extremes does not give enough room for the nobler energies of our nature. Aristotle seems to have been dimly aware of this weakness in his system when, at the opening of his seventh book, he spoke of a "heroic virtue" that rises above the measure of human nature.

Footnote: τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς ἀρετὴν ἡρωϊκήν τινα καὶ θείαν—Nic. Eth. Book vii.

7. I have already remarked (VIII. 1) that the theory of single equations or propositions includes questions that cannot be fully answered except in connection with the theory of systems of equations. We see this when we are asked to take a single equation and find, in terms of the remaining elements, the relation not of some single elementary class but of some compound class, one whose expression involves more than one element. The particular example that follows, and the general problem after it, are of this kind.

Ex. 2.—Let us go back to the symbolic expression of the definition of wealth used in Chap. VII., namely, w=st{p+r(1−p)}, where, as before,

w = wealth,
s = things limited in supply,
t = things transferable,
p = things productive of pleasure,
r = things preventive of pain;

and suppose we are asked to find from it how things that are transferable and productive of pleasure are related to the other elements of the definition, namely wealth, things limited in supply, and things preventive of pain.

The expression for things transferable and productive of pleasure is tp. Let us stand for this by a new symbol, y. We then have the equations w=st{p+r(1−p)},y=tp, and if we eliminate t and p from them, we can find y as a function of w, s, and r. That result, interpreted, will give the relation we want.

Bringing all the terms of these equations over to the left-hand side, we have w−stp−str(1−p)=0.y−tp=0.(3) Adding the squares of these equations together gives w+stp+str(1−p)−2wstp−2wstr(1−p)+y+tp−2ytp=0.(4) To eliminate t and p, we develop the left-hand side with respect to them, and get (w+s−2ws+1−y)tp+(w+sr−2wsr+y)t(1−p)+(w+y)(1−t)p+(w+y)(1−t)(1−p);(5) and the result of eliminating t and p is found by setting equal to 0 the product of the four coefficients of tp,t(1−p),(1−t)p, and (1−t)(1−p).

Or, by Prop. 3, the result of eliminating t and p from the equation above will have the form Ey+E′(1−y), where E is what we get by changing y into 1 in the given equation and then eliminating t and p, and E′ is what we get by changing y into 0 in the same equation and then eliminating t and p. In each case, the way to eliminate t and p is to multiply together the coefficients of the four constituents tp, t(1−p), and so on.

If we put y=1, the coefficients become as follows.

The first is w(1−s)+s(1−w).

The second is 1+w(1−sr)+s(1−w)r, which is equivalent to 1 by Prop. I.

The third and fourth are 1+w, which is equivalent to 1 by Prop. I.

So the value of E is w(1−s)+s(1−w). Again, putting y=0 in (5), we have for the coefficients:

The first is 1+w(1−s)+s(1−w), which is equivalent to 1.

The second is w(1−sr)+sr(1−w).

The third and fourth are w.

Multiplying these coefficients together gives E′=w(1−sr).

So the equation from which y is to be found is {w(1−s)+s(1−w)}y+w(1−sr)(1−y)=0,∴y=w(1−sr)w(1−sr)−w(1−s)−s(1−w); and expanding the right-hand side, y=00wsr+ws(1−r)+10w(1−s)r+10w(1−s)(1−r)+0(1−w)sr+0(1−w)s(1−r)+00(1−w)(1−s)r+00(1−w)(1−s)(1−r); and reducing this, we get y=ws(1−r)+00wsr+00(1−w)(1−s),(6)with w(1−s)=0.(7)

Read in words, this says two things.

First, things transferable and productive of pleasure consist of all wealth (limited in supply and) not preventive of pain, an indefinite amount of wealth (limited in supply and) preventive of pain, and an indefinite amount of what is not wealth and not limited in supply.

Second, all wealth is limited in supply.

In the solution above I have put in parentheses the part of the full description that is already implied by the separate relation (7) that comes with it.

8. The following problem is more general. It will give us an easy practical rule for problems like the last one.

General Problem.

Given any equation connecting the symbols x, y..w, z..

Required: to find the logical expression of any class described in any way by the symbols x, y.. in terms of the remaining symbols, w, z, and so on.

Let us keep to the case of just two symbols, x and y, on one side, and two symbols, w and z, on the other. That case is enough to establish the general Rule.

Let V=0 be the given equation, and let ϕ(x,y) stand for the class whose expression we want to find.

Put t=ϕ(x,y). Then x and y are to be eliminated from these two equations.

Now the equation V=0 can be expanded in the form Axy+Bx(1−y)+C(1−x)y+D(1−x)(1−y)=0,(1) where A, B, C, and D are functions of the symbols w and z.

Again, since ϕ(x,y) stands for a class or collection of things, it must consist of a constituent, or a series of constituents, whose coefficients are 1.

So if the full development of ϕ(x,y) is written in the form axy+bx(1−y)+c(1−x)y+d(1−x)(1−y), each of the coefficients a, b, c, d must be 1 or 0.

Now by transposing and squaring, we reduce the equation t=ϕ(x,y) to the form t{1−ϕ(x,y)}+ϕ(x,y)(1−t)=0; and expanding with respect to x and y, we get {t(1−a)+a(1−t)}xy+{t(1−b)+b(1−t)}x(1−y)+{t(1−c)+c(1−t)}(1−x)y+{t(1−d)+d(1−t)}(1−x)(1−y)=0; and adding this to (1), we have {A+t(1−a)+a(1−t)}xy+{B+t(1−b)+b(1−t)}x(1−y)+&c.=0.

Let the result of eliminating x and y have the form Et+E′(1−t)=0, Then, by what has been said, E will be the reduced product of what the coefficients of the expansion above become when t=1 , and E′ the product of the same factors, reduced in the same way, when t=0.

So E will be the reduced product (A+1−a)(B+1−b)(C+1−c)(D+1−d). Look at any one factor of this expression, say A+1−a. When a=1 it becomes A, and when a=0 it becomes 1+A, which reduces to 1 by Prop. I. From this we may conclude that E is the product of the coefficients of those constituents in the development of V whose coefficients in the development of ϕ(x,y) are 1.

Moreover, E′ will be the reduced product (A+a)(B+b)(C+c)(D+d). Look at any one of these factors, say A+a. It becomes A when a=0, and reduces to 1 when a=1 ; and the same goes for the others. So E will be the product of the coefficients of those constituents in the development of y, whose coefficients in the development ϕ(x,y) are 0. Putting these two cases together, we can lay down the following Rule.

9. To find, from a logical equation, how any class expressed by a given combination of the symbols x, y, and so on, is related to the classes represented by the other symbols in that equation.

Rule.—Expand the given equation with respect to the symbols x, y. Then form the equation Et+E′(1−t)=0, in which E is the product of the coefficients of all those constituents in the development whose coefficients in the expression of the given class are 1, and E′ is the product of the coefficients of those constituents in the development whose coefficients in the expression of the given class are 0. The value of t found from this equation, by solving it and interpreting the result, will be the expression we want.

Note.—In proving this Rule we assumed that V consists only of positive terms. But it is easy to show that this condition is unnecessary, that the Rule is general, and that the given equation really needs no preparation at all.

10. Ex. 3.—Take the same definition of wealth as in Example 2. We want an expression for things transferable, but not productive of pleasure, t(1−p), in terms of the other elements, represented by w, s, and r.

The equation w−stp−str(1−p)=0, gives, when squared, w+stp+str(1−p)−2wstp−2wstr(1−p)=0; and developing the left-hand side with respect to t and p, (w+s−2ws)tp+(w+sr−2wsr)t(1−p)+w(1−t)p+w(1−t)(1−p)=0.

It is best to write the coefficients as in the following equation: {w(1−s)+s(1−w)}tp+{w(1−sr)+sr(1−w)}t(1−p)+w(1−t)p+w(1−t)(1−p)=0

Let the function to be found, t(1−p), be represented by z. Then the full development of z with respect to t and p is z=0tp+t(1−p)+0(1−t)p+0(1−t)(1−p). So, by the last problem, we have Ez+E′(1−z)=0;where E=w(1−sr)+sr(1−w);E′={w(1−s)+s(1−w)}×w×w=w(1−s);∴{w(1−sr)+sr(1−w)}z+w(1−s)(1−z)=0. So, z=w(1−s)2wsr−ws−sr=00wsr+0ws(1−r)+10w(1−s)r+10w(1−s)(1−r),+0(1−w)sr+00(1−w)s(1−r)+00(1−w)(1−s)r+00(1−w)(1−s)(1−r).Or, z=00wsr+00(1−w)s(1−r)+00(1−w)(1−s),with w(1−s)=0.

So things transferable and not productive of pleasure are either wealth (limited in supply and preventive of pain); or things that are not wealth, but are limited in supply and not preventive of pain; or things that are not wealth and are unlimited in supply.

The following results, found in the same way, are easy to check:

Things limited in supply and productive of pleasure which are not wealth are intransferable (cannot be transferred).

Wealth that is not productive of pleasure is transferable, limited in supply, and preventive of pain.

Things limited in supply which are either wealth or productive of pleasure, but not both, are either transferable and preventive of pain, or intransferable.

11. A great many curious examples could be taken from natural history. But I do not think such applications would have any value of their own. For instance, they would throw no light on the true principles of classification in zoology. To discover those, we need some foundation of positive knowledge: some acquaintance with the structure of living things, and with how their parts are fitted to their purposes. That kind of knowledge can only come from the outside means of observation and analysis. Still, take any collection of propositions in natural history, and a great many logical problems present themselves, whatever system of classification is used. In making up such examples, it is perhaps better to leave out, as superfluous, the property of a class or species that its name already suggests. An example is the ring-structure of the annelida, the class of animals that includes the earthworm and the leech.

Ex. 4.—1. The annelida are soft-bodied, and either naked or enclosed in a tube.

2. The annelida consist of all invertebrate animals having red blood in a double system of circulating vessels.

Assumea = annelida;
s = soft-bodied animals;
n = naked;
t = enclosed in a tube;
i = invertebrate;
r = having red blood, &c.

Then the propositions are expressed by the equations a=vs{n(1−t)+t(1−n)};(1)a=ir;(2) and to these we may add the condition they imply, that nothing is both naked and enclosed in a tube, nt=0.(3)

Eliminating v, and reducing the system to a single equation, we have a[1−sn(1−t)−st(1−n)]+a(1−ir)+ir(1−a)+nt=0.(4)

Suppose we want to find how soft-bodied animals enclosed in tubes stand, by virtue of the premises, with respect to the following elements: having red blood, having an outer covering, and having a backbone.

We must first eliminate a. The result is ir{1−sn(1−t)−st(1−n)}+nt=0.

Then (IX. 9), developing with respect to s and t, and reducing the first coefficient by Prop. 1, we have nst+ir(1−n)s(1−t)+(ir+n)(1−s)t+ir(1−s)(1−t)=0.(5)

So if we put st=w, we find nw+ir(1−n)×(ir+n)×ir(1−w)=0; or, nw+ir(1−n)(1−w)=0;∴w=ir(1−n)ir(1−n)−n=0irn+ir(1−n)+0i(1−r)n+00i(1−r)(1−n)+0(1−i)rn+00(1−i)r(1−n)+0(1−i)(1−r)n+00(1−i)(1−r)(1−n);or, w=ir(1−n)+00i(1−r)(1−n)+00(1−i)(1−n).

So soft-bodied animals enclosed in tubes consist of all invertebrate animals that have red blood and are not naked, together with an indefinite remainder made up of invertebrate animals that do not have red blood and are not naked, and of vertebrate animals that are not naked.

In exactly the same way, the following reduced equations have been drawn from the development (5). Their interpretation is left to the reader. s(1−t)=irn+00i(1−n)+00(1−i)(1−s)t=00(1−i)r(1−n)+00(1−r)(1−n)(1−s)(1−t)=00i(1−r)+00(1−i).

In none of these examples have I tried to show off the power of the method in any special way. That power, I believe, can only be fully displayed in connection with the mathematical theory of probability (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition). But I would make a suggestion to anyone who wants to form a fair opinion on this point. Work through the following problem by the rules of ordinary logic before looking at its solution. And remember that whatever complexity it has could be multiplied without limit. The only effect would be to make its solution by the method of this book more laborious, but no less certain.

Ex. 5. Suppose that observing a certain class of natural productions has led to the following general results.

First, in whichever of these productions the properties A and C are missing, the property E is found, together with one of the properties B and D, but not with both.

Second, wherever the properties A and D are found while E is missing, the properties B and C will either both be found or both be missing.

Third, wherever the property A is found together with either B or E, or both, there either the property C or the property D will be found, but not both. And conversely, wherever the property C or D is found on its own, there the property A will be found together with either B or E, or both.

We are asked to find two things. First, what can be concluded in any particular case from the known presence of the property A, with respect to the properties B, C, and D; and also whether any relations hold among the properties B, C, and D on their own. Second, what can be concluded in the same way about the property B and the properties A, C, and D.

Notice that in each of the three data, what we are told about the properties A, B, C, and D is tangled up with another element, E, about which we want to say nothing in our conclusion. So we will need to eliminate the symbol for the property E from the system of equations that expresses the given propositions.

Let us represent the property A by x, B by y, C by z, D by w, and E by v. The data are then x‾z‾=qv(yw‾+wy‾);(1)v‾xw=q(yz+y‾z‾);(2)xy+xvy‾=wz‾+zw‾;(3) where x‾ stands for 1−x, and so on, and q is a symbol of an indefinite class. We eliminate q from the first and second equations separately, and add the results to the third equation, reduced by (5), Chap. VIII. We get x‾z‾(1−vyw‾−vwy‾)+v‾xw(yz‾+zy‾)+(xy+xvy‾)(wz+w‾z‾)+(wz‾+zw‾)(1−xy−xvy‾)=0.(4)

From this equation v must be eliminated, and then the value of x found from the result. For this purpose it will be convenient to use the method of Prop. 3 of the present chapter.

So let the result of the elimination be represented by the equation Ex+E′(1−x)=0.

To find E, put x=1 in the left-hand side of (4). We find v‾w(yz‾+zy‾)+(y+vy‾)(wz+w‾z‾)+(wz‾+zw‾)v‾y‾.

Eliminating v, we have (wz+w‾z‾){w(yz‾+zy‾)+y(wz+w‾z‾)+y‾(wz‾+zw‾)}; and when this is actually multiplied out, subject to the conditions ww‾=0, zz‾=0, and so on, it gives E=wz+yw‾z‾

Next, to find E′, put x=0 in (4). We have z(1−vyw‾−vy‾w)+wz‾+zw‾. Eliminating v from this, and reducing the result by Propositions 1 and 2, we find E′=wz‾+zw‾+y‾w‾z‾;

and so, finally, we have (wz+yw‾z‾)x+(wz‾+zw‾+y‾w‾z‾)x‾=0;(5) from which x=wz‾+zw‾+y‾w‾z‾wz‾+zw‾+y‾w‾z‾−wz−yw‾z‾ and so, by development, x=0yzw+yzw‾+yz‾w+0yz‾w‾+0y‾zw+y‾zw‾+y‾z‾w+y‾z‾w‾; or, collecting the terms that stand in the same vertical column, x=zw‾+z‾w+y‾z‾w‾;(6) which reads as follows.

In whatever substances the property A is found, there will also be found either the property C or the property D, but not both; or else the properties B, C, and D will all be missing. And conversely, wherever the property C or the property D is found on its own, or the properties B, C, and D are all missing together, there the property A will be found.

It also turns out that there is no separate relation among the properties B, C, and D on their own.

Second, we are to find y. Developing (5) with respect to that symbol, we get (xwz+xw‾z‾+x‾wz‾+x‾zw‾)y+(xwz+x‾wz‾+x‾zw‾+x‾z‾w‾)y‾=0; and proceeding as before, y=x‾w‾z‾+00(x‾wz+xwz‾+xzw‾),(7) together with xzw=0;(8)x‾z‾w=0;(9)x‾zw‾=0;(10)

Solving (10), we reduce it to the form x‾z=00w; and from it we have the separate relation: If the property A is absent and C present, D is present. Again, adding (8) and (9) and solving gives xz+x‾z‾=00w‾.

So, for the general solution and the remaining separate relation, we have the following.

First, if the property B is present in one of the productions, then either the properties A, C, and D are all absent, or exactly one of them is absent. And conversely, if they are all absent it may be concluded that the property B is present (7).

Second, if A and C are both present or both absent, D will be absent, quite independently of whether B is present or absent (8) and (9).

I have not attempted to verify these conclusions.

Chapter 10: Of the Conditions of a Perfect Method

1. We have now discussed primary propositions at length, and we are about to take up secondary propositions. This point of transition between the two great divisions of the science of logic is a good place to pause. While we look back over some of the steps we have taken, we can ask what it is that makes a method perfect in a subject like the one we have been studying. I do not mean only the perfection that lies in power. I mean also the perfection that rests on our sense of what is fitting and beautiful. A careful analysis of the question would probably lead us to something like this conclusion. A perfect method should not only be efficient, doing well the work it was designed to do. It should also show a certain unity and harmony in all its parts and processes. This ideal would be most fully reached if the very forms of the method pointed back to the fundamental principles they are built on, and, if possible, to the one fundamental principle beneath them all. When we apply these thoughts to the science of reasoning, it may be wise to look beyond the analytical processes alone. We should ask what is best not only in the manner or form of deduction, but also in the system of data, or premises, from which the deduction is made.

2. As far as power alone goes, there is no doubt that the first of the methods developed in Chapter VIII. is, within its proper range, a perfect one. Bringing in arbitrary constants frees us from depending on the forms of the premises, and from any conditions among the equations that represent them. But it seems to bring in a foreign element. It is a more laborious form of solution than the second method of reduction proved in the same chapter, and a less elegant one too. There are, however, conditions under which that second method takes on a more perfect form than it usually has. Suppose we made the one fundamental condition, expressed by the equation x(1−x)=0, the universal pattern for every form, so that every expression we work with obeyed the law of duality just as a single class symbol does. That would give a unity of character to both the processes and the results which could not be had in any other way. If brevity or convenience were the only things that made a method valuable, adopting such a principle would bring no advantage. To force this character onto every step of a solution would sometimes take no small labour of preliminary reduction. Still, it is interesting to know that it can be done. It is even of some importance to know the conditions under which a solution of this kind would turn up on its own. Some of these points are considered in this chapter.

Proposition I.

3. To reduce any equation among logical symbols to the form V=0, in which V satisfies the law of duality, V(1−V)=0. It was shown in Chap. V. Prop. 4, that this condition holds whenever V is the sum of a series of constituents. It is also clear from Prop. 2, Chap. VI. that certain equations are all equivalent. These are the equations which, when we move everything to one side to get the form V=0 and then develop the left-hand side, produce the same series of constituents with coefficients that are not zero. The particular numbers those coefficients happen to be make no difference.

So the aim of this Proposition can always be reached in three steps. Bring all the terms of an equation over to the left-hand side. Expand that side fully. Then, in the result, change every coefficient that is not zero into unity (that is, 1), leaving alone those that are 1 already.

But developing functions that contain many symbols leads to expressions inconveniently long. It is worth showing, then, how this source of complexity can be avoided in the only cases that actually come up in practice.

The great primary forms of equations were discussed in Chapter VIII. They are— X=vY,X=Y,vX=vY. We have seen that whenever the conditions X(1−X)=0,Y(1−Y)=0, hold, that is, whenever X and Y each obey the law of duality, the first two of these equations lead us to the forms X(1−Y)=0,(1)X(1−Y)+Y(1−X)=0;(2) the first saying that there is nothing which is X and not Y, the second that there is nothing which is X and not Y, and nothing which is Y and not X. Under the same circumstances it can be shown that the last of them gives v(X(1−Y)+Y(1−X))=0;(3) and all of these results clearly satisfy, on their left-hand sides, the condition V(1−V)=0.

These are the forms and conditions in which the equations of a properly expressed logical system actually present themselves. So it is always possible, by the method above, to bring them under the required law. But although each separate equation may satisfy the law this way, their equivalent sum (VIII. 4) may not. It remains to show how the condition can be imposed on the sum too.

Let us write the equation formed by adding together the separate reduced equations of the system as v+v′+v″,&c.=0,(4) an equation which by itself is equivalent to the whole system it came from. We suppose v,v′,v″, &c. to be class terms (IX. 1) satisfying the conditions v(1−v)=0,v′(1−v′)=0,&c. Now the full interpretation of (4) would be found by developing its left-hand side with respect to all the elementary symbols x, y, &c. that it contains, and setting equal to 0 every constituent whose coefficient is not zero. In other words, we would set equal to 0 every constituent found in any one of v, v′, v″, &c. Those constituents fall into groups. First come those found in v. Second, those not found in v but found in v′. Third, those found in neither v nor v′ but found in v″. And so on. So they will be exactly the constituents found in the expression v+(1−v)v′+(1−v)(1−v′)v″+&c.,(5) an expression in which no constituent appears twice, and which plainly satisfies the law V(1−V)=0.

For example, suppose we had the expression (1−t)+v+(1−z)+tzw, in which the terms 1−t, 1−z are bracketed to show that each is to be taken as a single class term. Following (5), we would reduce it to an expression satisfying the condition V(1−V)=0 in three moves. Multiply every term after the first by t. Then multiply every term after the second by 1−v. Last, multiply the term that remains after the third by z. The result is 1−t+tv+t(1−v)(1−z)+t(1−v)zw.(6)

4. So all logical equations can be reduced to the form V=0, with V satisfying the law of duality. But it would clearly be a higher degree of perfection if equations always came in this form without any preparation at all. Better still if they not only showed this form when first stated, but kept it intact after the additions we must make to reduce a system of equations to a single equivalent one. That they do not do this on their own is not really a defect of the method. It comes from the fact that our premises are not always complete, accurate, and independent. They are not complete when they involve material relations (as distinguished from formal ones) that are left unstated. They are not accurate when they imply relations that were not intended. Let us set those two points aside, since they concern us less here, and consider in what sense premises may fail to be independent.

5. A system of propositions may be called independent when no conclusion that can be drawn from one portion of the system can also be drawn from any other portion of it. Suppose the equations representing those propositions are all reduced to the form V=0, then this condition means that no constituent which can be made to appear in the development of one function V of the system can be made to appear in the development of any other function V′ of the same system. When the condition fails, the equations of the system are not independent. This can happen in various ways. Let all the equations satisfy the law of duality on their left-hand sides. Then if a positive term x appears in the expansion of one equation, and a term xy in the expansion of another, the equations are not independent. The term x can be developed further into xy+x(1−y), and so the equation xy=0 is contained in both equations of the system, that is, both of them say that there is nothing which is both x and y. Again, let a term xy appear in one equation and a term xz in another. Both can be developed so as to give the shared constituent xyz. Other cases are easy to imagine in which premises that look quite independent at first sight are not really so. Whenever equations of the form V=0 are not truly independent in this way, then even though each one may satisfy the law of duality, V(1−V)=0, the equivalent equation we get by adding them together will not satisfy that condition, unless enough reductions have been carried out by the method of this chapter. When, on the other hand, the equations of a system both satisfy this law and are independent of one another, their sum will satisfy the same law. I have dwelt on these points longer than would otherwise be necessary. I think it important to form for ourselves, and to keep before us in all our investigations, the pattern of an ideal perfection, the goal and the guide of future efforts. In inquiries of this kind, the chief aim in improving the method should be to make the transformation of equations easier, as far as brevity allows, so that the fundamental condition spoken of above becomes universal.

In connexion with this subject the following Propositions deserve attention.

Proposition II.

If the left-hand side of any equation V=0 satisfies the condition V(1−V)=0, and if the expression of any symbol t of that equation is found as a developed function of the other symbols, then the coefficients of the expansion can take only the forms 1, 0, 00, 10.

For if we expand the equation with respect to t, we get Et+E′(1−t),(1) where E and E′ are what V becomes when t is changed in it first to 1 and then to 0. So E and E′ will themselves satisfy the conditions E(1−E)=0,E′(1−E′)=0.(2) Now (1) gives t=E′E′−E, and the right-hand side of this is to be expanded as a function of the remaining symbols. Clearly the only numerical values that E and E′ can take in calculating the coefficients are 1 and 0. So only the following cases can arise:

First, E′=1, E=1, then E′E′−E=10.

Second, E′=1, E=0, then E′E′−E=1.

Third, E′=0, E=1, then E′E′−E=0.

Fourth, E′=0, E=0, then E′E′−E=00.

This makes the truth of the Proposition plain.

6. It is worth noting that the forms 1, 0, and 00 appear in the solution of equations whether or not the condition V(1−V)=0 holds. The coefficient 10 is different. The terms that carry this coefficient when the condition is satisfied may take any value other than the three values 1, 0, and 00 when it is not. It is allowed, and it would make for uniformity, to change any coefficient of a development that does not come in one of the four forms named in this Proposition into 10. We treat this as the proper symbol to show that the term it is attached to must be set equal to 0. I shall often do this.

Proposition III.

7. The result of eliminating any symbols x, y, &c. from an equation V=0, whose left-hand side identically satisfies the law of duality, V(1−V)=0, can be obtained by developing the given equation with respect to the other symbols, and setting equal to 0 the sum of those constituents whose coefficients in the expansion are equal to unity.

Suppose the given equation V=0 involves only three symbols, x, y, and t, and that x and y are to be eliminated. Let the development of the equation with respect to t be At+B(1−t)=0,(1) with A and B free of the symbol t.

By Chap. IX. Prop. 3, the result of eliminating x and y from the given equation will have the form Et+E′(1−t)=0,(2) in which E is the result of eliminating the symbols x and y from the equation A=0, and E′ the result of eliminating them from the equation B=0.

Now A and B must satisfy the condition A(1−A)=0,B(1−B)=0 So A (we look at this coefficient alone for now) will be either 0, or 1, or a single constituent, or the sum of some of the constituents that involve the symbols x and y. If A=0, clearly E=0. If A is a single constituent, or the sum of only some of the constituents involving x and y, then E will be 0 as well. The reason is that the full development of A with respect to x and y will contain terms with zero coefficients, and E is the product of all the coefficients. So when A=1, E is equal to A, but in every other case E is equal to 0. In the same way, when B=1, E′ is equal to B, but in every other case E′ is zero. So the expression (2) will consist of that part of (1), if there is any, in which the coefficients A, B are unity. And this reasoning is general. Suppose, for instance, that V involved the symbols x, y, z, t, and that we had to eliminate x and y. Then if the development of V with respect to z and t were zt+xz(1−t)+y(1−z)t+(1−z)(1−t), the result we want would be zt+(1−z)(1−t)=0, this being the part of the development whose coefficients are unity.

Hence, if from any system of equations we derive a single equivalent equation V=0, with V satisfying the condition V(1−V)=0, the ordinary processes of elimination can be dropped entirely, and the single process of development can take their place.

8. There may be no practical advantage in the method pointed out here. But it has a theoretical unity and completeness that make it worth attention, and so I shall give a later chapter (XIV.) to illustrating it. The progress of applied mathematics has offered other striking examples of whole systems of problems or equations being brought under the rule of some central law that runs through all of them.

9. From what has gone before, we can see that there is one class of propositions for which none of the special devices of preparation above are needed. It is the class marked by the following conditions:

First, That the propositions are of the ordinary kind, the kind implied by the copula is or are, with the predicates particular.

Secondly, That the terms of the proposition are meaningful without assuming any unstated relation among the elements that go into expressing those terms.

Thirdly, That the propositions are independent.

We may, if such speculation is not altogether idle, allow ourselves a guess. These may be the conditions that language would obey, as an instrument of expression and of thought, in the hands of unerring beings who said simply what they meant, without holding anything back on the one hand and without repeating themselves on the other. Considered both in relation to the idea of a perfect language and in relation to the processes of an exact method, these conditions deserve the student's attention equally.

Chapter 11: Of Secondary Propositions, and of the Principles of Their Symbolical Expression

1. We established in Chap. IV. that every logical proposition belongs to one of two great classes, Primary Propositions and Secondary Propositions. The preceding chapters have dealt with the first class. We now turn to Secondary Propositions, that is, propositions about other propositions, considered as true or false. The inquiry we are beginning will follow the same general order and course as the one we have already carried out. The two inquiries differ in the subjects of thought they deal with. They do not differ in the formal and scientific laws they reveal, or in the methods and processes built on those laws. We might, to some degree, have expected this. It fits everything we know of the uniformity of Nature, and everything we believe of the unchanging constancy of the Author of Nature, to suppose that the mind should have a harmony and uniformity no less real than the one the physical sciences reveal to us. This is a mind, after all, that has been given high powers, not only for dealing with the world around it, but for knowing itself and reflecting on the laws of its own make-up. Expectations like this must never become the main rule of our inquiries. Nor should they ever draw us away from the patient research by which we find out how things actually are within the particular field we are investigating. But once the grounds of a resemblance have been properly and independently established, it is not at odds even with purely scientific aims to reflect on that resemblance, to trace how far it reaches, and to receive whatever hints it seems to give us of truths not yet discovered. This does not set aside the need for a final appeal to fact. Nor does it stretch analogy beyond its proper job, which is to suggest relations that independent inquiry must then either confirm or reject.

2. Secondary Propositions are those which concern or relate to Propositions considered as true or false. We express the relations of things by primary propositions. But we can also make propositions themselves the subject of thought, and express our judgments about them. The expression of any such judgment is a secondary proposition. There is no proposition at all about which enough knowledge would not let us make one of two assertions: either that the proposition is true, or that it is false. Each of these assertions is a secondary proposition. "It is true that the sun shines" and "It is not true that the planets shine by their own light" are examples. In the first, the proposition "The sun shines" is asserted to be true. In the second, the proposition "The planets shine by their own light" is asserted to be false. Secondary propositions also include every judgment that expresses a relation or dependence among propositions. Conditional propositions belong here, such as "If the sun shine the day will be fair." So do most disjunctive propositions, such as "Either the sun will shine, or the enterprise will be postponed." The first example expresses how the truth of the proposition "The day will be fair" depends on the truth of the proposition "The sun will shine." The second expresses a relation between the two propositions "The sun will shine" and "The enterprise will be postponed": the truth of one shuts out the truth of the other. To the same class of secondary propositions we must also assign every proposition that asserts that several propositions are true together or false together, such as "It is not true both that 'the sun will shine' and that 'the journey will be postponed.'" These different elements can even be mixed in a single secondary proposition. It may contain both the disjunctive element, expressed by either, or, and the conditional element, expressed by if; and the propositions it connects may themselves be compound. Take this: If "the sun shine," and "leisure permit," then either "the enterprise shall be commenced," or "some preliminary step shall be taken." Here several propositions are joined together, not at random or without meaning, but so as to express a definite connection among them, a connection that concerns whether each is true or false. So by our definition this combination is a Secondary Proposition.

The theory of Secondary Propositions deserves careful study, both for its many applications and for the close and harmonious analogy, already mentioned, that it bears to the theory of Primary Propositions. I want to say a little more about each of these points.

3. First, the reasonings of everyday life take the form of secondary propositions at least as often as the form of primary ones. The moralist and the metaphysician, too, perhaps talk less often about things and their qualities than about principles and hypotheses, about truths and how truths are connected and related to one another. Our experience is narrow, and the conclusions it suggests on the great unsolved questions of morals and society show their human origin in more ways than one. Universal principles certainly exist. But the partial formulas that make up our knowledge of how those principles apply are subject to conditions, exceptions, and failures. So in the fields of inquiry that ought, by their subject matter, to be the most interesting of all, much of what we actually know is hypothetical. We shall see later that writers on speculative philosophy have tended strongly to adopt these same forms of thought. A general method for handling hypothetical propositions, and the other kinds of secondary propositions, will therefore open a more interesting field of applications than any we have met so far.

4. Second, the theory of Secondary Propositions is interesting for the close and remarkable analogy it bears to the theory of Primary Propositions. We shall see that the formal laws governing the operations of the mind are expressed in exactly the same way in both cases. So the mathematical processes built on those laws are the same as well, and the methods worked out in the earlier part of this book will still serve in the new applications we are about to take up. But while the laws and processes of the method stay the same, the rule of interpretation must be adapted to new conditions. In place of classes of things we shall have propositions. In place of the relations of classes and individuals we shall consider the connections of propositions, or of events. Still, however much the two systems differ in what they mean and how they are read, a harmonious relation will be seen to run through both. This analogy helps us overcome every difficulty that remains. It is also interesting to study for its own sake, and it is conclusive proof of the unity of character that marks the make-up of the human faculties.

Proposition I.

5. To investigate the nature of the connexion of Secondary Propositions with the idea of Time.

To begin this inquiry, we must state clearly what the analogy is that links Secondary Propositions to Primary ones.

Primary Propositions express relations among things. They treat those things as parts of a universe, and the matter of our discourse is confined within that universe's limits, whether or not those limits are the same as the limits of the actual universe. The relations expressed are essentially substantive, that is, relations among things themselves: some, all, or none of the members of one class are also members of another class. Every subject that primary propositions refer to, and every relation among those subjects that they express, is of this kind.

With secondary propositions we find ourselves dealing with a different kind both of subject and of relation. The subjects we deal with are themselves propositions. So we may ask: can we regard these subjects, too, as things, and assign them, by analogy with the earlier case, to a universe of their own? Again, the relations among these propositions are relations of being true or false at the same time, not of being the same thing. When we express the connection between two different propositions, we do not say that one is the other. Instead, depending on the meaning we want, we use forms of speech like these: "Either the proposition X is true, or the proposition Y is true"; "If the proposition X is true, the proposition Y is true"; "The propositions X and Y are jointly true"; and so on.

In considering relations like these, we do not need to explore the whole range of their possible meaning. That could draw us into metaphysical questions about causation, which lie beyond the proper limits of science. It is enough to find some meaning they certainly have, and which is adequate for logical deduction. Take as an example the conditional proposition "If the proposition X is true, the proposition Y is true." One meaning it certainly has is that the time in which the proposition X is true is time in which the proposition Y is true. This is only a relation of existing together, and it may or may not exhaust the meaning of the proposition. But it really is part of what the proposition states, and it is enough for every purpose of logical inference.

Everyday language supports this view, that secondary propositions are essentially connected with the notion of time. We limit a primary proposition with the word "some," but a secondary proposition with the word "sometimes." To say "Sometimes injustice triumphs" amounts to saying that there are times when the proposition "Injustice now triumphs" is true. There are, it is true, propositions whose truth is not limited to particular periods or occasions in this way. These are true through all time, and have been given the name "eternal truths." Every reader of Plato and Aristotle will know the distinction. Aristotle in particular uses it to contrast the abstract truths of science, such as the propositions of geometry, which are always true, with the chance relations of things as they appear, which are sometimes true and sometimes false. But the forms of language in which both kinds of proposition are expressed show that both depend on the idea of time: in the one case limited to some finite stretch, in the other stretched out to eternity.

6. Someone may object that in ordinary reasoning we are often quite unaware of this notion of time, even though it is built into the very language we use. The remark is fair, but it only shows that we usually reason with the help of words and the forms of a well-built language, without attending to the deeper grounds on which those forms were established. The course of this investigation will illustrate the same principle. I shall use the notion of time to work out the laws for expressing secondary propositions, and the laws by which the symbols that express them combine. But once those laws and forms are settled, the notion of time (essential, as I believe it is, for that purpose) can in practice be dropped. We can then pass from the forms of common language to the closely matching forms of the symbolic instrument of thought developed here, use its processes, and interpret its results, without being aware of the idea of time at all.

Proposition II.

7. To establish a system of notation for the expression of Secondary Propositions, and to show that the symbols which it involves are subject to the same laws of combination as the corresponding symbols employed in the expression of Primary Propositions.

Let the capital letters X, Y, Z, stand for the elementary propositions about whose truth or falsehood we want to assert something, or among which we want to express some relation in the form of a secondary proposition. And let the matching small letters x, y, z, stand for operations of the mind, in the following sense. Let x represent an act of the mind by which we fix our attention on that portion of time during which the proposition X is true; and let this be what we mean when we say that x denotes the time during which the proposition X is true. Let us also use the connecting signs +, -, =, and so on, in the following sense. Let x+y stand for the total of the portions of time during which the propositions X and Y are respectively true, those times being entirely separate from each other. In the same way, let x−y stand for the time that is left when we take away, from the portion of time during which X is true, the portion during which Y is true, that portion being (by supposition) included in the first. And let x=y mean that the time during which the proposition X is true is the same as the time during which the proposition Y is true. We shall call x the representative symbol of the proposition X, and so on for the others.

From these definitions it follows that we shall always have x+y=y+x, since each side will stand for the same total of time.

Next, let xy represent performing one after the other the two operations represented by y and x. That is, it stands for the whole mental operation made up of these steps. First, the mind selects the portion of time during which the proposition Y is true. Second, out of that portion of time, it selects whatever part of it is time during which the proposition X is true. The result of these two steps is to fix the mind's attention on the whole of the portion of time during which the propositions X and Y are both true.

From this definition it follows that we shall always have xy=yx.(1) For suppose we first mentally select the portion of time during which the proposition Y is true, and then, out of that, the part during which X is true. Or suppose we first select the portion of time during which the proposition X is true, and then, out of that, the part during which the proposition Y is true. Either way we reach the same final result: the portion of time during which the propositions X and Y are both true.

By carrying this reasoning further we can show that the laws by which the symbols x, y, z, and so on, combine, under the interpretation given them here, are expressed in exactly the same way as the laws by which the same symbols combine under the interpretation given them in the first part of this book. The reason for this identity is plain. In both cases we are studying the operations of the same faculty, or the same combination of faculties. The essential character of those operations does not change, whether we suppose them to be at work on the universe of things, which contains all existence, or on the whole of time, in which all events take place and to some part of which, at least, every assertion, truth, and proposition refers.

So, besides the laws already stated, we shall have, by (4), Chap. II., the law whose expression is x(y+z)=xy+xz;(2) that is, the time when X is true and either Y or Z is true is the time when X and Y are true together with the time when X and Z are true. And above all we shall have the fundamental law of duality, (2) Chap. II., whose expression is x2=x,or,x(1−x)=0;(3) that is, there is no time when X is both true and not true. This law separates the system of thought in logic from the system of thought in the science of quantity, and it gives the processes of logic a completeness and generality they could not otherwise have.

8. Again, this law (3), like the other laws, is satisfied by the symbols 0 and 1. So we are led, as before, to ask whether those symbols can be given a meaning in the present system of thought. The same reasoning we followed before shows that they can, and justifies the following two statements.

First, in the expression of secondary propositions, 0 represents nothing with respect to time; that is, no time at all.

Second, in the same system, 1 represents the universe, or the whole of time, that the discourse is taken to be about in any way.

In primary propositions the universe of discourse is sometimes limited to a small part of the actual universe of things, and sometimes is the whole of that universe. In the same way, in secondary propositions the universe of discourse may be limited to a single day, or to the passing moment, or it may take in the whole of time. It may, in the most literal sense, be "eternal." Indeed, unless the nature of the discourse states or implies some limit, the proper meaning of the symbol 1 in secondary propositions is "eternity," just as its proper meaning in the primary system is the whole universe of what actually exists.

9. Instead of using the symbols x, y, z, to represent the truth of propositions, we could just as properly use them to represent the occurrence of events. In fact, the occurrence of an event both implies and is implied by the truth of a proposition, namely the proposition which asserts that the event occurs. Either meaning of the symbol x carries the other with it. It will be very convenient to be able to use our symbols in whichever of these two equivalent meanings the circumstances of a problem make most suitable, and I shall take that liberty whenever it is needed. In problems of pure logic I shall treat the symbols x, y, and so on, as representing elementary propositions, among which the premises express some relation. In the mathematical theory of probability, which, as I said before (I. 12), rests on a foundation of logic, and which this work goes on to treat in a later portion (in the chapters on probability, not included in this edition), I shall use the same symbols for the simple events whose implied or required frequency of occurrence is among the things that theory reckons with.

Editor's note: Boole reads the symbol of a secondary proposition as the portion of time during which that proposition is true. Modern logic drops the idea of time altogether. Instead it gives each proposition one of just two truth values, true or false, written 1 or 0, which is exactly where Boole's own algebra of 0 and 1 lands. This chapter is the ancestor of what is now called propositional logic.

Proposition III.

10. To deduce general Rules for the expression of Secondary Propositions.

In the questions that arise from this Proposition, full proof is less necessary, because they match exactly the questions we have already settled for primary propositions. We shall first consider how to express terms, and then how to express the propositions that connect them.

Since 1 stands for the whole of time, and x for the portion of it during which the proposition X is true, 1−x will stand for the portion of time during which the proposition X is false.

Again, since xy stands for the portion of time during which the propositions X and Y are both true, combining this with the last remark leads us to the following interpretations.

The expression x(1−y) will represent the time during which the proposition X is true and the proposition Y false. The expression (1−x)(1−y) will represent the time during which the propositions X and Y are both false at once.

The expression x(1−y)+y(1−x) will express the time during which either X is true or Y true, but not both; for that time is the sum of the times when each is true on its own, without the other. The expression xy+(1−x)(1−y) will express the time during which X and Y are either both true or both false.

If another symbol z comes in, the same principles still apply. So xyz stands for the time when the propositions X, Y, and Z are all true at once; (1−x)(1−y)(1−z) for the time when they are all false at once; and the sum of these two expressions would stand for the time when they are either all true together or all false together.

The general principles of interpretation at work in these examples need no further illustration or fuller statement.

11. We can now set out and study the laws for expressing propositions, case by case. First, though, I want to draw attention to one principle of fundamental importance. The principles of expression laid down so far are perfectly general. They let us limit our assertions that propositions are true or false to any particular parts of the whole of time that makes up the universe of our discourse, whether that whole is an unlimited eternity, or a period with a fixed beginning and end, or the passing moment. Yet in the actual practice of human reasoning such limits are not usually used. When we assert that a proposition is true, we generally mean that it is true throughout the whole of the time our discourse refers to. And when several assertions that propositions are simply true or false are made together as the premises of a logical proof, they all refer to the same universe of time, not to particular, limited parts of it. In the realm of necessary truth that the exact sciences study, every assertion of a truth may be the assertion of an "eternal truth." In reasoning about passing events (some state of affairs in society, for instance), each assertion may be tied directly to the present time, "Now." But in both cases, unless something is stated to the contrary, each separate proposition refers to the same stretch of time. The cases we then have to consider are the following.

First, to express the proposition, "The proposition X is true."

Here we must express that, within the limits of time to which the matter of our discourse is confined, the proposition X is true. The time during which the proposition X is true is denoted by x, and the stretch of time our discourse refers to is represented by 1. So we have x=1(4) as the expression required: the time when X is true is the whole of time.

Second, to express the proposition, "The proposition X is false."

Here we must express that, within the limits of time our discourse refers to, the proposition X is false; in other words, that within those limits there is no portion of time during which it is true. The portion of time during which it is true is x. So the equation required will be x=0.(5) We could also get this result by setting the expression for the time during which the proposition X is false, namely 1−x, equal to the whole of time, 1. This gives 1−x=1,whence x=0.

Third, to express the disjunctive proposition, "Either the proposition X is true or the proposition Y is true," where it is implied that the two propositions exclude each other, that is, that only one of them is true.

The time during which either the proposition X is true or the proposition Y is true, but not both, is represented by the expression x(1−y)+y(1−x). So we have x(1−y)+y(1−x)=1,(6) as the equation required.

Suppose instead that in this proposition the words either, or, are not meant to be strictly exclusive, so that the propositions X and Y might both be true at once. Then we must add the term xy to the left-hand side of the equation above. We shall then have xy+x(1−y)+(1−x)y=1,or x+(1−x)y=1.(7) that is, at every time either X is true, or, if it is not, Y is.

Fourth, to express the conditional proposition, "If the proposition Y is true, the proposition X is true."

Since whenever the proposition Y is true the proposition X is true, it is necessary and sufficient here to express that the time during which the proposition Y is true is time during which the proposition X is true. In other words, it is some indefinite portion of the whole time during which the proposition X is true. Now the time during which the proposition Y is true is y, and the whole time during which the proposition X is true is x. Let v be a symbol of time indefinite. Then vx will represent an indefinite portion of the whole time x. So we shall have y=vx as the expression of the given proposition: the time when Y is true is some of the time when X is true.

12. When v is taken in this way as a symbol of time indefinite, vx may be understood to represent the whole of the time x, or an indefinite part of it, or no part of it at all; for any of these meanings can be produced by fixing the arbitrary symbol v in a particular way. If v is fixed to represent a time that includes the whole time x, then vx will represent the whole time x. If v is fixed to represent a time some part of which lies inside the time x, but which does not fill up that time, then vx will represent a part of the time x. Lastly, if v is fixed to represent a time no part of which is shared with any part of the time x, then vx will take the value 0, and will amount to "no time," or "never."

Now notice that the proposition "If Y is true, X is true" does not assert that either of the propositions X and Y is true. It fits equally well with several suppositions. It fits the supposition that the truth of the proposition Y is a condition the truth of the proposition X cannot do without; in that case we shall have v=1. It fits the supposition that Y expresses a condition which, when it is met, assures us that X is true, but that X can be true without that condition being met; in that case v stands for a time some part of which lies within the whole time x. And lastly it fits the supposition that the proposition Y is never true at all; in that case v represents some time no part of which is shared with any part of the time x. All these cases are covered by the general supposition that v is a symbol of time indefinite.

Fifth, to express a proposition that is both conditional and disjunctive.

The general form of a conditional proposition is "If Y is true, X is true," and by the last section its expression is y=vx. Following the usage we set up for primary propositions, we may properly call Y and X the terms of the conditional proposition they belong to. We may also adopt the language of ordinary logic, which calls the term Y, the one the word if is attached to, the "antecedent" of the proposition, and the term X the "consequent."

Now suppose that the terms, instead of being simple propositions as in the case above, are each, or either of them, disjunctive propositions, joining different terms with the words either, or. Here are some examples, in which X, Y, Z, and so on, stand for simple propositions.

First, if either X is true or Y is true, then Z is true.

Second, if X is true, then either Y is true or Z true.

Third, if either X is true or Y is true, then either Z and W are both true, or they are both false.

Clearly, in these cases the relation of the antecedent to the consequent is not affected by the fact that one or both of those terms is disjunctive. So all we need to do is find, by the principles already established, the proper expressions for the antecedent and the consequent, attach the indefinite symbol v to the consequent, and set the two equal. For the propositions above, this gives the following equations, in order: 1st. x(1−y)+(1−x)y=vz.2nd. x=v{y(1−z)+z(1−y)}.3rd. x(1−y)+y(1−x)=v{zw+(1−z)(1−w)} The rule shown here applies in general.

One can imagine cases in which the disjunctive and conditional elements enter a compound proposition in some other way than this. But I do not know of any that the natural needs of human reasoning ever actually present to us, so I shall not discuss them. Leaving them out will cause no serious difficulty. The principles underlying the applications above are perfectly general, and a little thought will adapt them to any case one can imagine.

13. The laws of expression just stated already contain the laws of interpretation. The equation x=1 must be understood to say that the proposition X is true; the equation x=0, that the proposition X is false. The equation xy=1 will say that the propositions X and Y are both true together; and the equation xy=0 that they are not both true together.

In the same way the equations x(1−y)+y(1−x)=1,x(1−y)+y(1−x)=0, will assert, respectively, the truth and the falsehood of the disjunctive proposition "Either X is true or Y is true." The equations y=vxy=v(1−x) will express, respectively, the propositions "If the proposition Y is true, the proposition X is true" and "If the proposition Y is true, the proposition X is false."

In the chapters that follow we shall often meet a case in which some terms on one side of an equation have the indefinite symbol v attached and others do not. The following example will illustrate it. Suppose we have y=xz+vx(1−z). This says that the time during which the proposition Y is true is made up of all the time during which X and Z are true together, plus an indefinite portion of the time during which X is true and Z false. From this we can see, first, that if Y is true, then either X and Z are true together, or X is true and Z false; and second, that if X and Z are true together, Y is true. The second of these may be called the reverse interpretation. It takes the antecedent from the right-hand side of the equation, and the consequent from the left-hand side. What makes this reverse reading possible is that the right-hand side has a term whose coefficient is unity (that is, 1). The general principle involved may be stated as follows.

14. Principle.—Any constituent term or terms in a particular member of an equation which have for their coefficient unity, may be taken as the antecedent of a proposition, of which all the terms in the other member form the consequent.

In plainer words: any compartment on one side of an equation that has 1 in front of it can serve as the "if" part of a proposition whose "then" part is everything on the other side. So the equation y=xz+vx(1−z)+(1−x)(1−z) would have the following interpretations.

Direct Interpretation.—If the proposition Y is true, then either X and Z are true, or X is true and Z false, or X and Z are both false.

Reverse Interpretation.—If either X and Z are true, or X and Z are false, Y is true.

These partial interpretations, taken together, express the whole meaning of the given equation.

15. Let me repeat a remark made earlier. The idea of time seems to be an essential element in the theory of how secondary propositions are interpreted. Yet in practice it can be set aside as soon as the laws of expression and of interpretation have been firmly established. Indeed, the forms those laws produce seem to match the forms of a perfect language. Imagine any known language freed from its idioms and stripped of everything superfluous. Then imagine expressing some proposition in that language in the simplest and most literal way, the way most faithful to the principles of pure and universal thought on which all languages are founded, which all of them display, but from which all of them have strayed more or less. Passing from such a language to the notation of algebra would mean nothing more than swapping one set of signs for another, with no essential change of form or character. For the elements among which a relation is expressed, whether things or propositions, we would write letters; for the disjunctive conjunction "or" we would write +; for the connecting copula, the sign of relation, we would write =. I need not follow this analogy further. How real and complete it is will become clearer as we study the forms of expression that turn up in later applications of this theory, and compare them more directly with that imperfect yet noble instrument of thought, the English language.

16. Before leaving the subject of this chapter, I want to add a few remarks on the general analogy between the theory of Primary Propositions and that of Secondary Propositions.

We could no doubt have founded the theory of Primary Propositions on the simple notion of space, in the same way that the theory of secondary propositions has been founded on the notion of time. If we had, the analogy we are considering might have agreed a little more closely with the view of those who regard space and time as merely "forms of the human understanding," conditions of knowledge that the very make-up of the mind imposes on everything it takes in. But this view cannot be proved. And it ties us to accepting "place," τὸ ποῦ (the Greek "where"), as an essential category of existence. Whether it is one or not lies, I suspect, beyond the reach of our faculties. But it can be shown, and I believe it has been shown, that the formal processes of reasoning in primary propositions do not require, as an essential condition, that the things we reason about appear in space. Those processes would apply just as strictly to forms of existence, if there are any, that lie beyond the realm of things extended in space. Something perhaps similar happens in many known examples in geometry and dynamics: we can set out the formal analysis of problems that rest on some intellectual conception of space different from the one our senses present, or the one our imagination can picture. So I believe that the idea of space is not essential to developing a theory of primary propositions. But I am inclined to think, though I wish to speak cautiously on a question so very difficult, that the idea of time is essential to establishing a theory of secondary propositions. There seem to be grounds for thinking that space might have appeared to the human mind differently from the way it does, without any change in the faculties involved in reasoning. There do not seem to be the same grounds, at least, for supposing that time could have appeared to us otherwise than it does. But let me set these speculations aside, since they may not be entirely free from presumption. Let it simply be affirmed that the real reason the symbol 1 represents, in primary propositions, the universe of things and not the space they occupy is this: the sign of identity =, joining the two sides of the equations, implies that the things the two sides represent are identical, not merely that they are found in the same portion of space. Let it be affirmed, in the same way, that the reason the symbol 1 in secondary propositions represents, not the universe of events, but the eternity in whose successive moments and periods they unfold, is this: the same sign of identity, joining the logical sides of the equations, implies, not that the events the two sides represent are identical, but that the times at which they occur are the same. These reasons seem to me to settle the immediate question of interpretation. In an earlier treatise on this subject (Mathematical Analysis of Logic, p. 49), I followed Wallis's theory of the Reduction of Hypothetical Propositions, and was led to interpret the symbol 1 in secondary propositions as the universe of "cases" or "conjunctures of circumstances." But that view requires us to define what a "case," or a "conjuncture of circumstances," means; and whatever that term contains beyond the notion of time is certainly foreign to the aims of formal logic, and restricts its processes.

Footnote: Our perception presents space to us as having three dimensions: length, breadth, and depth. But in a large class of problems, those about the properties of curved surfaces, the rotation of solid bodies about axes, the vibrations of elastic media, and so on, this limit to three looks arbitrary in the mathematical working. If one paid attention only to the processes of solution, one could find no reason why space should not exist in four dimensions, or in any greater number. The intellectual procedure in the imaginary world this suggests can be grasped by the clear light of analogy. Aristotle sets out the existence of space in three dimensions, and the views on it held by the religious and philosophical mind of antiquity, as follows:— Μέγεθος δὲ τὸ μὲν ἐφ’ ἓν, γραμμή τὸ δ’ ἐπὶ δύο ἐπίπεδον, τὸ δ’ ἐπὶ τρία σῶμα· καὶ παρὰ ταῦτα οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλο μέγεθος, διὰ τὸ τρία πάντα εἶναι καὶ τὸ τρὶς πάντῃ. Καθάπερ γάρ φασι καὶ οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι, τὸ πᾶν καὶ τὰ πάντα τοῖς τρισὶν ὥρισται. Τελευτὴ γὰρ καὶ μέσον καὶ ἀρχὴ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἔχει τὸν τοῦ παντός· ταῦτα δὲ τὸν τῆς τριάδος. Διὸ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως εἰληφότες ὥσπερ νόμους ἐκείνης, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἁγιστείας χρώμεθα τῶν θεῶν τῷ ἀριθμῷ τούτῳ.—De Caelo, 1. (In English: "Of magnitude, what extends one way is a line, two ways a plane, three ways a body; and besides these there is no other magnitude, because three is all, and 'three ways' is 'every way.' For, as the Pythagoreans also say, the whole and all things are bounded by threes: end, middle, and beginning hold the number of the whole, and that number is the triad. So, having taken it from nature as one of her laws, we use this number in the worship of the gods as well.")

Chapter 12: Methods in Secondary Propositions

1. We have already seen (XI. 7) that the literal symbols of logic combine by the same laws whether they express primary propositions or secondary ones. The only difference between the two cases is a difference of interpretation. We have also established (V. 6) a general principle: whenever two different systems of thought and interpretation are tied to the same system of formal laws (that is, of laws governing how the symbols are combined and used), then everything that happens in between is the same in both. By "in between" I mean the processes that lie between writing down the first conditions of a problem and interpreting its symbolic solution. Primary and secondary propositions share exactly this kind of common formal law. So the processes we established and illustrated for the first kind of proposition will apply to the second kind without any change at all.

2. In particular, the two fundamental processes of elimination and development obey the same laws for secondary propositions as for primary ones. Again, we saw (Chap. VI. Prop. 2) how to interpret any equation among primary propositions that contains no fractions. We develop it into a series of constituents, and set equal to 0 every constituent whose coefficient is not zero. The same method works for the equations of secondary propositions. And the interpreted result it finally leads to is, as before (VI. 6), a system of denials that hold together. There is one difference. In the primary case those denials deny that certain classes of things exist. In the secondary case they deny the truth of certain combinations of the elementary propositions that make up the terms of the premises. And just as in primary propositions the system of denials could be converted into various other forms of proposition (VI. 7), &c., we shall find that the same conversion is possible here. Again the only difference lies not in the form of the equations but in the nature of their interpretation.

3. Further, in primary propositions we can find the expression of any one element of a system of equations in terms of the remaining elements (VI. 10), or in terms of any chosen few of them, and interpret that expression as a logical inference. The same thing can be done by the same means for secondary propositions, the difference of interpretation alone excepted. The steps are no different from the corresponding steps for primary propositions: eliminating the elements we want to banish from the final solution, reducing the system to a single equation, solving it algebraically, and developing the solution into a form that can be interpreted.

To clear away any possible difficulty, however, it may help to gather into a general Rule the different cases that arise in working with secondary propositions.

Rule.—Express the given propositions in symbols (XI. 11).

From each equation in which it appears, eliminate separately the indefinite symbol v (VII. 5).

Eliminate the remaining symbols that you want to banish from the final solution. Before each elimination, always reduce to a single equation all the equations in which the symbol or symbols to be eliminated appear (VIII. 7). Collect the resulting equations into a single equation V=0.

Then proceed according to the particular form in which you want to express the final relation, as follows.

First, if you want it in the form of a denial, or a system of denials, develop the function V, and set equal to 0 all those constituents whose coefficients are not zero.

Second, if you want it in the form of a disjunctive proposition, set equal to 1 the sum of those constituents whose coefficients are zero.

Third, if you want it in the form of a conditional proposition whose antecedent is a simple element, such as x or 1−x, find the algebraic expression of that element, and develop that expression.
