Fourth, if you want it in the form of a conditional proposition whose antecedent is a compound expression, such as xy, xy+(1−x)(1−y), &c., set that expression equal to a new symbol t. Then find t as a developed function of the symbols that are to appear in the consequent, either by the ordinary methods or by the special method of (IX. 9).

Fifth, interpret the results by (XI. 13, 14).

Suppose we only want to find out whether one particular elementary proposition x is true or false. Then we must eliminate every symbol except x. If the result is the equation x=1, the proposition is true; if x=0, it is false; if 0=0, the premises are not enough to decide whether it is true or false.

4. Ex. 1.—Cicero's treatise On Fate (De Fato), which survives only in fragments, contains a curious discussion of the following prediction: "Si quis (Fabius) natus est oriente Canicula, is in mari non morietur." That is, "If anyone (Fabius) was born at the rising of the dogstar, he will not die at sea." I shall apply the method of this chapter to it. Let y represent the proposition, "Fabius was born at the rising of the dogstar," and x the proposition, "Fabius will die in the sea." When I say that x represents the proposition "Fabius will die in the sea," I mean only that x is a symbol assigned (XI. 7) to that proposition in such a way that the equation x=1 asserts its truth and the equation x=0 denies it. Reading the symbols as times, as in the last chapter, x stands for the time during which "Fabius will die in the sea" is true, and y for the time during which "Fabius was born at the rising of the dogstar" is true. The equation we have to discuss will be y=v(1−x).(1) that is, the time for which the first proposition is true is some part of the time for which the second is false: if Fabius was born at the dogstar's rising, he will not die at sea. First, let us reduce the given proposition to a denial, or a system of denials (XII. 3). Moving the right-hand side across, we have y−v(1−x)=0. Eliminating v, y{y−(1−x)}=0,or, y−y(1−x)=0,or, yx=0.(2) This result means: "It is not true that Fabius was born at the rising of the dogstar and will die in the sea." Cicero calls this form of proposition "Conjunctio ex repugnantibus" (a conjunction of things that cannot go together, denied). He remarks that Chrysippus hoped by this form to escape a difficulty he believed he saw in contingent statements about the future, that is, statements about things that may or may not happen: "Hoc loco Chrysippus aestuans falli sperat Chaldaeos caeterosque divinos, neque eos usuros esse conjunctionibus ut ita sua percepta pronuntient: Si quis natus est oriente Canicula is in mari non morietur; sed potius ita dicant: Non et natus est quis oriente Caniculâ, et in mari morietur. O licentiam jocularem! ... Multa genera sunt enuntiandi, nec ullum distortius quam hoc quo Chrysippus sperat Chaldaeos contentos Stoicorum causa fore."—Cic. De Fato, 7, 8. In English: here Chrysippus, sweating over the problem, hopes that the Chaldaean astrologers and the other diviners can be talked out of announcing their findings as "if" statements, such as "If anyone was born at the rising of the dogstar, he will not die at sea," and will say instead, "It is not the case both that someone was born at the rising of the dogstar and that he will die at sea." What playful license! ... There are many ways of stating a thing, and none more twisted than this one, which Chrysippus hopes the Chaldaeans will accept for the Stoics' sake.

5. Next, let us reduce the given proposition to a disjunctive form. The constituents that do not appear on the left-hand side of (2) are x(1−y),(1−x)y,(1−x)(1−y). So we have y(1−x)+x(1−y)+(1−x)(1−y)=1.(3) This means: either Fabius was born at the rising of the dogstar and will not perish in the sea; or he was not born at the rising of the dogstar and will perish in the sea; or he was not born at the rising of the dogstar and will not perish in the sea.

In cases like this one, however, where some constituents differ from each other in only a single factor, it is most convenient, as we have seen (VII. 15), to gather those constituents into a single term. If we combine the first and third terms of (3) in this way, we have (1−y)x+1−x=1; and if we combine the second and third in the same way, we have y(1−x)+1−y=1. These two forms of the equation give, respectively, the interpretations:

Either Fabius was not born under the dogstar and will die in the sea, or he will not die in the sea.

Either Fabius was born under the dogstar and will not die in the sea, or he was not born under the dogstar.

Clearly these interpretations say exactly the same as the earlier one.

Now let us find, in the form of a conditional proposition, what follows from the supposition that "Fabius will perish in the sea."

In equation (2), which is what remains of the original equation once v has been eliminated, we must try to find x as a function of y.

We have x=0y=0y+00(1−y) on expansion, or x=00(1−y); that is, the time in which Fabius dies at sea lies somewhere within the time in which he was not born at the dogstar's rising. Interpreted: If Fabius dies in the sea, he was not born at the rising of the dogstar.

These examples go some way to illustrate the connection we have established in the previous chapters between primary and secondary propositions. That connection has two marks: the processes are identical, and the interpretations are analogous.

6. Ex. 2.—The second book of Plato's Republic contains a remarkable argument meant to prove that the Divine Nature cannot change. It is a very fine example of two things at once. It shows the careful induction from familiar instances by which Plato arrives at general principles, and the clear, connected logic by which he then deduces from them the particular conclusions he wants to establish. The argument is contained in the following dialogue:

"Must not that which departs from its proper form be changed either by itself or by another thing? Necessarily so. Are not things which are in the best state least changed and disturbed, as the body by meats and drinks, and labours, and every species of plant by heats and winds, and such like affections? Is not the healthiest and strongest the least changed? Assuredly. And does not any trouble from without least disturb and change that soul which is strongest and wisest? And as to all made vessels, and furnitures, and garments, according to the same principle, are not those which are well wrought, and in a good condition, least changed by time and other accidents? Even so. And whatever is in a right state, either by nature or by art, or by both these, admits of the smallest change from any other thing. So it seems. But God and things divine are in every sense in the best state. Assuredly. In this way, then, God should least of all bear many forms? Least, indeed, of all. Again, should He transform and change Himself? Manifestly He must do so, if He is changed at all. Changes He then Himself to that which is more good and fair, or to that which is worse and baser? Necessarily to the worse, if he be changed. For never shall we say that God is indigent of beauty or of virtue. You speak most rightly, said I, and the matter being so, seems it to you, O Adimantus, that God or man willingly makes himself in any sense worse? Impossible, said he. Impossible, then, it is, said I, that a god should wish to change himself; but ever being fairest and best, each of them ever remains absolutely in the same form."

The premises of this argument are the following.

First, if the Deity suffers change, He is changed either by Himself or by another.

Second, if He is in the best state, He is not changed by another.

Third, the Deity is in the best state.

Fourth, if the Deity is changed by Himself, He is changed to a worse state.

Fifth, if He acts willingly, He is not changed to a worse state.

Sixth, the Deity acts willingly.

Let us express the elements of these premises as follows.

Let x represent the proposition, "The Deity suffers change."

Let y represent the proposition, "He is changed by Himself."

Let z represent the proposition, "He is changed by another."

Let s represent the proposition, "He is in the best state."

Let t represent the proposition, "He is changed to a worse state."

Let w represent the proposition, "He acts willingly."

Written in symbols, and with the indefinite class symbols v eliminated, the premises then give the following equations:

xyz+x(1−y)(1−z)=0,(1)sz=0,(2)s=1,(3)y(1−t)=0,(4)wt=0,(5)w=1.(6)

Read aloud, they say: (1) it is never true that He suffers change and is changed both by Himself and by another, nor that He suffers change and is changed by neither; (2) He is never both in the best state and changed by another; (3) He is in the best state; (4) He is never changed by Himself without being changed to a worse state; (5) He never both acts willingly and is changed to a worse state; (6) He acts willingly.

Keeping x, I shall eliminate in turn z, s, y, t, and w (the order in which those symbols occur in the system above), and interpret each result as it comes.

Eliminating z from (1) and (2), we get xs(1−y)=0.(7) Eliminating s from (3) and (7), x(1−y)=0.(8) Eliminating y from (4) and (8), x(1−t)=0.(9) Eliminating t from (5) and (9), xw=0.(10) Eliminating w from (6) and (10), x=0.(11)

From equation (8) onward, these give the following results.

From (8) we have x=00y, so If the Deity suffers change, He is changed by Himself.

From (9), x=00t: If the Deity suffers change, He is changed to a worse state.

From (10), x=00(1−w): If the Deity suffers change, He does not act willingly.

From (11): The Deity does not suffer change. This is Plato's result.

I have remarked before that the order of elimination makes no difference. Let us test that fact here by eliminating the same symbols in the reverse order, beginning with w. The resulting equations are

t=0,y=0,x(1−z)=0,z=0,x=0;

and they give the following interpretations, one for each equation:

God is not changed to a worse state. He is not changed by Himself. If He suffers change, He is changed by another. He is not changed by another. He is not changed.

So we reach the same conclusion by a different route.

As a display of the power of the method, these examples are of little value. But they illustrate its nature and character just as well as more complicated cases would.

7. One last instance of the analogy between the system of primary propositions and that of secondary propositions deserves mention. In the secondary system, too, the fundamental equation, x(1−x)=0, can be interpreted. It says that there is no time during which the proposition is both true and false; that is, it expresses the axiom, A proposition cannot be true and false at the same time. Compare this with the corresponding interpretation for classes of things (III. 15). If we solve the equation in the form x=01−x=00x, and develop it, it gives, in the two systems, the axioms "A thing is what it is" and "If a proposition is true, it is true." Both are forms of what has been called "the principle of identity." People have held the most opposite opinions about the nature and value of these axioms. Some have treated them as the very core and essence of philosophy. Locke gave them a chapter headed "On Trifling Propositions." Both views, I think, mix truth with error. If such propositions are put in place of experience, or used as material for the empty, wordy quarrels of the schools, they are worse than trifling. But seen as closely bound up with the very laws and conditions of thought, they rise to an importance that is at least speculative.

Footnote: Essay on the Human Understanding, Book IV. Chap. viii.

Chapter 13: Clarke and Spinoza

1. In this chapter and the next I mean to follow a definite plan. I shall examine the actual premises involved in proving some of the general propositions of the two treatises named above, whether those premises are stated outright or only implied. By the actual premises I mean every proposition that the argument assumes without proving and uses as part of the foundation on which its final conclusion is built. Once I have found these premises, I shall express them in the language of symbols. Then, by the methods developed in the earlier chapters of this work, I shall deduce from them the most important inferences they contain, beyond the particular inferences the authors themselves drew. In some cases I shall change the premises: I shall leave out some fact or principle they contain, or add or substitute some new proposition, and then work out how the final conclusions are affected by the change. In all this it is not my task to ask, except in passing, how far the metaphysical principles laid down in these famous works deserve our trust. My task is only to find out what conclusions may rightly be drawn from given premises. And in doing that, I want to show the complete freedom we have in choosing both the elements of the final propositions and the order in which they appear: that is, in deciding which elementary propositions to declare true or false, and which to declare true or false under given restrictions, or in given combinations.

2. The main practical difficulty of this inquiry will not lie in applying the method once the premises are fixed. It will lie in finding out what the premises are. Even in what are regarded as the most rigorous examples of reasoning on metaphysical questions, we shall sometimes find that different trains of thought are blended together. We shall find that some particular but essential parts of a proof are given in parentheses, or off to the side of the main argument; that the meaning of a premise is to some degree ambiguous; and, not rarely, that arguments judged by the strict laws of formal reasoning are incorrect or inconclusive. In such cases it may be very hard to determine the true premises of a proof and set them out clearly. But this is a difficulty that everyone must overcome who wants to know whether a particular conclusion is proved or not, whatever form they intend to give the reasoning that follows. So it is not a difficulty peculiar to the method of this work, though it shows itself more plainly with this method than with any other. The connection is in fact so close that, using the method of this treatise, we cannot even guess whether a conclusion is valid until we have clearly grasped and exactly stated every premise it rests on. In the more usual way of proceeding, on the other hand, nothing is more common than to examine a few steps of a train of argument and from them form a vague general impression of the whole, without any such preliminary and thorough analysis of the premises it involves.

This need to pin down exactly the real premises of a proof should not be thought of as a drawback, especially because, once it is done, every source of doubt or ambiguity is gone. With the method of this treatise, the order in which the premises are arranged, the way they are connected, and every similar circumstance may be treated as a matter of indifference. The process of inference is then carried out with a precision that might almost be called mechanical.

3. The "Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God" consists of a series of propositions, or theorems. Each is proved from premises that can mostly be sorted into two distinct kinds. The first kind is facts of observation, such as the existence of a material world, the phenomenon of motion, &c. The second kind is hypothetical principles, whose authority and universal reach are supposed to be recognized à priori. It is of course on the truth of the second kind that the validity of the proof really depends, assuming the reasoning is correct. But whatever may be thought of its claims on that score, there is no question that, as an intellectual achievement, the work stands very high. Its trains of argument are not generally very clearly arranged, but they are almost always examples of correct logic, and they show a subtlety of understanding and a force of reasoning that have seldom been equalled and perhaps never surpassed. In them we see the culmination of the intellectual efforts that were stirred up in the field of metaphysical inquiry at a time when the rule of hypothetical principles was less questioned than it is now, and when the rigorous proofs of the newly risen school of mathematical physics seemed to offer a model for such efforts to follow. For this reason, not to mention the dignity of their subject, they seem to me to deserve serious attention, and I do not think it a vain or pointless task to spend a careful analysis on some of them.

4. The Ethics of Benedict Spinoza is a treatise whose object is to prove that God and the universe are identical, and to build on that doctrine a system of morals and of philosophy. Its main argument is extremely hard to analyse. The difficulty is not that its separate propositions are complicated. It is that it uses vague definitions, and axioms so unclear that it is hard to decide whether we ought to accept them or reject them. The reasoning of Dr. Samuel Clarke is partly verbal; that of Spinoza is verbal to a much greater degree. Perhaps that is why, to some minds, Spinoza's reasoning has seemed to have a formal force to which in reality it has no fair claim. These points, however, will be considered in their proper place.

Clarke's Demonstration.

Proposition I.

5. "Something has existed from eternity."

The proof is as follows:—

"For since something now is, 'tis manifest that something always was. Otherwise the things that now are must have risen out of nothing, absolutely and without cause. Which is a plain contradiction in terms. For to say a thing is produced, and yet that there is no cause at all of that production, is to say that something is effected when it is effected by nothing, that is, at the same time when it is not effected at all. Whatever exists has a cause of its existence, either in the necessity of its own nature, and thus it must have been of itself eternal: or in the will of some other being, and then that other being must, at least in the order of nature and causality, have existed before it."

Let us now analyse this proof. Its first sentence breaks down into the following propositions:

1st. Something is.

2nd. If something is, either something always was, or the things that now are must have risen out of nothing.

The next part of the proof argues that the second of these alternatives, namely "The things that now are have risen out of nothing," is impossible. Formally, it breaks down as follows:

3rd. If the things that now are have risen out of nothing, something has been effected, and at the same time that something has been effected by nothing.

4th. If that something has been effected by nothing, it has not been effected at all.

This second part of the argument seems to be simply an assumption of the point to be proved, or an attempt to make that point clearer by stating it in different words.

The third and last part of the proof gives a separate proof of one of two things: either of the original proposition to be proved, namely "Something always was," or of the point argued in the second part, namely that the hypothesis "the things that now are have risen out of nothing" cannot stand. It breaks down as follows:—

5th. If something is, either it exists by the necessity of its own nature, or it exists by the will of another being.

6th. If it exists by the necessity of its own nature, something always was.

7th. If it exists by the will of another being, then the proposition, that the things which exist have arisen out of nothing, is false.

This last proposition is not stated in this form in Dr. Clarke's text. But his stated conclusion, that another Being existed first, is plainly meant to amount to a denial of the proposition that the things which now are have risen out of nothing.

So the proof consists of two distinct trains of argument. One is made up of what I have called the first and second parts of the proof; the other is made up of the first and third parts. Let us consider the second of these trains.

The premises are:—

1st. Something is.

2nd. If something is, either something always was, or the things that now are have risen out of nothing.

3rd. If something is, either it exists in the necessity of its own nature, or it exists by the will of another being.

4th. If it exists in the necessity of its own nature, something always was.

5th. If it exists by the will of another being, then the hypothesis, that the things which now are have risen out of nothing, is false.

We must now express these propositions in symbols.

Letx =Something is.
y =Something always was.
z =The things which now are have risen from nothing.
p =It exists in the necessity of its own nature (that is, the something spoken of above).
q =It exists by the will of another Being.

It should be understood that writing Let x= "Something is" means no more than that x is the representative symbol of that proposition (XI. 7). The equations x=1 and x=0 then declare, respectively, that it is true and that it is false.

The equations of the premises are:—

1st.x = 1;
2nd.x=v{y(1−z)+z(1−y)};
3rd.x=v{p(1−q)+q(1−p)};
4th.p=vy;
5th.q=v(1−z);

and when we eliminate the various indefinite symbols v, we get 1−x=0;(1)x[yz+(1−y)(1−z)]=0;(2)x[pq+(1−p)(1−q)]=0;(3)p(1−y)=0;(4)qz=0.(5)

6. First, I shall examine whether any conclusions can be deduced from these equations about the truth or falsehood of the single propositions represented by the symbols y, z, p, q, namely of the propositions "Something always was;" "The things which now are have risen from nothing;" "The something which is exists by the necessity of its own nature;" "The something which is exists by the will of another being."

To do this, we must eliminate in turn every symbol except y, then every symbol except z, &c. The equation that results each time will show whether any such separate relation exists.

To eliminate x from (1), (2), and (3), we need only put the value of x given by (1) into (2) and (3). The results are yz+(1−y)(1−z)=0.(6)pq+(1−p)(1−q)=0.(7) That is, of the two propositions in each pair, exactly one is true.

To eliminate p, we add (4) and (7), which gives p(1−y)+pq+(1−p)(1−q)=0;(8) and from this we find (1−y)(1−q)=0.(9) that is, it is not the case both that nothing always was and that the something does not exist by the will of another Being.

To eliminate q from (5) and (9), we have qz+(1−y)(1−q)=0; and from this we find z(1−y)=0.(10) Only the two equations (6) and (10) now remain. Adding them gives yz+1−y=0. Eliminating z from this equation, we have 1−y=0,or, y=1.(11) Eliminating y from the same equation, we have z=0.(12) The interpretation of (11) is:

Something always was.

The interpretation of (12) is:

The things which are have not risen from nothing.

Next let us go back to the system (6), (7), together with the two equations (4) and (5), and find the two equations that involve p and q respectively.

To eliminate y, we have from (4) and (6) p(1−y)+yz+(1−y)(1−z)=(0); and from this (p+1−z)z=0,or, pz=0.(13) that is, it is not the case both that the something exists in the necessity of its own nature and that the things which now are have risen from nothing.

To eliminate z from (5) and (13), we have qz+pz=0; and from this we get 0=0. So there remains only equation (7). Eliminating q from it, we get 0=0 as the final equation in p.

So no conclusion can be drawn from the premises asserting simply that the proposition "The something which is exists in the necessity of its own nature" is true, or that it is false. And since eliminating p gives the same result, 0=0, as the final equation in q, it follows also that no conclusion can be drawn from the premises about the simple truth or falsehood of the proposition "The something which is exists by the will of another Being."

As for relations connecting more than one of the propositions represented by the elementary symbols, we need only consider the one expressed by equation (7), which connects p and q. The propositions represented by the other symbols are absolutely true or false on their own, independent of any connection of this kind. Put into the form p(1−q)+q(1−p)=1, is, the interpretation of (7) is:

The something which is, either exists in the necessity of its own nature, or by the will of another being.

I have set out the details of this analysis at a length that is perhaps needlessly full and wordy. I did so because in the examples that follow I mean rather to indicate the steps by which the results are reached than to risk repeating myself tiresomely. The conclusions the method has produced here are easily checked by ordinary reasoning.

The reader will have no difficulty in applying the method to the other train of premises in Dr. Clarke's first Proposition, and deducing from them the first two of the conclusions this analysis has reached.

Proposition II.

7. Some one unchangeable and independent Being has existed from eternity.

The premises from which this proposition is proved are the following:

1st. Something has always existed.

2nd. If something has always existed, either there has existed some one unchangeable and independent being, or the whole of existing things has been comprehended in a succession of changeable and dependent beings.

3rd. If the universe has consisted of a succession of changeable and dependent beings, either that series has had a cause from without, or it has had a cause from within.

4th. It has not had a cause from without (because it includes, by hypothesis, all things that exist).

5th. It has not had a cause from within (because no part is necessary, and if no part is necessary, the whole cannot be necessary).

Leaving out, purely for brevity, the supporting proofs given in parentheses in the fourth and fifth premises, we may represent the premises as follows: Let x= Something has always existed.y=There has existed some one unchangeable and independent being.z=There has existed a succession of changeable and dependent beings.p=That series has had a cause from without.q=That series has had a cause from within. Then we have the following system of equations, namely: 1st. x=1;2nd. x=v{y(1−z)+z(1−y)};3rd. z=v{p(1−q)+(1−p)q};4th. p=0;5th. q=0: which, when we eliminate each indefinite symbol v separately, gives 1−x=0;(1)x{yz+(1−y)(1−z)}=0;(2)z{pq+(1−p)(1−q)}=0;(3)p=0;(4)q=0.(5) Eliminating x, p, q, and y from this system leads to the equation z=0. And eliminating x, p, q, and z leads in the same way to the equation y=1. The interpretations of these equations are, respectively:

1st. The whole of existing things has not been comprehended in a succession of changeable and dependent beings.

2nd. There has existed some one unchangeable and independent being.

The second of these is the proposition Dr. Clarke proves. This analysis has settled every one of the propositions represented by the literal symbols x, y, z, p, q as absolutely true or absolutely false. So there is no need to look for any further relations connecting them.

Clarke gives another proof of Prop. II., which for brevity I pass over. It is worth noticing that the "impossibility of infinite succession," which Clarke proves as part of his argument, has commonly been assumed as a fundamental principle of metaphysics and carried over to questions other than causation. Aristotle uses it to establish that there must be first principles of demonstration, and that there must be an end (the good) in human actions, &c. There is perhaps no principle he appeals to more often in his writings. The schoolmen (the philosophers of the medieval universities) used it in the same way to prove that genera and species cannot be ranked one under another without end, and so that universals must exist. It seems that our inability to form a definite and complete conception of an infinite series, that is, to grasp it as a whole, has been confused with a logical inconsistency, or a contradiction in the idea itself.

Footnote: Metaphysics, III. 4; Anal. Post. I, 19, et seq.

Footnote: Nic. Ethics, Book I. Cap. II.

8. The analysis of the next argument depends on the theory of Primary Propositions.

Proposition III.

That unchangeable and independent Being must be self-existent.

The premises are:—

1. Every being must either have come into existence out of nothing, or it must have been produced by some external cause, or it must be self-existent.

2. No being has come into existence out of nothing.

3. The unchangeable and independent Being has not been produced by an external cause.

To express these in symbols, let us take x=Beings which have arisen out of nothing.y=Beings which have been produced by an external cause.z=Beings which are self-existent.w=The unchangeable and independent Being. Then we have x(1−y)(1−z)+y(1−x)(1−z)+z(1−x)(1−y)=1,(1)x=0,(2)w=v(1−y),(3) and eliminating v from the last of these, wy=0.(4) that is, the unchangeable and independent Being is not among the beings produced by an external cause.

Whenever, as here, a symbol's value is given as 0 or 1, the best way to eliminate it is by simple substitution. So eliminating x gives y(1−z)+z(1−y)=1;(5)or, yz+(1−y)(1−z)=0.(6) Now adding (4) and (6), and eliminating y, we get w(1−z)=0,∴w=vz; and the interpretation of this is,—The unchangeable and independent being is necessarily self-existing.

The interpretation of (5), in the form it has as it stands, is,—Every being has either been produced by an external cause, or it is self-existent.

9. In Dr. Samuel Clarke's remarks on this proposition there is a remarkable argument meant to prove that the material world is not the self-existent being just spoken of. The passage I mean is the following:

"If matter be supposed to exist necessarily, then in that necessary existence there is either included the power of gravitation, or not. If not, then in a world merely material, and in which no intelligent being presides, there never could have been any motion; because motion, as has been already shown, and is now granted in the question, is not necessary of itself. But if the power of gravitation be included in the pretended necessary existence of matter: then, it following necessarily that there must be a vacuum (as the incomparable Sir Isaac Newton has abundantly demonstrated that there must, if gravitation be an universal quality or affection of matter), it follows likewise, that matter is not a necessary being. For if a vacuum actually be, then it is plainly more than possible for matter not to be."—(pp. 25, 26).

A careful examination shows that the actual premises involved in this proof are the following:

1st. If matter is a necessary being, either the property of gravitation is necessarily present, or it is necessarily absent.

2nd. If gravitation is necessarily absent, and the world is not subject to any presiding Intelligence, motion does not exist.

3rd. If the property of gravitation is necessarily present, the existence of a vacuum is necessary.

4th. If the existence of a vacuum is necessary, matter is not a necessary being.

5th. If matter is a necessary being, the world is not subject to a presiding Intelligence.

6th. Motion exists.

Of these premises, the first four are stated in the proof. The fifth is implied in the way its first and second sentences are connected. The sixth states a fact that the author does not seem to have thought it necessary to state, but which is clearly part of the ground of his reasoning. Let us represent the elementary propositions as follows: Let x=Matter is a necessary being.y=Gravitation is necessarily present.t=Gravitation is necessarily absent.z=The world is merely material, and not subject to any presiding Intelligence.w=Motion exists.v=A vacuum is necessary. Then the system of premises is represented by the following equations, in which q is used as the symbol of an indefinite time: x=q{y(1−t)+(1−y)t}.tz=q(1−w).y=qv.v=q(1−x).x=qz.w=1. If we eliminate the symbols q from these, we get the following system, namely: x{yt+(1−y)(1−t)}=0.(1)tzw=0.(2)y(1−v)=0.(3)vx=0.(4)x(1−z)=0.(5)1−w=0.(6) Now if we eliminate w, v, z, y, and t from these equations, we obtain the equation x=0, which expresses the proposition, Matter is not a necessary being. This is Dr. Clarke's conclusion. If we try to eliminate any other set of five symbols (except the set v, z, y, t, and x, which would give w=1), we get a result of the form 0=0. So there are no other conclusions stating that any of the elementary propositions marked by single symbols is absolutely true or absolutely false.

Of conclusions expressed by equations in two symbols, there is only the following one, namely:— If the world is merely material, and not subject to a presiding Intelligence, gravitation is not necessarily absent. This conclusion is expressed by the equation tz=0, whence z=q(1−t). Suppose that in this analysis we drop the last premise, the one stating the fact that motion exists, and leave untouched the hypothetical principles contained in the other premises. Then some remarkable conclusions follow. I shall turn to these in the next chapter.

10. Of the rest of Dr. Clarke's argument I shall give only the substance and the connections, briefly. I shall dwell only on certain parts of it that are more complex than the others and better illustrate the method of this work.

In Prop. IV. it is shown that the substance or essence of the self-existent being is incomprehensible. The drift of the reasoning is that we do not know the essential nature of anything else, and so, much less, the essence of the self-existent being.

In Prop. V. it is argued that "though the substance or essence of the self-existent being is itself absolutely incomprehensible to us, yet many of the essential attributes of his nature are strictly demonstrable, as well as his existence."

In Prop. VI. it is argued that "the self-existent being must of necessity be infinite and omnipresent;" and it is maintained that his infinity must be "an infinity of fulness as well as of immensity." The ground the proof rests on is that an absolute necessity of existence must be independent of time, place, and circumstance, free from limitation, and so exclude all imperfection. And from this it is inferred that the self-existent being must be "a most simple, unchangeable, incorruptible being, without parts, figure, motion, or any other such properties as we find in matter."

The premises actually used may be set out as follows:

1. If a finite being is self-existent, it is a contradiction to suppose it not to exist.

2. A finite being may, without contradiction, be absent from one place.

3. That which may without contradiction be absent from one place may without contradiction be absent from all places.

4. That which may without contradiction be absent from all places may without contradiction be supposed not to exist.

Let us take x=Finite beings.y=Things self-existent.z=Things which it is a contradiction to suppose not to exist.w=Things which may be absent without contradiction from one place.t=Things which without contradiction may be absent from every place. Expressing the premises and eliminating the indefinite symbols, we have xy(1−z)=0.(1)x(1−w)=0.(2)w(1−t)=0.(3)tz=0.(4) Eliminating t, w, and z in turn, we get xy=0, ∴y=00(1−x); and the interpretation of this is,—Whatever is self-existent is infinite.

In Prop. VII. it is argued that the self-existent being must of necessity be One. The proof runs in this order: the self-existent being is "necessarily existent"; "necessity absolute in itself is simple and uniform, and without any possible difference or variety"; all "variety or difference of existence" implies dependence; and therefore "whatever exists necessarily is the one simple essence of the self-existent being."

The conclusion is also made to follow from these premises:—

1. If there are two or more necessary and independent beings, either of them may be supposed to exist alone.

2. If either may be supposed to exist alone, it is not a contradiction to suppose the other not to exist.

3. If it is not a contradiction to suppose this, there are not two necessary and independent beings.

Let us represent the elementary propositions as follows:— x=there exist two necessary independent beings.y=either may be supposed to exist alone.z=it is not a contradiction to suppose the other not to exist. Proceeding as before, we then have x(1−y)=0.(1)y(1−z)=0.(2)zx=0.(3) Eliminating y and z, we have x=0. So, There do not exist two necessary and independent beings.

11. It is well known that objections to the premises on which these last two propositions rest were raised by Bishop Butler, in some celebrated letters. When the "Demonstration" was published, Butler was a student at a nonconformist academy (a college for Protestants outside the Church of England). His letters, with Dr. Clarke's replies, are usually printed at the back of editions of the work. The real question at issue is whether the principle holds that "whatsoever is absolutely necessary at all is absolutely necessary in every part of space, and in every point of duration." Clarke's reasoning assumes this principle, and he states it outright in his reply to Butler's first letter. In his second letter Butler says: "I do not conceive that the idea of ubiquity is contained in the idea of self-existence, or directly follows from it, any otherwise than as whatever exists must exist somewhere." That is to say, necessary existence implies existence in some part of space, but not in every part. Dr. Clarke never seems to have managed to answer this objection effectively. The whole correspondence is extremely curious and interesting. Butler's objections are exactly the ones that would occur to a sharp mind convinced that the successful search for truth depends mainly on sifting first principles, not on any mechanical skill in reasoning. And Dr. Clarke's replies, though they cannot be accepted as satisfactory, show to a remarkable degree the particular intellectual power that is evident in the work from which the discussion arose.

12. In Prop. VIII. it is argued that the self-existent and original cause of all things must be an Intelligent Being.

The main argument offered for this proposition runs as follows. The cause is more excellent than the effect. So the self-existent being, as the cause and origin of all things, must contain in itself the perfections of all things; and intelligence is one of the perfections shown in a part of the creation. It is further argued that this perfection is not a modification of shape, divisibility, or any of the known properties of matter, for these are not perfections but limitations. To this is added the à posteriori argument, the argument from the evidence of design in the structure of the universe.

There is also attached, however, a separate argument for the existence of an intelligent self-existent being, based on the observed existence of motion in the universe. I shall set out this proof briefly and apply the method of this treatise to it.

Leaving out unimportant explanations, the argument is as follows:—

"’Tis evident there is some such a thing as motion in the world; which either began at some time or other, or was eternal. If it began in time, then the question is granted that the first cause is an intelligent being.... On the contrary, if motion was eternal, either it was eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being, or it must of itself be necessary and self-existent, or else, without any necessity in its own nature, and without any external necessary cause, it must have existed from eternity by an endless successive communication. If motion was eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being, this also is granting the question as to the present dispute. If it was of itself necessary and self-existent, then it follows that it must be a contradiction in terms to suppose any matter to be at rest. And yet, at the same time, because the determination of this self-existent motion must be every way at once, the effect of it would be nothing else but a perpetual rest.... But if it be said that motion, without any necessity in its own nature, and without any external necessary cause, has existed from eternity merely by an endless successive communication, as Spinoza inconsistently enough seems to assert, this I have before shown (in the proof of the second general proposition of this discourse) to be a plain contradiction. It remains, therefore, that motion must of necessity be originally caused by something that is intelligent."

The premises of this argument may be arranged as follows:

1. If motion began in time, the first cause is an intelligent being.

2. If motion has existed from eternity, either it has been eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being, or it is self-existent, or it must have existed by endless successive communication.

3. If motion has been eternally caused by an eternal intelligent being, the first cause is an intelligent being.

4. If it is self-existent, matter is at rest and not at rest.

5. That motion has existed by endless successive communication, and that at the same time it is not self-existent, and has not been eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being, is false.

To express these propositions, let us take— x=Motion began in time (and therefore)1−x=Motion has existed from eternity.y=The first cause is an intelligent being.p=Motion has been eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being.q=Motion is self-existent.r=Motion has existed by endless successive communication.s=Matter is at rest. The equations of the premises are then— x=vy.1−x=v{p(1−q)(1−r)+q(1−p)(1−r)+r(1−p)(1−q)}.p=vy.q=vs(1−s)=0.r(1−q)(1−p)=0. The fourth equation gives q=0, since nothing can be both at rest and not at rest. Putting this value for q into the other equations, we get the system x=vy,p=vy,1−x=v{p(1−r)+r(1−p)},r(1−p)=0, and eliminating the indefinite symbols v from this, we have the final reduced system, x(1−y)=0,(1)(1−x){pr+(1−p)(1−r)}=0,(2)p(1−y)=0.(3)r(1−p)=0.(4) We shall first look for the value of y, the symbol that appears in Dr. Clarke's conclusion. First, eliminating x from (1) and (2), we have (1−y){pr+(1−p)(1−r)}=0.(5) Next, to eliminate r from (4) and (5), we have r(1−p)+(1−y){pr+(1−p)(1−r)}=0,∴{1−p+(1−y)p}×(1−y)(1−p)=0; and so (1−y)(1−p)=0.(6) Last, eliminating p from (3) and (6), we have 1−y=0,∴y=1, which expresses the conclusion we were looking for, The first cause is an intelligent being.

Let us now examine what other conclusions can be deduced from the premises.

If we put the value just found for y into equations (1), (2), (3), (4), they reduce to the following pair of equations, namely, (1−x){pr+(1−p)(1−r)}=0,r(1−p)=0.(7) Eliminating x from these equations, we have r(1−p)=0, whence r=vp, which expresses the conclusion, If motion has existed by endless successive communication, it has been eternally caused by an eternal intelligent being.

Again, eliminating r from the same pair, we have (1−x)(1−p)=0,or, 1−x=vp, which expresses the conclusion, If motion has existed from eternity, it has been eternally caused by some eternal intelligent being.

Last, eliminating p from the same original pair, we get (1−x)r=0, which, solved in the form 1−x=v(1−r), gives the conclusion, If motion has existed from eternity, it has not existed by an endless successive communication.

Solved in the form r=vx, the same equation leads to the equivalent conclusion, If motion exists by an endless successive communication, it began in time.

13. The reader will now notice that the first and the last of these four conclusions do not agree. From the hypothesis that motion exists by an endless successive communication, two consequences were drawn. First, that it has been eternally caused by an eternal intelligent being. Second, that it began in time. These are plainly at odds. And yet both are rigorous deductions from the original premises. The conflict between them is not logical. It is what is technically called a material conflict, one that lies in the meaning of the words rather than in the form of the argument. Still, the conflict could have been stated formally in the premises. We could have added a formal proposition saying that "whatever is externally caused by an eternal intelligent being, does not begin in time." Had we done so, no such conflict as now appears in our conclusions could have arisen. Formal logic can take account only of relations that are formally expressed (VI. 16). So in particular cases it may become necessary to state, in a formal way, some connection among the premises that is already contained in the very meaning of the language used, even though nobody has said it out loud.

To show what this means, let us add to the equations (2) and (4) the equation px=0, which expresses the condition just mentioned. We then have (1−x){pr+(1−p)(1−r)}+r(1−p)+px=0.(8) Eliminating p from this, we find simply r=0, which expresses the proposition, Motion does not exist by an endless successive communication. If we now put the value of r back into (8), we have (1−x)(1−p)+px=0, or, 1−x=p; and this gives the interpretation, If motion has existed from eternity, it has been eternally caused by an eternal intelligent being, together with the converse of that proposition.

In Prop. IX. Clarke argues that "the self-existent and original cause of all things is not a necessary agent, but a being endued with liberty and choice." The proof rests mainly on two grounds: that this cause possesses intelligence, and that there exist final causes (purposes in nature), which imply design and choice. To the objection that the supreme cause acts by necessity to produce what is best, Clarke replies that this is a necessity of fitness and wisdom, not a necessity of nature.

14. In Prop. X. he argues that "the self-existent being, the supreme cause of all things, must of necessity have infinite power." The ground of the demonstration is that, since "all the powers of all things are derived from him, nothing can make any difficulty or resistance to the execution of his will." He sets limits to this infinite power. It does not extend to the "making of a thing which implies a contradiction," or to doing that "which would imply imperfection (whether natural or moral) in the being to whom such power is ascribed." But it does extend to the creation of matter, and to the creation of an immaterial, thinking substance, gifted with a power of beginning motion and with a liberty of will or choice. On the strength of this doctrine of liberty, Clarke holds that we can give a satisfactory answer to "that ancient and great question, πόθεν τὸ κακὸν, what is the cause and original of evil?" I shall set out his argument on this point briefly. It runs as follows:

"All that we call evil is either an evil of imperfection, as the want of certain faculties or excellencies which other creatures have; or natural evil, as pain, death, and the like; or moral evil, as all kinds of vice. The first of these is not properly an evil; for every power, faculty, or perfection, which any creature enjoys, being the free gift of God,…it is plain the want of any certain faculty or perfection in any kind of creatures, which never belonged to their natures is no more an evil to them, than their never having been created or brought into being at all could properly have been called an evil. The second kind of evil, which we call natural evil, is either a necessary consequence of the former, as death to a creature on whose nature immortality was never conferred; and then it is no more properly an evil than the former. Or else it is counterpoised on the whole with as great or greater good, as the afflictions and sufferings of good men, and then also it is not properly an evil; or else, lastly, it is a punishment, and then it is a necessary consequence of the third and last kind of evil, viz., moral evil. And this arises wholly from the abuse of liberty which God gave to His creatures for other purposes, and which it was reasonable and fit to give them for the perfection and order of the whole creation. Only they, contrary to God's intention and command, have abused what was necessary to the perfection of the whole, to the corruption and depravation of themselves. And thus all sorts of evils have entered into the world without any diminution to the infinite goodness of the Creator and Governor thereof."—p. 112.

The main premises of this argument can be stated as follows.

First, all reputed evil (what is called evil) is either evil of imperfection, or natural evil, or moral evil.

Second, evil of imperfection is not absolute evil.

Third, natural evil is either a consequence of evil of imperfection, or it is compensated with greater good, or it is a consequence of moral evil.

Fourth, whatever is either a consequence of evil of imperfection, or is compensated with greater good, is not absolute evil.

Fifth, all absolute evils are included among reputed evils.

To express these premises, let us take w= reputed evil.x= evil of imperfection.y= natural evil.z= moral evil.p= consequence of evil of imperfection.q= compensated with greater good.r= consequence of moral evil.t= absolute evil. We treat the premises as primary propositions whose predicates are all particular, so that each subject is only some part of its predicate class. And we take the words either, or as absolutely disjunctive, meaning that each alternative excludes the others. We then have the following equations: w=v{x(1−y)(1−z)+y(1−x)(1−z)+z(1−x)(1−y)}x=v(1−t).y=v{p(1−q)(1−r)+q(1−p)(1−r)+r(1−p)(1−q)}p(1−q)+q(1−p)=v(1−t).t=vw. If we eliminate the symbol v from each of these separately, we have w{1−x(1−y)(1−z)−y(1−x)(1−z)−z(1−x)(1−y)}=0,(1)xt=0,(2)y{1−p(1−q)(1−r)−q(1−p)(1−r)−r(1−p)(1−q)}=0,(3){p(1−q)+q(1−p)}t=0,(4)t(1−w)=0.(5)

Suppose we want to find, first, what conclusion the premises allow us to draw about absolute evils, in their dependence on moral evils and on the consequences of moral evils.

For this we must find t in terms of z and r.

So the symbols w, x, y, p, q must be eliminated. The work is easy, because any set of these equations can be reduced to a single equation simply by adding them.

Eliminating w from (1) and (5), we have t{1−x(1−y)(1−z)−y(1−x)(1−z)−z(1−x)(1−y)}=0.(6) Eliminating p from (3) and (4) gives yqr+yqt+yt(1−r)(1−q)=0.(7) Eliminating q from this gives yt(1−r)=0.(8) that is, nothing is at once natural evil, absolute evil, and not a consequence of moral evil. Eliminating x between (2) and (6) gives t{yz+(1−y)(1−z)}=0.(9) Eliminating y from (8) and (9) gives t(1−z)(1−r)=0. This is the only relation that holds among the elements t, z, and r. It says that there is no absolute evil which is neither moral evil nor a consequence of moral evil. From it we get t=0(1−z)(1−r)=00zr+00z(1−r)+00(1−z)r+0(1−z)(1−r)=00z+00(1−z)r; and its interpretation is, Absolute evil is either moral evil, or it is, if not moral evil, a consequence of moral evil.

Any of the results reached along the way to this solution will also yield interpretations. From (8), for example, we might deduce t=0y(1−r)=00yr+00(1−y)r+00(1−y)(1−r)=00yr+00(1−y); which means, Absolute evils are either natural evils, which are the consequences of moral evils, or they are not natural evils at all.

Many other conclusions can be drawn from the given equations, in answer to any questions we care to put. I shall give a few examples of these, without showing the intermediate steps of the solution.

Quest. 1.—Can any relation be deduced from the premises connecting the following elements: absolute evils, consequences of evils of imperfection, and evils compensated with greater good?

Ans.—No relation exists. If we eliminate all the symbols but t, p, q, the result is 0=0, an identity that says nothing.

Quest. 2.—Is any relation implied between absolute evils, evils of imperfection, and consequences of evils of imperfection?

Ans.—The final relation between x, t, and p is xt+pt=0; so that t=0p+x=00(1−p)(1−x). Therefore, Absolute evils are neither evils of imperfection, nor consequences of evils of imperfection.

Quest. 3.—What is the relation of natural evils to evils of imperfection and to evils compensated with greater good?

We find pqy=0,∴y=0pq=00p(1−q)+00(1−p). Therefore, Natural evils are either consequences of evils of imperfection which are not compensated with greater good, or they are not consequences of evils of imperfection at all.

Quest. 4.—How do those natural evils which are not moral evils stand in relation to absolute evils and to the consequences of moral evils?

If y(1−z)=s, we find, after elimination, ts(1−r)=0;∴s=0t(1−r)=00tr+00(1−t). Therefore, Natural evils, which are not moral evils, are either absolute evils, which are the consequences of moral evils, or they are not absolute evils at all.

The following conclusions were found in the same way. In each one, the subject shows what things a description was asked for, and the predicate shows which elements the description was meant to involve:

Absolute evils, which are not consequences of moral evils, are moral and not natural evils.

Absolute evils which are not moral evils are natural evils, which are the consequences of moral evils.

Natural evils which are not consequences of moral evils are not absolute evils.

Last, let us look for a description of the evils which are not absolute, in terms of natural and moral evils.

The final equation we obtain is 1−t=yz+00y(1−z)+00(1−y)z+(1−y)(1−z). Read directly, this equation states a necessary truth. Read in reverse, it gives something remarkable: Evils which are both natural and moral, and evils which are neither natural nor moral, are not absolute evils.

This conclusion may not express a truth. But it is certainly contained in the given premises, as formally stated.

15. Let us now take from the same argument a somewhat fuller set of premises. And this time let us suppose that the words either, or are not absolutely disjunctive. So by the phrase "either evil of imperfection, or natural evil, or moral evil," we will mean whatever has one or more of these qualities.

Let the premises be these:

1. All evil (w) is either evil of imperfection (x), or natural evil (y), or moral evil (z).

2. Evil of imperfection (x) is not absolute evil (t).

3. Natural evil (y) is either a consequence of evil of imperfection (p), or it is compensated with greater good (q), or it is a consequence of moral evil (r).

4. Whatever is a consequence of evil of imperfection (p) is not absolute evil (t).

5. Whatever is compensated with greater good (q) is not absolute evil (t).

6. Moral evil (z) is a consequence of the abuse of liberty (u).

7. That which is a consequence of moral evil (r) is a consequence of the abuse of liberty (u).

8. Absolute evils are included in reputed evils.

We express these premises in the usual way and eliminate the indefinite symbols v. This gives the following equations: w(1−x)(1−y)(1−z)=0,(1)xt=0,(2)y(1−p)(1−q)(1−r)=0,(3)pt=0,(4)qt=0,(5)z(1−u)=0,(6)r(1−u)=0,(7)t(1−w)=0.(8) Each of these equations satisfies the condition V(1−V)=0.

The following results are easily deduced:

Natural evil is either absolute evil, which is a consequence of moral evil, or it is not absolute evil at all.

All evils are either absolute evils, which are consequences of the abuse of liberty, or they are not absolute evils.

Natural evils are either evils of imperfection, which are not absolute evils, or they are not evils of imperfection at all.

Absolute evils are either natural evils, which are consequences of the abuse of liberty, or they are not natural evils, and at the same time not evils of imperfection.

Consequences of the abuse of liberty include all natural evils which are absolute evils and are not evils of imperfection, together with an indefinite remainder of natural evils which are not absolute, and of evils which are not natural.

16. These examples are enough to illustrate the method. The reader can easily supply others if they are wanted. We now go on to examine the most essential parts of Spinoza's demonstration. His definitions and axioms, from the opening of the first book of the Ethics, are these.

Definitions.

1. By a cause of itself (causa sui), I understand that of which the essence involves existence, or that of which the nature cannot be conceived except as existing.

2. That thing is said to be finite or bounded in its own kind (in suo genere finita) which may be bounded by another thing of the same kind; e. g. Body is said to be finite, because we can always conceive of another body greater than a given one. So thought is bounded by other thought. But body is not bounded by thought, nor thought by body.

3. By substance, I understand that which is in itself (in se), and is conceived by itself (per se concipitur), i.e., that whose conception does not require to be formed from the conception of another thing.

4. By attribute, I understand that which the intellect perceives in substance, as constituting its very essence.

5. By mode, I understand the affections of substance, or that which is in another thing, by which thing also it is conceived.

6. By God, I understand the Being absolutely infinite, that is the substance consisting of infinite attributes, each of which expresses an eternal and infinite essence.

Explanation.—I say absolutely infinite, not infinite in its own kind. For to whatever is only infinite in its own kind we may deny the possession of (some) infinite attributes. But when a thing is absolutely infinite, whatsoever expresses essence and involves no negation belongs to its essence.

7. That thing is termed free, which exists by the sole necessity of its own nature, and is determined to action by itself alone; necessary, or rather constrained, which is determined by another thing to existence and action, in a certain and determinate manner.

8. By eternity, I understand existence itself, in so far as it is conceived necessarily to follow from the sole definition of the eternal thing.

Explanation.—For such existence, as an eternal truth, is conceived as the essence of the thing, and therefore cannot be explained by mere duration or time, though the latter should be conceived as without beginning and without end.

Axioms.

1. All things which exist are either in themselves in se or in another thing.

2. That which cannot be conceived by another thing ought to be conceived by itself.

3. From a given determinate cause the effect necessarily follows, and, contrariwise, if no determinate cause be granted, it is impossible that an effect should follow.

4. The knowledge of the effect depends upon, and involves, the knowledge of the cause.

5. Things which have nothing in common cannot be understood by means of each other; or the conception of the one does not involve the conception of the other.

6. A true idea ought to agree with its own object. (Idea vera debet cum suo ideato convenire.)

7. Whatever can be conceived as non-existing does not involve existence in its essence.

Other definitions are implied, and other axioms are quietly assumed, in some of the demonstrations. Take Prop. I., "Substance is prior in nature to its affections." Its proof consists of nothing but a reference to Defs. 3 and 5. Yet it seems to assume a further axiom: "That by which a thing is conceived is prior in nature to the thing conceived." Again, the demonstration of Prop. V. assumes that the converse of this axiom is true. Many other examples of the same kind occur. So it is impossible, by the processes of logic alone, to deduce all the conclusions of the first book of the Ethics from the axioms and definitions set at its head, which are the ones given above. In the brief analysis that follows, I shall try to set out in their proper order what seem to me to be the real premises, whether stated or implied, and to show how they lead to the conclusions Spinoza reached.

17. My view, then, is that in the course of his demonstration Spinoza divides the universe of possible existence in several parallel ways, as follows.

First, into things which are in themselves, x, and things which are in some other thing, x′. Since these two classes together make up the universe, we have x+x′=1; (Ax. I.)or, x=1−x′.

Second, into things which are conceived by themselves, y, and things which are conceived through some other thing,y′; so that y=1−y′. (Ax. II)

Third, into substance, z, and modes, z′; so that z=1−z′. (Def. III. V.)

Fourth, into things free, f, and things necessary,f′; so that f=1−f′. (Def. VII.)

Fifth, into things which are causes and self-existent, e, and things caused by some other thing, e′; so that e=1−e′. (Def. I. Ax. VII.) And his reasoning proceeds on the principle, sometimes stated and sometimes assumed, that these divisions are not only parallel but equivalent: that they cut the universe along the same line. Thus in Def. III., substance is made equivalent to that which is conceived by itself; so that z=y. Again, Ax. IV., as Spinoza actually applies it, makes a cause the same thing as that by which a thing is conceived; so that y=e. Again, in Def. VII., things free are identified with things self-existent; so that f=e. Last, in Def. V mode is made identical with that which is in another thing; so z′=x′, and therefore z=x. All these results can be gathered into one series of equations: x=y=z=f=e=1−x′=1−y′=1−f′=1−z′=1−e′. Any two members of this series joined by the sign of equality express a conclusion that legitimately follows from his system, whether or not Spinoza drew it himself. Thus the equation z=1−e′, that is, substance is the same as what is not caused by another thing, expresses the sixth proposition of his system: One substance cannot be produced by another. In the same way the equation z=e, expresses his seventh proposition, "It pertains to the nature of substance to exist." There is no need to follow this train of deduction further. Spinoza uses it chiefly to deduce, according to his views, the properties of the Divine Nature, having first tried to prove that the only substance is God. In the steps of this process there seem to me to be some fallacies, which depend chiefly on the ambiguous use of words. I must draw attention to them here.

18. In Prop. V. Spinoza tries to show that "There cannot exist two or more substances of the same nature or attribute." The proof is in effect as follows. If there are more substances than one, they are told apart either by their attributes or by their modes. If by attributes, then there is only one substance with any given attribute. If by modes, then once we set these aside as not essential, no real ground of distinction is left. So there exists only one substance of the same attribute. But the assumptions made here do not agree with those found in other parts of the treatise. By Def. IV., the intellect grasps substance by means of attribute. By Def. VI., a substance may have many attributes. So one substance could conceivably be told apart from another by differing in some of its attributes, while the others stay the same.

In Prop. VIII. Spinoza tries to show that all substance is necessarily infinite. The proof goes like this. There exists only one substance of one attribute, Prop. V.; and it belongs to its nature to exist, Prop. VII. So it will be of its nature to exist either as finite or as infinite. But not as finite. For by Def. II. it would then have to be bounded by another substance of the same nature, which would also have to exist necessarily, Prop. VII. Then there would be two substances of the same attribute, which is absurd, Prop. V. Therefore substance is infinite.

In this demonstration the word "finite" is confused with the expression "finite in its own kind," Def. II. The proof thus assumes that nothing can be finite unless it is bounded by another thing of the same kind. That is not the ordinary meaning of the word. Spinoza's use of "finite" tends to make space the only form of substance, and all existing things mere affections (states) of space. This, I think, is really one of the ultimate foundations of his system.

The first scholium (explanatory remark) attached to this Proposition is remarkable. I give it in the original words: "Quum finitum esse revera sit ex parte negatio, et infinitum absoluta affirmatio existentiae alicujus naturae, sequitur ergo ex sola Prop. VII. omnem substantiam debere esse infinitam." That is: since being finite is in truth partly a negation, and being infinite the absolute affirmation of the existence of some nature, it follows from Prop. VII. alone that every substance must be infinite. Now this is really an assertion of the principle that Clarke affirmed and Butler disputed (XIII. 11): that necessary existence implies existence in every part of space. This principle will probably be found at the base of every attempt to prove, à priori, the existence of an Infinite Being.

From the general properties of substance stated above, together with the definition of God as the substance consisting of infinite attributes, Spinoza's particular doctrines about the Divine Nature follow necessarily. Substance is self-existent, free, and causal in its very nature; it is the thing in which other things are, and by which they are conceived. So the same properties are asserted of the Deity. He is self-existent, Prop. XI.; indivisible, Prop. XIII.; the only substance, Prop. XIV.; the Being in which all things are, and by which all things are conceived, Prop. XV.; free, Prop. XVII.; the immanent cause of all things (the cause that acts from within them), Prop. XVIII. The proof that God is the only substance is drawn from Def. VI., which is read as declaring that "God is the Being absolutely infinite, of whom no attribute which expresses the essence of substance can be denied." Every conceivable attribute is thus assigned to Him by definition. And Prop. V. has settled that there cannot exist two substances of the same attribute. It follows that God is the only substance.

The "Ethics" of Spinoza, like much of his other writing, is set out in geometrical form, as a chain of definitions, axioms, and propositions. Even so, it does not give the symbolic method of this book much useful practice. Of course any train of reasoning can be handled by that method once its ultimate premises have been correctly identified. But here such treatment hardly differs from the processes of the original demonstrations, except in using letters for words. Reasoning that consists so largely of a play on terms defined as equivalent is not often met with. I have given a few pages here to setting it out more because of the interest of its subject than because of the merits of its demonstrations, however highly some people value them.

19. I do not think anyone can come away from reading the arguments of Clarke and Spinoza without a deep conviction that every attempt is futile to establish, entirely à priori, the existence of an Infinite Being, His attributes, and His relation to the universe. The basic principle of all such speculations is that whatever we can clearly conceive must exist. Even if that principle is granted to be true, it fails to do what it is meant to do. For how shall the finite comprehend the infinite? Yet before any solid ground can be laid for knowing, à priori, things infinite and eternal, we must grant that such a conception is possible, and in some sense more than simply removing the limits from the existence we experience through the senses. Spinoza affirms the reality of such knowledge plainly and explicitly: "Mens humana adaequatum habet cognitionem aeternae et infinitae essentiae Dei" (Prop. XLVII., Part 2nd), that is, the human mind has an adequate knowledge of the eternal and infinite essence of God. Compare this with Prop. XXXIV., Part 2nd: "Omnis idea quae in nobis est absoluta sive adaequata et perfecta, vera est;" (every idea which in us is absolute, or adequate and perfect, is true); and with Axiom VI., Part 1st, "Idea vera debet cum suo ideato convenire" (a true idea must agree with its object). What is more, he makes this kind of knowledge the essential part of all other knowledge: "De natura rationis est res sub quadam aeternitatis specie percipere" (Prop. XLIV., Cor. II., Part 2nd), that is, it is of the nature of reason to perceive things under a certain form of eternity. Suppose it were said that the human mind tends to rise in contemplation from the particular toward the universal, from the finite toward the infinite, from the passing toward the eternal; and that this tendency suggests to us, with high probability, that more exists than the senses perceive or the understanding grasps. That statement might be accepted as true, at least for a great many minds. But there is a class of speculations whose character must be explained partly by other causes. One is impatience with knowledge that is only probable or limited, which is so often all we can really reach. Another is a desire for absolute certainty, where we have been granted only hints enough to mark out the path of duty before us, but not enough to satisfy the demands of the speculative intellect. A third, perhaps, is dissatisfaction with the present state of things. When these motives gain too much weight, the more sober method of analogy and probable induction falls into neglect. Yet that method is, beyond all question, the one best suited to our present condition. To infer an intelligent cause from the abundant evidence of design all around us; to rise to the idea of a moral Governor of the world from studying the make-up and the moral provisions of our own nature: these are only the feeble steps of an understanding limited in its faculties and in its materials of knowledge. But they are worth more than the ambitious attempt to reach a certainty that cannot be had on the ground of natural religion. And as these were the most ancient foundations, so they are still the most solid ones, Revelation being set apart, for the belief that the course of this world is not abandoned to chance and inexorable fate.

Chapter 14: Example of Analysis

1. Let us go back to the remarkable system of premises used in the previous chapter to prove that "Matter is not a necessary being." This time we will drop the sixth premise, namely "Motion exists," and look at some of the consequences that follow from the premises that remain. In effect, we accept Dr. Clarke's hypothetical principles as true, but suppose ourselves ignorant of the fact that motion exists. There may be cases where picking out part of the premises of an argument in this way leads to interesting consequences. That is not, however, my reason for taking up this example again. The premises we will actually use are these—

1. If matter is a necessary being, either the property of gravitation is necessarily present, or it is necessarily absent.

2. If gravitation is necessarily absent, and the world is not subject to any presiding intelligence, motion does not exist.

3. If gravitation is necessarily present, a vacuum is necessary.

4. If a vacuum is necessary, matter is not a necessary being.

5. If matter is a necessary being, the world is not subject to a presiding intelligence.

As before, we represent the elementary propositions by letters, as follows: x=Matter is a necessary being.y=Gravitation is necessarily present.w=Motion exists.t=Gravitation is necessarily absent.z=The world is merely material, and not subject to a presiding intelligence.v=A vacuum is necessary.

When we express the premises in symbols and eliminate the indefinite class symbols (q), we get the following system of equations: xyt+xy‾t‾=0,tzw=0,yv‾=0,vx=0,xz‾=0; Here, to save space, y‾ stands for 1−y, t‾ for 1−t, and so on; so also 1−t‾=t, 1−y‾=y, and so on. Read aloud, the five equations say: matter is never a necessary being while gravitation is both necessarily present and necessarily absent, or while it is neither; gravitation is never necessarily absent in a merely material world where motion exists; gravitation is never necessarily present without a vacuum being necessary; a vacuum is never necessary while matter is a necessary being; and matter is never a necessary being without the world being merely material.

The left-hand sides of these equations contain only positive terms, so we can combine them into a single equation by adding them together (VIII. Prop. 2), namely: xyt+xy‾t‾+yv‾+vx+xz‾+tzw=0, What remains is to reduce the left-hand side so that it satisfies the condition V(1−V)=0, the law of duality, which holds when the left-hand side is a sum of constituents with no constituent counted twice.

To do this, we first develop the left-hand side with respect to the symbols x and y. The result is— (t+v‾+v+z‾+tzw)xy+(t‾+v+z‾+tzw)xy‾+(v‾+tzw)x‾y+tzwx‾y‾=0. Our goal will be reached if we reduce the four coefficients of this development to equivalent forms that themselves satisfy the required condition.

Take the first coefficient. Since v+v‾=1, it is 1+t+z‾+tzw, and this reduces to unity (IX. Prop. 1), because a sum of class terms that contains the whole universe is the whole universe.

The second coefficient is t‾+v+z‾+tzw; and its reduced form (X. 3) is t‾+tv+tv‾z‾+tv‾zw. Here each term after the first has been cut down to the part not already covered by the terms before it.

The third coefficient, v‾+tzw, reduces by the same method to v‾+tzwv. The last coefficient, tzw, needs no reduction. So the development becomes xy+(t‾+tv+tv‾z‾+tv‾zw)xy‾+(v‾+tzwv)x‾y+tzwx‾y‾=0;(1) and this is the reduced form we were looking for.

2. Now by the principle stated in Prop. III., Chap. X., we can find the whole relation connecting any particular set of the symbols in this equation. We develop the equation with respect to the symbols in question, and keep in the result only those constituents whose coefficients are unity. So if we choose the symbols x and y, we are led at once to the equation xy=0, that is, matter is never a necessary being while gravitation is necessarily present. From this we have y=00(1−x), that is, the cases in which gravitation is necessarily present are some of the cases in which matter is not a necessary being. In words: If gravitation is necessarily present, matter is not a necessary being.

Next let us look for the relation between x and w. Developing (1) with respect to those symbols, we get (y+t‾y‾+tvy‾+tv‾z‾y‾+tv‾zy‾)xw+(y+t‾y‾+tvy‾+tv‾z‾y‾)xw‾+(v‾y+tzvy+tzy‾)x‾w+v‾yx‾w‾=0. The coefficient of xw, and that one alone, reduces to unity. For tv‾z‾y‾+tv‾zy‾=tv‾y‾, and tvy‾+tv‾y‾=ty‾, and t‾y‾+ty‾=y‾, and lastly, y+y‾=1. Each step joins two terms that differ only in one letter being present in one and absent in the other, and that letter drops out. This is always how such reductions go. So we get xw=0,∴w=00(1−x), that is, the cases in which motion exists are some of the cases in which matter is not a necessary being. In words: If motion exists, matter is not a necessary being.

If we develop (1) in the same way with respect to x and z, we get the equation xz‾=0,∴x=00z, which says: If matter is a necessary being, the world is merely material, and without a presiding intelligence.

This, admittedly, is just the fifth premise over again. But it shows that there is no other relation connecting the two elements it involves.

If we look for the whole relation connecting the elements x, w, and y, we find, by developing (1) with respect to those symbols and proceeding as before, xy+xwy‾=0. That is, matter is never a necessary being while gravitation is necessarily present; nor is it ever a necessary being while motion exists and gravitation is not necessarily present. Suppose we are asked to find from this what follows from the hypothesis "Motion does not exist," as it bears on two questions: whether matter is necessary, and whether gravitation is necessarily present. We find w=−xyxy‾,∴1−w=xxy‾=10xy+xy‾+00x‾;or, 1−w=xy‾+00x‾, with xy=0. The direct interpretation of the first equation is this: If motion does not exist, then either matter is a necessary being and gravitation is not necessarily present, or matter is not a necessary being.

The reverse interpretation is: If matter is a necessary being, and gravitation not necessary, motion does not exist.

In exactly the same way, if we looked for the full relation between x, z, and w, we would find xzw+xz‾=0. That is, matter is never a necessary being in a merely material world where motion exists, nor in a world that is not merely material. From this we can deduce z=xw‾+00x‾, with xw=0.

So: If the world is merely material, and not subject to any presiding intelligence, then either matter is a necessary being and motion does not exist, or matter is not a necessary being.

And, reversely, If matter is a necessary being, and there is no such thing as motion, the world is merely material.

3. We could of course extend the same method to find the consequences of any complex hypothesis u. Take, for instance, "The world is merely material, and without any presiding intelligence (z), but motion exists" (w), and ask what it implies about any other open questions raised in the original premises, such as "Matter is a necessary being" (x), or "Gravitation is a necessary quality of matter" (y). To do this we would join to the general equation (1) a new equation, u=wz, which says that u stands for the cases where the world is merely material and motion exists. We would then reduce the system thus formed to a single equation, V=0, in which V satisfies the condition V(1−V)=0. Then we would proceed as above to find the relation between u, x, and y, and finally u as a developed function of x and y. But it is much better to use the methods of Chapters VIII. and IX. Here I will simply point out a few results, with the main steps of how they are deduced, and leave checking them to the reader, if the reader wishes.

In the problem just mentioned, we find the relation connecting x, y, w, and z to be xw+xw‾y+xw‾y‾z‾=0. That is, matter is never a necessary being while motion exists; nor while motion does not exist and gravitation is necessarily present; nor while motion does not exist, gravitation is not necessarily present, and the world is not merely material. If we now write u=wz, and then eliminate the symbols w and z by the general problem of Chap. IX., we find xu+xyu‾=0, and from this u=10xy+0xy‾+00x‾; and so wz=00x‾ with xy=0. That is: If the world is merely material, and without a presiding intelligence, and at the same time motion exists, matter is not a necessary being.

Now we have already shown that if motion exists, matter is not a necessary being. So this conclusion actually tells us less than we had already found (by inference) to be true. All the same, it is the proper and complete answer to the question that was asked, which was simply to find the consequences of a certain complex hypothesis.

4. So even from the limited set of premises before us, it would be easy to deduce a great variety of further inferences, taking as the given condition any combination of the elementary propositions we like. If the condition is inconsistent with the premises, the form of the solution will show it: the method will assign the value 0 to the combination of symbols that expresses the proposed condition. If, on the other hand, the condition puts no restriction at all on the propositions whose relation we are looking for, so that every combination of those propositions is equally possible, the form of the solution will show that too. Here are examples of each case.
